But some hares, made wary by the fox's malice, flee its play and fear its approach as an enemy. They say that a fox about to cross frozen lakes judges the thickness of the ice by putting its ear to it, and does not dare to cross the ice unless it finds it sufficiently strong, says Pliny. A fox in hunger, out of desperation, is said to imitate the barking of dogs. It also, when hungry and finding nothing to eat, feigns death, and, lying on its back, draws breath with its tongue hanging out. Then birds, coming down carelessly as if to a corpse, are seized and devoured, its mouth open. The fox is said to run in winding paths, so that its tracks are not detected by hunters. For the fox is named as if 'volupis' [the rolling one], because it is agile on its feet and never runs in a straight path. Foxes mate lying on their sides, with the female embracing the male. The fox's member has a bone inside it.

The varius is a small beast, a little larger than the weasel. It has its name from a fitting reason: it is white on the belly, and has on its back an ash-grey color so elegant that you would marvel at the beast, remarkable in its very creation. It is of the kind of the pirolus: it dwells in trees and rears its young there. Men and women of both sexes are accustomed to glory in the pelts of these beasts as adornment for their garments, especially cloaks; and indeed, while man glories in another's pelt, not his own by nature, the beast itself glories not at all in its own pelt.
In which it is given us to understand that we ought not to glory in our own good deeds as if from ourselves, especially since the Lord says: Without me you can do nothing.

The wisent [zubro] is a most ferocious beast, of the kind of wild bulls. It is a very large beast, reaching a length of fifteen cubits. It has darkish hair. Its horns are very large, three cubits long, and so wide and ample that they become vessels for drinks at the tables of the wealthy. They are of the greatest speed, and have wrongly acquired, in those regions, the Latin name 'tiger,' because of their swiftness. For those who say this are mistaken, since the tiger is a rather small and very swift beast, dwelling in the East. But this creature is found in Bohemia. Wisents, as has been said, are very large animals, and of such speed that the dung they discharge with force, thrown back, they catch on their horns and hurl it far behind them. Once discharged in great quantity, this dung blinds and weakens the pursuing dogs and renders them entirely useless. When they encounter a man or dog in their path, they toss it up on their horns, and for a long time throw it high and catch it again on their horns, until they utterly kill it, battered to pieces. It is deceived by this trick of the hunter, since there is no other art of hunting by which it can easily be caught: once the wisent is first tired out by dogs and hunters, the hunter, with a spear, positions himself against it near a large tree, and, when the wisent sees him, it runs at the tree and, in its foolishness, thinks with its forehead and horns that it can knock it down and thereby overwhelm the man; but since it cannot, and the hunter is always protected by the tree, meanwhile the hunter pierces the sides of the struggling beast with his spear-point and casts down, by human wit, one otherwise unconquerable by human strength. There is another kind of wisent, which the Poles call 'thurones': smaller in form, but superior in speed.

The zybo is an animal exceedingly cruel toward the death of men and beasts. It has the size of a wolf. On its neck there are hairs like a horse's hairs, and it has stiff hairs along its whole spine. It imitates the voices of men, and with these voices it often deceives men who do not know its malice. For, hiding in the depths of the forests, taught some word, it entices passersby, whom, as they draw near, it preys upon. It also enters the tombs of the dead and delights there in the filth of corpses: for it gladly feeds on human flesh. It also deceives dogs in this way: it imitates their barking, and when the dogs hear it, they suspect a companion, and, when they draw near, are torn apart by the zybo. Some say that the zybo is of the kind of the hyena beast, and this indeed seems so in its habits.

In general, concerning birds: the northern eagle, the harpy, the agothiles, the heron, the little heron, geese, ducks, the hawk, the amraham, the linnet, the merlin, the lark, the halcyon, birds of paradise, the aeriophylon, the eagle-owl, the buzzard, the bittern, the bustard, the barnacle goose, also called 'bernece,' the caladrius, the cynamolgus, the swan, the cariste, storks, the coretes, the crested lark, the raven, crows, the little crow, the cuckoo, the coredulus, the dove, the carcates, the quail, the goldfinch, the crochillos, the diomedian bird, the dariata, the egitus, the heron [erodius], the phoenix, the coot, the fatator, the fetis, the fig-pecker; on the medicine and illnesses of noble birds; the falcon, the griffin, the gracocenderon, the bustard [gosturdi], the crane, the glutis, the cock, the hen, the wild cock, the jay, the jackdaw, the ibis, the iboz, the incendula, the swallow, the isidia [and its variant isopigis], the kyliodromos, the kam, the kacolas, the komor, the kaches, the gull, the lucidum also called hyrcene, the nightingale [lucinia], the linacos, the lagepus, the kite, the magnales, the melanchoriphus, the morplex, the mennonides, the meauce, the merilliones, the bee-eater [merops], the blackbird, the jackdaw [monedula], the merganser, the sparrowhawk, the night-heron, the nepa, the pelican [onocrotalus], the othus, the osma, the oriole, the pelican [pellicanus], the purple gallinule, the peacock, the partridge, the spoonbill [platea], the plovers, the magpie, the woodpecker, the sparrow, the nightingale [phylomena], the parrot, the ostrich, the screech-owl, starlings, the turtledove, the trago, thrushes, the bat, lapwings, the owl [ulula], the hoopoe, the vulture, the zelencides. Here end the chapters. Here begins the fifth book, on the nature of birds.

Aristotle: a bird of good wing, that is, swift in flying, has poor feet, that is, weak ones, as the swallow and the like. Every bird and every animal that emits a sound and a voice has much noise and chattering at mating time, except man. Small-bodied birds cry out more than large-bodied birds, and this at mating time. Every winged creature with curved claws has thighs and a chest stronger than other winged creatures. Likewise all winged creatures have toes, some joined, which swim - as the goose -, some separate - as the eagle-owl or the magpie. Every winged creature having a curved claw has a good flight, and every winged creature that has a claw on the leg - as the cock - has a poor and weak flight. The seed of birds is at first white, then red like blood, then yellow. Some have said that wind-eggs, that is, those that come without mating, as sometimes happens with hens or geese - such eggs, I say, as some have said, come from the surplus of eggs produced from mating. But those who said this were mistaken, since hens have often been seen to lay without a cock's mating. But it should be noted that such eggs are tasteless and small. Every bird with hooked claws lives on flesh; others feed on fruits and worms and reptiles. Every bird that swims in the water, having webbing between its toes, walks in flocks. Every bird with toes on its feet eats flesh. Every bird that hunts prey hunts a kind other than its own species, and in this they differ from fish (only the sparrowhawk is without this mercy). All birds with a long neck drink and raise their head, until the water descends into the belly. Many birds too weak for extended flight, dreading winter, flee to the valleys in warm places, and before their departure they fortify themselves by eating much and growing fat, and through this they can better endure the want of hunger in winter. For many birds lie through the whole winter in caves and hollows of the valleys, namely in places where there is constant warmth. There, I say, they lie as if half-dead, huddled together, and, the warmth aided by their numbers, live without any food for a long time, sustained more by the Creator than by life itself. After winter they come out gradually, according to their strength. The flesh of birds that eat flesh is tastier than other flesh, unless perhaps something in their nature specifically opposes this. Every bird with hooked feet that lives on prey does not fly in flocks with its own kind. All fledgling birds, when they are small, have long bellies and navels; and as they grow, these shorten. The reason for their length may be this: since, as they lay disposed in the egg, enclosed in the shell, they could not excrete their food, so for some time after birth they remain thus. Fledglings, too, while still small, hold their heads raised upward, and the reason is this, that, hanging expectantly for food at uncertain times, they suppose their mother to be present. When they grow older, they lower their heads, as if preparing for the time when, in due season, they will seek food not from their mother but by themselves on the ground. Birds do not descend upon a foul-smelling carcass unless it has a good taste; but if it has a good taste, then, lured by the good flavor, they do not avoid the stench in the carcass. Birds love clear, living, and running waters. All birds with hooked claws do not drink water: and the reason is that they eat flesh, which is moister than the food of other birds. And such birds have a slender and delicate body, and large wings for flight. For no animal lacking a soft and light lung drinks much. All birds take a long draught in drinking, except the cock, the swallow, and birds that dwell in water. The sicknesses of birds are known from their wings, since, when they are ill, the position of their wings is disturbed and, in a bad condition, they hang downward. Universally, male birds live longer than females, and the reason is that females are more often weakened to death by the brooding of birds [i.e., by incubation]. All birds with hooked claws sit unwillingly on stones except for a short time, and nature has taught them this so that the roughness of the stone does not blunt their claws. Every bird with hooked claws has sharper sight than other birds, and the reason is that it must see its food from a distant place. And for this reason too the hook-clawed bird flies higher in the air, so that it can spot its food from afar. But birds that stay on the ground do not need to have sharp sight, like the hen and similar birds, since they see their food close by on the ground. A bird that closes its eyes closes them only by the lower eyelid, because of the hardness of the skin covering the head. [Those animals that live on small stones and sand - like birds - generally have no stomach. But they must have something harder, I mean the liver, which is stronger than the stomach itself for digesting, and can bear the roughness of sand and the crushing of small stones. For it is fortified, both outwardly and inwardly, with a very strong sinew, and in the middle is fit, with its most solid flesh, for digestion.] No bird has a bladder, because of the scantness of its drinking, but chiefly because the surplus of water passes, in all birds, into feathers.

Birds need much sight because of the governance of their life. As the Experimentator says, wild birds are less moist than domestic birds and have more tender flesh, easier to digest. They nest in thorny places. They make round nests, rough outside, soft within. When struck, they raise themselves upward. They grieve at the loss of their young, and yet rebuild in the same places. When they rise from the ground, they turn to face the wind. They steer themselves by their tails.

As the great Basil says in the Hexameron, which he wrote in Greek: just as fish cut through the water, moving forward with the motion of their fins, but direct their turns by the rudder of the tail, so too birds are believed to break through the air with their wings in flying. Among birds there is the greatest variety. For some are gregarious, except birds of prey, none of which associates with others except for mating. Others live communally, like doves, starlings, cranes, jackdaws, of which some are found governing themselves without leaders, others are kept under guidance, as cranes. There is also another distinction among them: some we see are certainly migrants, others native; some, driven by winter, depart for foreign lands for the sake of food, most become tame and patient, except the more timid ones, which cannot bear the touch of a hand. Some live around dwellings, others delight in deserted places and mountains. There is also great difference among birds in their voices, and each has its own peculiar quality. For some are talkative and chattering, others silent, some tuneful and noisy, others shrill, having no song at all; some are naturally imitative, or trained by human instruction, others have a single, unchangeable sound of voice. The cock is wanton, the peacock careful, the dove lustful, the hen domestic, the partridge cunning and jealous. And altogether there is manifold variety among them in their actions and habits; and there are as many kinds of habits among birds as there are kinds of birds. Every bird with long legs has a long neck; but if it has short legs, it will also have a short neck, except birds that have skin between their toes - like the goose. All hook-clawed birds have a sharp breast, and by this they fly better, since birds with a broad breast move much air and by this fly more slowly. Every bird that mates and lays eggs at only one time of the year has very small testicles, except during mating season: for then its testicles grow beyond what can be estimated. The beaks of flesh-eating birds are curved, so that they can hold what they grasp, and the strength of such birds is in their beaks and claws, and for this reason a hard beak suits the governance of their life: for nature always seeks perfection.

Pliny: birds alone move by various paths, on land and in the air. Some walk, as crows; some hop, as sparrows; some run, as partridges; others throw their feet before them, as storks and cranes. They spread their wings and, hovering, beat them at rare intervals; some more frequently, some less. Melius Turbo first established aviaries, enclosing birds of every kind, to whom nature had assigned the sky more freely. All birds are born feet first, contrary to other animals, which are born head first. Fecundity is greater in small birds than in large ones.

Volatile creatures are born twice, as Isidore says. For eggs are first produced, then formed and given life by the warmth of the mother's body. They say the power of eggs is so great that wood soaked in egg does not burn, nor does cloth burn against it. Mixed also with lime, it is said to glue together fragments of glass. Isidore says these two things, but they are much disputed among us: heavier birds feed on grain, high-flying ones on flesh alone. Birds that produce many young give birth most quickly. But the larger the animal, the longer it is formed in the womb.

div.head: 2. De aquila et diversis generibus aquilarum

cit.quote: The eagle, as Augustine says, is the noblest of birds, being the queen of birds. It is large, and lives on prey and flesh. Its eyesight is so sharp and steady that it can gaze upon the sun's rays without being dazzled; whence it gladly sits turned toward the sun. It holds its young up by their claws against the sun's rays. Those it sees keeping a steady gaze it preserves and feeds, as worthy of their kind; but those it sees turning their gaze away, it casts out as degenerate.

Some have thought, as Ambrose says, that this happens from disgust at the trouble of raising them. I do not think this at all should be believed, but rather that it is done by a test of judgment, lest the deformity of the offspring, among all birds, dishonor its kind. It condemns it, however, not from harshness of nature but from the integrity of its judgment, nor does it disown it as its own, but rejects it as if belonging to another. Yet a common bird bears and excuses, by its mercy, this severity of the royal bird. For the bird called the coot, which is called 'phene' in Greek, takes up this cast-off and rejected eagle chick and joins it with its own brood; and, mixing it among its own, feeds and nourishes it with the same food as its own young.

The eagle, as Aldhelm says, when weighed down by old age, marks out a most cold spring and, opposite it, flies up on high, rising above all the clouds. And from the heat of the nearby sun the mist of its eyes is consumed, and at once, descending swiftly with the very heat's onset, it plunges three times into the coldest waters, and, rising from them, at once seeks its nest and, among its now grown young, is seized as if by a kind of fever from the imbalance of cold and heat as it hunts for prey, and, sweating, sheds its feathers, and is warmed by its own young, and fed, until, recovering its down and feathers, it is renewed.

Augustine: its beak, too, which becomes so excessively hooked that it can scarcely take food even with effort, it strikes naturally against a rock, and, by striking, knocks off the hook and is restored for feeding.

Eagles are without harsh cries or murmuring. They nest on mountains, on steep crags, or in tall trees. Pliny: seeing a fish in the sea, it plunges headlong upon it, its wings beating the water, and its breast too.

James: it keeps in its nest a stone called 'aetites,' or, as some hold, jet, useful for many remedies. This stone, as if pregnant, has within it a small stone, like an offspring sounding within. Against the excessive heat which the eagle naturally has, it is said to keep this stone in its nest, lest the eggs be spoiled by too much heat and perish; for the heat of fire cannot harm the aetites stone.
Other philosophers say too, as the Experimentator relates, that it places two precious stones called 'indi' in its nest, without whose presence it cannot give birth.
On the eagle's brow are two stones, effective against demons. If you place an eagle's beak by your head at night, you will dream of whatever you wish.

The eagle, as the same Experimentator says, fasts for many days. It teaches its young to lick blood. When it perches, it always looks at its claws, lest they have grown too curved. The eagle shares its prey with other birds and allows them to eat with it; but let them beware: if the food placed before them is not enough for it, it seizes one of the birds feeding with it and eats it. The crow sometimes pursues the eagle, and when the eagle has long ignored it, it at last seizes the crow with its claws.

Aristotle says that the eagle generally has two chicks, and yet lays three eggs; but after producing three, it casts one down and thus rears only two. It has sometimes, however, been seen that the eagle has three chicks. But, as the same Aristotle says, this is not from three eggs; rather, the eagle rears three chicks from only two eggs, two from one egg, and one from the other.

The feathers of eagles, as Pliny says, when mixed with the feathers of other birds, seem, as if by a certain natural instinct, indignant, and do not tolerate them, but consume them. The eagle's wings are straight and extended, but curved at the tip. This alone among birds is never struck by lightning: this Pliny says of eagles. The eagle has a larger right foot than left. The eagle drives off its grown young, chasing away rivals for prey, that is. They do not carry off captured prey at once, but first set it down and, having tested its weight against their strength, go off. Eagles fight with stags and beat them with their wings, until they drive them backward over cliffs. On the other hand, stags kick up much dust into the eagles' eyes. Their fiercest fight, however, is with the dragon. But when the dragon prevails, it sometimes binds the eagle's wings in a manifold coil. There is a most wicked kind of eagle, which, weary of raising them, expels its young before their time.

The reason for this, as Aristotle says, is that after the brooding period it becomes so weakened that it cannot hunt prey, and its claws become so curved that it cannot hold prey, and its wings whiten and become so heavy that it can scarcely fly. There is, however, another bird, which is naturally merciful and devoted, which, taking pity, rears and feeds the abandoned young of others and encourages them to gain strength for flight. The eagle does not sit long upon a stone, lest the sharpness of its claws be blunted. The eagle builds its nest in the highest trees or on cliffs, where an evil beast cannot easily reach. But if a dragon, or a man, or some beast, or bird wishes to disturb or seize its young, it fights for them with wondrous spirit and, exposing itself to the danger of death, is not easily overcome, but carefully guards its young and does not abandon them, until they know themselves and can protect themselves. It is also said of the eagle that it has a certain foreknowledge, so that, however far it is placed from its young, it senses the approach of enemies to its young. The eagle lifts its young onto its shoulders, so as to encourage them to fly. All noble birds, at the sight of an eagle, become greatly afraid and lose their boldness that day, nor can they easily fly to hunt prey.

The Gloss says of the gyrfalcon that it catches the eagle, and in this its boldness is blamed, for its guilt of majesty injures the eagle, queen of birds - signifying obstinate subordinates, who unjustly harass their superiors, not heeding what is said: Be subject in all fear to your masters, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the perverse.

The northern eagle is a large and great bird, dwelling in the north. This bird always lays two eggs, as Pliny says, suspended among the tops of branches. And, having caught a hare or a fox, it strips off its hide little by little and wraps its eggs in that fur, and places them under the warmth of the sun, and thus leaves its eggs and does not brood them, but waits until they break open from natural ripeness at the emergence of the chicks. Then, returning to its young for the first time, it feeds them until they reach full strength.

The harpy is a bird, as Aldhelm says, in the remote parts of the world, in a place called the Strophades, in a wilderness by the Ionian Sea. It is nearly always insatiable with raging hunger. It has hooked claws, always ready for tearing and seizing. It has a human face only, but nothing of human virtue in itself. For it rages with a ferocity beyond human measure. It is said to kill the first man it sees in the wilderness. Then, when by chance it finds water and beholds its own face in the water, soon, perceiving that it has killed a man like itself, it grieves immoderately, and this sometimes even unto death, and mourns the slain for the whole of its life. This bird, sometimes tamed, speaks, trained to a human voice, but lacks reason.

The goatsucker [agothiles] is a bird of the East, which takes its name from the fact itself. For Michael, who translated Aristotle's book On Animals, says that 'agothilez' in Arabic means, in Latin, 'one who sucks the milk of goats.' It is a large bird, which lays two or three eggs. This bird seeks out goats full of milk and places itself beneath their udders, and with its broad beak, which it has been created for this purpose, sucks milk from the udders like a kid. And this is quite remarkable about them: when they have sucked the udders, the milk is destroyed in them and the goats' udders dry up.
Pliny also says that from this same sucking the goats lose their sight. He calls these birds 'caprimulgae.'

The heron, as James, Isidore, and Ambrose say, is a bird named as if 'ardua' [steep], because of its high flights. For it dreads rainstorms and for this reason flies above the clouds, so that it cannot feel the tempest of the winds. When, then, it flies higher, it signifies a coming storm. This bird, though it seeks its food in the waters, nevertheless places its nest in woods and tall trees.

It is said, moreover, that it strives with all its might to defend its young in the nest with wondrous firmness. Hawks are hostile to them, as the Experimentator says. But the heron turns its rear toward the hawk and discharges its dung, at whose touch the hawk's feathers rot. It has a single intestine, like the stork. Some call this bird 'tantalus.' Most of these birds have an ash-grey color, though some are white.

Pliny: there is a certain kind of these whose males, in mating, are so distressed, crying out loudly, that blood pours from their eyes in pain; nor do the females suffer less in giving birth. Pliny calls this kind of bird 'ardeolae.'

There is said to be a certain kind of heron, whose birds differ from the others only by their broad beak. The beak, at its front part, is as broad as half a cubit, so that it exceeds the measure of three fingers, and this seems to have been created for this purpose alone, that they may seek their livelihood from it more conveniently. This bird lives on fish, which, once every effort to escape is foiled, it seizes with its beak and swallows.

This kind especially has a sky-blue color and the size of a heron; but there are others that shine entirely white. There is also a kind of these, as Pliny says, that has only one eye, with which it can see; from this it happens that it can be caught more quickly by the fowler.

Geese, or 'auce,' as the Book of Properties says, are birds of an eagle's size. Among them, those that are wild seek the high freedom of the air properly their own, and are of a bluish-grey color. They fly like cranes, in orderly formation, like letters. They direct their flights according to the blowing of the winds, either the south wind or the north. When the north wind blows, they seek the south, knowing well that colder weather threatens. Unless meanwhile, feeding as they go, they graze, they scarcely rest from flight. For flight is so delightful to them that they rarely sleep. But for domestic geese, on the contrary, flight is burdensome, grazing is their chief occupation, and resting and sleeping their special pleasure. They announce the hours of the night with their cries, like the cock.
[an account, attributed to Isidore, is condensed to a fragment here:] that a goose, by its cry at midnight, roused the guards and thus freed the citadel of the Capitol from danger.

The great Basil and Ambrose: rightly, then, Rome, do you owe to the goose the power by which you rule; your gods were sleeping, the geese were watching. For this reason, in those days, you sacrifice to the goose, and not to Jupiter. For your gods yield to the geese, by whom they know themselves to have been defended, lest they too be captured by the enemy.

Pliny: a goose is recorded to have attached itself as a perpetual companion to the philosopher Lacydes, so that it never wished to be separated from him, by night or day, in public or in private. Geese give birth in water, and mate in spring, or, if they are accustomed to mate in winter, after the solstice. At most they lay sixteen eggs, at least seven. If someone steals their eggs, they keep laying until they are exhausted. They do not hatch eggs not their own. It is most useful, in brooding, to set nine or eleven eggs beneath them. For their goslings, contact with nettle is deadly. The remedy against nettle is a root placed in the bedding beneath the brooding bird.
Geese sometimes lay without mating, but these are eggs without chicks, as Aristotle says.
They hiss to defend their young, as the Experimentator says.

For goslings not yet strong, one goose always keeps watch with neck erect, lest a marauding eagle come from above. They distinguish between an eagle and a vulture, which is indeed difficult for a man to do. They live for many years. The Egyptians say that they have geese among them that have lasted since the time of Pharaoh. This is marvelous, however - if true - because even if the body could last, the eyes, by reason, could not last so long, since every excess of what is perceptible corrupts the sense; for example: the excess of perceptible light, which is in the sun, harms the sense of the eyes most of all, and cannot long remain without corruption, unless - as is told of eagles - the failing of nature is somehow renewed. But we have nowhere read that the goose's nature is renewed. White geese are more fertile, spotted or dark ones less so, as Palladius says, since they passed from a wild to a domestic kind. The goose, delighting in company, scarcely fattens when alone.

Their flesh is hard to digest. They bathe more often before rain. When geese being fattened in confinement are left alone, deprived of company, they scarcely fatten further, from the sadness of solitude.

There is a kind of goose, as Pliny says, whose fat, kept in a bronze vessel with cinnamon, buried in much snow and steeped in icy cold, is useful for the most excellent kind of medicine, called Commagum. There is another kind of them, which, apart from the ostrich, is the largest among birds, but so heavy that it can be caught by hand, immobile upon the ground, and this especially in its final growth, when it has not yet reached full maturity. The mountains of the Alps and the northern region, where men are rarely seen, produce this kind.

The duck, as the Book of Properties says, is a bird somewhat larger than a cock. The male has a neck and head of green color; its beak is broad, its wings marked with white, green, and black, and it has a white ring around its neck. It has red and broad feet, with which it paddles in the water. For it delights in river waters and can scarcely live without them, especially since dry food chokes it more quickly.

Ducks alone, as Pliny says, of the same kind, rise straight up into the air, and, drawing their bodies fully together with their feet, make for the sky. Their young, as soon as they leave the egg, are so agile that, even should their mother die or be lost, they can live without a nurse. At first, not fully recognizing their offspring, they utter uncertain, sobbing cries and anxiously call them together; at last, lamenting around ponds and pools as the chicks dive in. Finally, when the young begin to follow their mother too insistently, recognizing their own offspring, they lead them out to pasture. Ducks, geese, and other water birds purge themselves with the herb sideritis. In fighting, the duck strikes the ground, nor is its fighting heavy or violent. Males, sometimes when many are gathered together, are carried by such madness of lust that, mating one after another in rivalry, they kill the single female duck.

[on trapping ducks:] the fowler places several tame female ducks in a place where wild ones are to be caught. Then, as the wild ducks fly overhead, the fowler releases a tame male duck he had kept in his bosom, so that by flying it may lure the wild ones. When the female ducks remaining see the male fly off, calling out, they try to call him back, nor are they disappointed in their desire: for as soon as the male hears them, having enticed the wild ducks into his company, he returns to the females. And so the wild ducks are entangled in nets along with the others that remain. There is also another way of catching ducks, by baiting hooks and setting them where the ducks are accustomed to settle, so that they are caught in the depths.

The hawk, as the Book of Properties says, is a very noble bird, indeed larger, but much slower than the goshawk, yet more cautious in guarding itself. For it is more measured in flight and wondrously well-formed.

When it has caught a bird, it at once pierces it in the side with its beak, so as to be satisfied with the heart alone; whence its master rewards the victor with the bird's heart alone, keeping the rest for his own uses. The hawk, once stripped of its old feathers, spreads its wings to the south wind, so as to recover new ones, and this so that its pores may open to the sun's heat and its feathers grow back more easily. For nature is nearly everywhere the mistress of usefulness, in the things of the world that die and are born. [When it is healthy, it holds its feathers taut; when sick, drooping.] The hawk is carried on the left hand, as the Experimentator says, so that it may fly toward the right to seize something.

This bird, when it sees that its young can attempt flight, as Ambrose says, does not bring them food, but beats them with its wings and throws them from the nest; and thus drives the tender ones to hunt, lest, grown up, they become lazy. What wonder, if creatures accustomed to seizing are loath to nourish.
The hawk, cooked in rose oil, is most effectively curative, as Pliny says, for ailments of the limbs.

The wild hawk seizes domestic birds and devours them at once, but the tame hawk seizes wild birds and keeps them for its master. It catches hares in this way: with its left foot fixed to the ground, it seizes the running creature with its right, and this so that the little hare, which is indeed stronger, cannot escape by force. And it should be noted that the hawk attacks the hare's head first, and takes away its sight with its claws at the outset. The hawk's feathers, violently plucked out, do not easily grow back, because of the dryness and sparseness of the pores. Whence it often suffers constipation and cannot digest its food. And so it is given feathers to purge its food, so that it may be lighter for flight. But feathers that fall out naturally grow back more easily on the hawk, because the place is ripe and more abundant in moisture.

The hamraham is a bird of the East, as Aristotle says, which nests on mountains where man cannot climb; and so its nest is never found, and its young very rarely. For the young do not descend to the lower places unless they are fully strong in every way and resemble their mother. And for this reason the sophist Arothinius takes this as an argument, saying that the hamraham comes from another, distant land, since no one has ever seen its young. Let the wretched hypocrite blush, who, if he does some good, is eager to display it, and, seeking praise from men, receives his reward in the present. These birds follow armies for the sake of corpses: for they live on flesh; nor do they lay more than two eggs.

The achantis is a bird, as Pliny says. It is nourished on a diet of grass, and for this reason it holds horses in hatred. When it sees them come upon it as it grazes and tear up the grass, it flees, and avenges itself as best it can, mocking the horses' whinnying by imitating their neighs with its own voice. This bird, though small in body, is nevertheless fecund, for it produces twelve chicks at once.

The merlin, as Pliny says, is small, and breaks crows' eggs; whose young are troubled by foxes. But the merlin plucks at the fox cubs and the vixen herself. And when the crows see this, they help the foxes, as against a common enemy. This bird lives among thorns; and for this reason it hates asses, which devour the flowers and leaves of the thorn-bush.

The lark, as the Book of Properties says, is a bird named 'from praise' [a laude], because with wondrous delight, its wings spread in the air, it rejoices, with the modulation of its voice, in the gentle air of a joyful and calmer season.
[crested lark - a fragmentary note]

For under a clouded or rainy sky it scarcely ever sings. It announces, with a jubilant voice, the day coming at dawn. Sitting on the ground it scarcely ever sings; it sings, however, while ascending. As the Experimentator says, it ascends gradually, but descends suddenly, like a falling stone. In descending it draws its wings to its body and steers itself with a light motion of its tail. Caught by man in its youth, it is kept in a cage, where, even if it sometimes sings, by the ruffling of its feathers, even as it sings its melodies, it openly shows that it is being wronged, in that, though singing, it is not allowed to reach the free air.

It fears the hawk so greatly that, when attacked by it, it flies into a man's bosom or offers itself, pressed to the ground, to be caught by his hand, well aware that man is more likely to pity it than the hawk; and rightly, since the one sometimes shows mercy to the captive, the other never does.
The lark is caught by hand when it sees a decoy, unless suspended by a thread on a rod above. So too other little birds, when they crowd together in a thornbush.

Halcyons, as Pliny says, are small birds, larger than a sparrow. They dwell in the sea and rear their young there. They are of an azure color, live on fish, and are partly purple, with white feathers mixed in, with a slender and long neck. They can very rarely be seen except around the solstices. They breed in winter, at a time when the sea is still navigable for large ships. They make nests shaped like a ball, which cannot be cut with iron, but can be broken by a strong blow, like dry sea-foam; yet what they are made of cannot be discovered. This alone among all wild birds breeds in wintertime; but birds accustomed to dwell in houses with men, like the hen and the dove and the like, breed at indiscriminate times; and the reason is that they are safe, protected by the shelter of houses from the harshness of cold.

Ambrose: this bird, the halcyon, then, in wintertime lays its eggs in the sand, and this when the sea rises highest and the waves crash most violently against the shores, so that, by the marvel of a sudden calm, the grace of this bird might shine forth all the more. For where the sea has been stormy, once the eggs are laid, it quickly grows calm, and all the storms of wind subside, and it is peaceful for sailing. The sea remains still until the halcyon has brooded her eggs. Seven days is the brooding period, after which she brings forth her chicks. She adds another seven days as well, in which to nourish her offspring, until they begin to grow. Do not marvel at so short a time of nourishment, since the whole matter is completed in so few days. So great a grace has this tiniest of birds from God, that sailors observe these fourteen days of presumed calm, which they also call the 'halcyon days,' in which they dread no disturbance of stormy weather.

This bird signifies those who, in time of prosperity, confess themselves idle and, as it were, without fruit; but when they see adversities rising against them, then for the first time they trust that they have the fruit of rewards. Whence it is said that the apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus. By their merits it sometimes happens that the desired fruit is not denied to their merits, and a time of peace is granted by the merciful Lord, who indeed does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear, but with the temptation also makes a way of escape, that we may be able to endure.

The aeriophylon, commonly called 'aelion,' is a bird whose name seems drawn from the fact itself: for it is a Latin and Greek name, said to come from 'air' and 'philos' (which means love), as if 'lover of the air.' For this bird is the noblest of birds. It catches fawns and roe-kids, and this by tearing with its claws, first gouging out the beast's eyes, and thus, its brain pierced through, killing it. It has reddish feathers, a long tail, claws, a beak, and very large legs; it is a little larger than the eagle, mighty in flight and swiftest in its wings. It dwells in the clear open sky, and this so much that it scarcely ever, or only briefly, settles or rests on the ground. Raised often above the clouds, it takes its food in the air, in the manner of birds of prey; and if a bird crosses its path in the air, it is seized by it without delay and, driven by the force of its impact, is cast down from the highest air to the ground; yet no man can see who has struck down the dead bird from the air. For the aeriophylon flies so high that it can rarely be seen by man; and especially since its sight is often blocked by clouds. Yet in clear weather it is sometimes seen, and this by those with sharp eyesight. While it is still a fledgling, before it knows itself, it is caught by men who wish to tame it, and thus it is trained for hunting. And its nature is so changed from its wild alienation that it thinks its condition to be nowhere but in the houses, among men, where it was raised. Whence it happens that, contrary to the custom of other noble birds, it remains on perches and in houses without any tethers. They fly sociably, two by two, and divide the prey they have caught.

Birds of paradise are winged creatures so commonly named, not because they come from paradise, but because of their remarkable beauty they are so called. For they are of such splendor and glory that no color is thought lacking to them. Their size is that of a goose, their voice so sweet and gentle that it can stir devotion and joy in a man. If it is ever caught and ensnared, it groans and does not cease lamenting, until restored to freedom. It gladly dwells along the river Nile and is rarely found elsewhere. There are also other birds in those same regions called birds of paradise, from the fact that it is not known whence they come or whither they go. For their mating is never seen, but at certain times, gathered together, they leave the lands they had inhabited before crossing over, and thus depart. Their color is dark and somewhat reddish, and their size smaller than jackdaws.

The eagle-owl has a name composed from the sound of its voice. By this bird other birds are caught. And it signifies sinners, who sin openly to the scandal of men and cause their neighbor to sin by bad example. As the Experimentator says, the eagle-owl drinks doves' eggs. It hunts mice. Dwelling in churches, it drinks oil from the lamps and yet befouls it with its droppings. When attacked by those birds that live in the light, it defends itself lying on its back with the claws of its feet. These birds signify, in the church, insolent and dissolute clergy, who, though they live off the rich benefice of the church, defile it with the filth of lust and scandals, and, when reproached by the good, rage against them with cruelty of spirit. It is indeed a bird burdened only with feathers, but always held by heavy sloth. It frequents tombs by night and day, and, always dwelling in caves, flees the light.
Pliny says that it comes out of the egg tail-first, because the mother applies the part of the body to be brooded to bear the weight of the head.

The buzzard, as the Book of Properties says, is a bird of the hawk kind, but a little darker. It is exceedingly slow and sluggish in flight. It lives on prey, however, which it can catch through cunning or by some weakness or sluggishness holding it back. This bird is most sweet in flavor and taste when taken as food.

The bittern, as the Book of Properties says, is a bird so named from the sound of its voice. It has long legs, an extended neck, a long and sharp beak like the heron's; it differs from the heron only in color, for it is very similar to the color of the earth.

It dwells around ponds, eager for fish as food. This bird stands so still on the shore, in the heat of the sun, in a place where it knows fish frequent, that, unless you watch closely, you would think it a dead bird or a motionless object. Whence it happens that it is less suspected by unwary fish. But though it has a long neck, it makes it short by curving it, so that, when fish, unsuspecting, approach it as it seems to be thinking of nothing and sitting in secure remoteness, it draws them to itself by extending its neck. This bird, when it knows it is caught in a snare, feigns stillness. And when the fowler comes and thinks to catch it by hand, it, seizing him unexpectedly with the weapon of its beak, which it uses with great power, wounds him by tearing. For, as the Experimentator says, it has a long and very sharp beak, which, sleeping and waking, it always keeps raised to defend itself. When the hawk thinks to seize it, it rushes onto its beak to its death. It eats frogs and venomous things. This alone, in springtime, gives out a horrible cry instead of a song. And it is said to be unable to do this unless it plunges its head into the water, so that the density of the element within it renders its captured voice resonant, like a kind of thundering. Its flesh, when roasted at the fire, gives off a marvelous smell. Whence it happens that this bird often graces the tables of the rich. Its fat is said to be useful for remedies.

The bustard is a bird that takes its name from the fact itself. For it is a bird the size of an eagle, which, slow in flight, makes two or three leaps on the ground before it rises into the sky, whence it is said to have the name 'bis-tarda' [twice-slow]. This bird has a hooked beak and claws like an eagle's. It feeds on flesh, but does not seize prey in flight at all. But if they find a sheep or some defenseless animal anywhere, several of these birds gather and cast down and kill what they find, and so gorge themselves on its flesh. They also feed most gladly on carcasses. This bird is almost the only one, among those that eat flesh, that also grazes on plants, and this most gladly on the pea, while it is still green. On its wings it has white color, and on the tail; in the rest of its coloring it resembles the eagle. It lays its eggs on the ground and broods them there, while the crop is still standing in the field; and this is the reason it does not nest in trees: because it cannot fly high.

We call 'bonosae' the birds dwelling in the regions of Germany. Their flesh is black outside, white within. When the mating season stirs their desire, the male runs with open mouth, until it foams at the mouth. Then the female comes and takes the foam in her mouth, and from this conceives and lays eggs. They are the size of pheasants. Their flesh is delicate and close in flavor to the partridge.

div.head: 23. De barliatibus que et ‘bernece’ dicuntur et sunt aves arborum

cit.quote: Barnacle geese, as Aristotle says, grow from wood, and are the birds the common people call 'bernescas,' having a similar nature.

Aristotle says, moreover, in the book On Animals: a certain investigator, he says, saw in the sea an animal wondrous beyond measure, whose formation was like the formation of wood, and it was black, round, uniform in thickness, and had many wings on it, that is, a multitude of winged birds. It is said, moreover, that when fir wood falls into the waters of the sea, in the course of time, when it begins to rot, it gives off from itself a thick moisture, and from that thickened moisture small forms of birds are shaped, the size of larks, at first bare. Then, ripening, they grow feathers and, hanging by their beaks to the wood, float on the sea until maturity, until, stirring themselves, they break free, and so grow and become strong up to their proper form. We have seen trustworthy men who have testified that they saw these birds still hanging on the wood, and of which we ourselves have seen many. They have an ash-grey and black color, are smaller than geese, and have feet like a duck's, but black.

bibl.author: Historia orientalis Iacobi de Vitriaco Iacobus de Vitriaco

cit.quote: Bishop James of Acre, in his History of the East, says something not unlike this. For he says that there are trees along the seashore, from which these birds are produced, hanging with their beaks fixed to the trees, but after the time of maturity has come, they fall at once from the trees and (growing by stages) begin to fly like other birds. Unless they quickly find water as they fall, they cannot live; for in the waters is their nourishment and their life. Thus far James. It should be noted concerning these birds that they hang not at the top of the branches, but on the bark and trunks of the trees. They grow by the moisture of the tree and the infusion of dew, until, having feathers and the strength of life, they break away from the bark. And this indeed is certain concerning these birds, that in our part of the world, around Germany, they neither breed by mating nor are bred by mating, nor has any man among us ever seen their mating. They live on grasses and herbage like geese, but cannot at all forgo drink when eating dry food. Some Christians, in regions where these birds are abundant, have been accustomed, even in our own age, to eat the flesh of these birds during Lent.

bibl.author: Constitutiones Concilii quarti Lateranensis Innocentius III papa

cit.quote: But Pope Innocent III, at the general Fourth Lateran Council, further forbade this practice.

The caladrius, as James and Isidore say, is a bird entirely white. The inner part of its thigh removes cloudiness from the eyes. The caladrius's nature, moreover, is such that, if it is sometimes brought to a sick man, it makes those standing by certain whether the sick man will die or live. For if it looks away from the sick man's face and turns its eyes aside, it is a sign of death. But if it does not turn its eyes away, it is a sign of life. For it gazes into his face and gathers into itself all the illnesses of that sick man, and flies into the air, and there burns up the illnesses and disperses them, and at once the sick man is healed.

Alexander is said to have found these birds in Persia. Kings of old used to keep these birds enclosed in royal courtyards. Of these birds, and similarly of those which the blessed Brendan found on a certain lofty and most beautiful tree, one of which answered him that they were spirits doing their penance there in the form of birds - whether this is true or impossible we leave to the present reader to judge.

The cinnamon-bird, as Solinus says, is a bird in Arabia, which weaves its nest [spherical and narrow at the entrance - as Aristotle says] high in trees, out of the sprigs of cinnamon. Since it is not easy to reach this nest, because of the height and fragility of the branches, the inhabitants of that land bring down the precious masses of cinnamon with lead-weighted darts. [The bird is larger than a sparrow, of a sky-blue color mixed with yellow. Its life is sustained by fish.]

The swan is a bird which the Greeks call 'olor.' It is called 'olor,' moreover, from the fact that it is entirely white in feather: for no one recalls a black swan. For 'holos' in Greek means 'whole' in Latin. 'Cygnus' is named from singing, because it pours forth the sweetness of song in modulated tones. And they say it sings sweetly for this reason, that it has a long and bending neck, and the voice, struggling through such a long and winding passage, must necessarily produce varied modulations. They say that in the Hyperborean regions, at the leading song of the Cyranean birds, very many swans fly up and sing in fitting harmony.

The swan has white feathers but black flesh. It naturally precedes its own death with a song of joy and rejoicing as it is about to die. When swans are about to migrate to another place for the sake of food, gathered together, they travel in such swimming formation that they are carried forward by the thrust of their beaks, by which they more easily cleave the air than if they pushed with their foreheads. From the rear they gradually spread out, and the flock is drawn out in a wedge. They rest their necks upon those in front, and, when the leader tires, they take him up at the rear.

At mating time, male and female caress one another and bend their heads alternately with their necks, as if for an embrace. Without delay, once they have mated, the male, aware of having hurt the female, flees from her; but she, impatient, pursues the fleeing male. Yet this resentment does not persist for long, but, the hurt ceasing, is calmed, and, her mind at rest and ceasing to pursue the male, after mating she purifies herself, plunging into the water with frequent motion of tail and beak. As the Experimentator says, the swan's strength lies in its wings. When death is imminent, it fixes a feather in its brain and thus sings sweetly. It is of a choleric constitution, and therefore prone to anger. It swims with one foot and steers itself with the other, like a rudder. Raised among fish, it is harmless to them. It eats little in proportion to the size of its body. It has very tiny teeth in its beak, with which it cuts its food. It nests over the water, attentive in raising its young. It is a bird impatient of burdens, as Marcus Varro says, and does not gladly fly, but delights in resting on ponds. Struck on the head it dies easily, though it can endure many other injuries.
Caryatid birds, as Solinus says, are birds that fly into flames unharmed, so that neither their feathers nor their flesh yield at all to the flames of fire.
Storks, as Isidore says, are birds of an ash-grey color.
They are so named, as Solinus says, from the sound they make by clacking, which comes from the mouth rather than the voice.

[a fragmentary passage compares this to the cock's crowing:] the cock, moreover, [crows] for four reasons: for the arrival of a mate, and this in gladness; for birds flying overhead, and this in fear; out of anger, and this in defense; for victory, as a cock does, and this in triumph. The stork lays eggs or raises chicks according to the scarcity or sufficiency of food: if there is abundance, more; if there is scarcity of food, fewer, yet no fewer than three, unless perhaps one of the laid eggs has perished. The stork, seeing a heavy storm or hail approaching - for irrational creatures are keener at discerning what weather will bring - places itself over its young with wings spread and its mouth turned toward the storm, and often endures dangers for their sake.
[a fragmentary note:] crows go before their army [i.e., their flock].

Ambrose says, and the great Basil, that they are carried from the regions of the East and travel, like cranes, in formation, and that crows help them and share in fighting against hostile birds, which is evident from the fact that they return to their usual places bloodied with wounds.

So great is the honor given to them for the destruction of serpents in Thessaly that it was a capital offense to kill a stork, just as to kill a man, as Pliny relates. Their affection for their young is so great that, while they diligently brood their nests, they shed their feathers from constant sitting; but the young too show no less remarkable devotion to their mothers. For as long a time as the mothers spend raising their young, for just as long are they in turn nourished by their young. Whence it is also called the 'devoted bird.' They return to their nests each year. But wherever they refuse to return to their accustomed nests, the ignorant common people suppose the abandoned dwelling to become like a deserted resting-place. The stork seems to have a head very prone to catarrh, since water drips almost continually from its beak, and this more so in winter.

This kind of bird lies in wait for serpents in many ways, and though it eats them and other venomous things, nevertheless, as Aldhelm says, it does not die. It eats toads, however, only in great hunger, and in this the natural evil of the toad is noted.

The stork's stomach is a remedy against poisons, as Pliny says. They say that one of their brood casts itself down, feathered, to the master of the place where they bred, as a kind of tribute; but perhaps it is more from weariness of raising it. Where they go, or whence they come, is still unknown.

Preparing to depart, as Solinus says, they gather in a certain place, so that none of their kind is left behind except as a captive. In Asia there is a field where, gathered together, they murmur among themselves, and tear apart the one who arrives last, and thus depart. Nor is there any doubt that storks are devoted followers of chastity and keep the bond of marriage faithfully with one another. As evidence of this, though nothing certain, the common people have nonetheless taught something memorable. They say that a certain man of shrewd wit had, for a long time, a pair of storks living, as is their custom, in a high place of his house. It happened that, while the female's mate had gone off to feed, another male came upon her and defiled her by adulterous union. Without delay, as the adulterer departed, the adulteress at once plunged herself into a distant pool and purified herself with water. And when her mate returned from feeding, he did not notice in his spouse the crime of adultery, washed away by the water. The husband of the house, though the mate was thus repeatedly deceived, often noticed what had happened. And one day he came, when, after the adultery, the adulteress, according to her custom, was striving to wash herself at the pool, and the master of the house kept her away from the pool. Without delay her male, returning from feeding, discovered the filth of adultery upon his mate, and, concealing it for the time, went away. And returning the next day, he brought with him a great multitude of storks. These, attacking her one by one, tore the wretched adulteress apart in a cruel death. If, then, mere water could do this in the stork, what can the water of baptism, with the power of the words, do even in a man, defiled with infinite filth? And the same power belongs to the tear of contrition.
The 'choretes' is a bird, according to Pliny. This bird has a perpetual enmity with the crow.

But the crow, its turn returned, never ceases to oppose it in kind. Persisting stubbornly, then, in this mutual hatred, they never cease plotting ambushes against one another; and so, when the dark night has given its opportune rest, by its silence, to all other creatures, even then these two do not cease to harm one another, but, leaving their nests, seek out each other's eggs greedily in turn and, if they find them, steal them. They do the same to each other's chicks, and in many other ways these cruel birds torment one another.

The crested lark is a small bird, nearly similar to the lark, as the Book of Properties says. It is dusky in color, and unremarkable in feather, but gladdens its hearers with the wondrous modulation of its voice. Whence it happens that, caught by men, it is enclosed in cages. But, forgetful of its captivity and misfortune, it scarcely lets one hour of the day pass without song; indeed, it seems to count it a delight to be captive in such a way, so that it attends to nothing else, is not anxious for food nor for the present life, but, needing only one thing, rejoices to pass its time in songs and to be roused at every hour by the varied voices of birds. For it imitates the voices of all birds, and you could not tell, if you did not see the bird, whether it was the crested lark's own voice or that of the bird it imitates.

And in this is specially signified the joy of contemplatives, even in the present life, since, scarcely and rarely mindful of their exile, because of the sweetness of God, they seem, according to the Apostle, already to have their citizenship in the heavens.

The raven, as Isidore says, is a bird of black color, so named from the sound of its voice. For it knows how to make no other sound but 'cras, cras.' The female broods the eggs and the male brings her food.

As Augustine says, the raven does not feed the chicks hatched from its eggs until, examining them, it sees them turning black in feather. For seven days, then, they are said to remain without any nourishment of food, but on the seventh day they turn black.

Ravens cast some of their young out of the nest, weary of raising them. Under the reign of Tiberius, a young raven flew down from a very high tower into a shoemaker's shop that stood nearby. Kept as a pet by the shop's owner and trained early to speech, it would fly out every morning toward the Forum and greet, by name, Tiberius, then Germanicus and Drusus Caesar, and then the Roman people passing by. One day, returning to the shop, it was killed by a certain man stirred by envy. Without delay, when this was heard in the Forum, the people grieved, and, its killer having been killed in vengeance, the whole assembly of the Roman people celebrated the raven's funeral rites so grandly that it seemed as if one of the princes had died. It has also been discovered of ravens that, if they find water in some deep place, where, because of the shortness of their neck, they could not reach it, they at once gather small stones and drop them into the water, until the water rises enough that they can reach it with their beak and satisfy their desired thirst. Ravens breed before the solstice; they lay eggs for sixty days, chiefly in thirst. [It lives, moreover, for very many years, and so does the whole raven kind.] They are said to conceive and give birth through the mouth. Ravens are said to become pregnant if it happens that they eat a raven's egg.

As the Experimentator says, the females of certain ravens brood their eggs in the sun, and the males bring them food. A raven never rears only two chicks, but more. The raven is noisy and forms various sounds, namely sixty-four, as Fulgentius says. They sometimes mate in flight. The raven eats the eagle-owl's eggs by day, and the eagle-owl eats the raven's eggs by night; the raven, however, is stronger by day, the eagle-owl by night. There is a certain kind of raven in the East that fights with the ass and the bull; for when these flee, the raven flies above them and dashes itself with force against their eyes and, when it can, strikes the fleeing creature's eyes with its beak; and thus, blinding them, renders them useless to their masters; and consequently their carcasses, killed and skinned, become food for birds. And thus a base bird conquers strong animals; and a base woman brings down strong men. The raven naturally loves the fox, and so helps it against the bird called the achilos: for the achilos is the raven's enemy.
Crows, as Pliny says, are of the same kind. They too are seized by sickness at the solstice.

As the Experimentator says, crows attack noble birds as if they were their enemies, and this often to their own harm. For when noble birds have long tolerated the crows' repeated attacks, at last, overcome by impatience, they tear the troublesome birds apart. These alone, flying beside their young for some time, feed them, whom they follow with careful attendance, and are anxious lest the tender ones by chance fail. They bring food and do not abandon their duties of nourishing for a long time. Let men, then, learn to love their children from the practice and devotion of crows.

The crow gladly feeds on nuts. And when it sometimes cannot overcome the hardness of a nut with its beak, flying high, it drops the nut among rocks once, and again, and often, until, cracked, it can break it open. When the female crow is brooding, the male feeds her.
The 'cornica' [great crow], as Pliny says, is a very large bird in the regions of the East. Though this bird is large, it does not have very many feathers in proportion to its body's size.

And this is the reason: since not every bird lacks a bladder, and the surplus of the water it drinks passes into feathers, this bird's surplus of drink does not pass into feathers, but - as is believed - into the lung, which this bird has large, fleshy, and full of blood, and it is like the lung found in a cow.

The cuckoo, as the Book of Properties says, is a base bird. It is so called from the sound of its voice. In singing it does not change its voice, but always repeats the same one. It has nearly the color of the turtledove, but a different nature. It is a most sluggish bird and unstable in its dwelling-place. It lays its eggs in the nest of a little bird of another kind, and removes from that foreign nest a number of eggs equal to the number of its own eggs that it lays there, namely so that the little bird, finding no surplus in the number, does not reject them as foreign. Thus the deceived little bird broods the added egg of a foreign kind and rears its young, nor is it clever enough to distinguish the offspring from its own chicks, smaller in form, by its size.

And so, as Pliny says, while the cuckoo, still weak, sits with the other chicks in the nest, it nevertheless, by a natural greediness, snatches food from the other chicks before them, and by this abundance grows fatter than the rest and becomes sleeker. The foster-mother, charmed by its elegance, delights in its form and marvels at herself for having borne such a creature. She condemns all her own chicks by comparison to it, and lets herself be consumed with admiration for it. And this is its reward to her: not knowing its ignorance, it finds its ignorance out. For when the supposed mother has raised the cuckoo and nourished it to the strength of flight, the cuckoo, in return, rises up against its foster-mother and kills her as she follows it. The cuckoo is said to be stripped of its feather-covering in winter. It enters either a burrow in the ground or hollows of trees, and there gathers in summer what it will live on in winter.

Pliny relates something about the cuckoo, not asserting it, but rather refuting the false opinions of the pagans: There is another marvel, he says, that they tell about the cuckoo: that in the place where one first hears a cuckoo, if the right foot's outline is traced and the footprint dug up, fleas will not be bred wherever it is scattered.

Isidore relates something about the cuckoo, but quite doubtful: These birds, he says, have their time of coming, being carried on the shoulders of kites because of their short and weak flights, lest, exhausted by the long stretches of the sky, they fail. Their saliva breeds cicadas.
The 'coredulus' [heart-eater] is a bird, as Isidore says, named as if 'eating the heart.' For, living on flesh and prey, it especially longs to be sated on the heart.

This signifies, indeed, God himself, who, through the wise faithful soul, admonishes, saying: Give me your heart, my son. On which Augustine says: For he buys so dearly that he alone ought to possess it.
The dove, as Augustine says, is a gentle bird. It does not tear with its beak.
It is without gall, as Bede says.

Yet Aristotle says that it has gall, but not in the place where other animals have it: for it has it in the intestine. The contradiction with Bede, who says it has no gall, is resolved by understanding: not in the place where other animals have it.

It stirs love with a kiss, goes about in flocks, harms no one with its beak, does not live on carrion, feeds on pure grain, has a moan instead of a song, and nourishes the young of others. The dove recovers its sight nine times over. It nests high up, as James and Bede say, where evil beasts cannot reach. Let your citizenship, then, O faithful soul, be in the heavens.

It rests more gladly over the waters that reflect the hawk, so as both to quench its thirst and to watch in the water for the shadow of the approaching hawk: Blessed, then, is the man who dwells in the wisdom of scripture and meditates in justice and reflects with understanding on the watchfulness of God. For he shall be fed with the bread of life and understanding, and shall drink the water of saving wisdom.

There is a certain tree of the East, as Isidore says, which in Greek is called 'peredixion,' but in Latin 'around the right.' The fruit of this tree is sweet, in which doves marvelously delight. They are also sheltered by its shade and branches. In those same regions there is a certain kind of dragon, which lies in wait for these doves. But the dragon itself naturally so dreads this tree that it fears even to touch its shadow. As the doves sit in the tree, then, the dragon lies in wait at a distance and watches, to see if any of them leaves the tree and becomes its prey. But if the shadow falls on the left side, the dragon attacks from the right; if on the right, from the left. Understand the dragons as demons, the doves as faithful souls, the peredixion tree as the cross of Christ, whose 'around the right' is his mother, and the tree's shadow the sign of the cross.

The wood-pigeon is a kind of dove, which [is of a sky-blue color, has a white ring around its neck, and an exceptional brightness]; having lost its bodily mate, it goes about alone among the other doves, seeking no green place to rest, nor does it seek bodily union any further. James: across the sea, toward the East, there are doves which, performing the office of messengers, carry the letters of their masters under their wings, crossing many stretches of land in a short time. They are, moreover, very necessary, especially when, through enemy lands, other messengers dare not pass. Aristotle: doves are of the greatest chastity and know no adultery.

They do not break faith, as Pliny says, and love a shared home, and, unless single or widowed, do not leave their chaste home. It is certain, however, that there are some doves that have never known a male, and others that, having had one and lost him, remain widows. Such doves, however, avoid the shared home of those doves that are joined in pairs, so as not to be troubled by the disturbances of males, and flee, and dwell among ruined walls. Females sometimes endure even unjust, overbearing males, since there is suspicion of adultery. Then the throat is full of complaint, and cruel blows from the beak; but soon, in reconciliation, there is kissing, and, around mating, entreaties, and flattery with frequent circling of the feet. [A domestic dove always carries something to enlarge the nest, every time she comes down from it.] Love for the offspring is often equal in both. The parents spit out into the chicks' mouths, from their throat, earth gathered more salted, preparing seasoning for the food. Doves always rear two chicks, bearing a male first, and after three days a female. Both brood in turns: the female broods from midday until morning, and the male the rest of the time. On the eighteenth day they hatch.

As the Experimentator says, the dove first pierces the shell and then splits it apart. When doves find a stray dove, they gather it to themselves. They eat small stones for the tempering of the stomach (for they are of a very hot nature). They fight with raised feathers. They have very hot dung, which they cast out of the nest and teach their young to cast out too. The blood of a dove, a swallow, and a turtledove, taken from beneath the right wing, applied to the eye, heals it; for it is sharp and has the power to dissolve.

Among the chicks, eggs are often also found, and while some fly off, others are just hatching. These chicks themselves breed at three months old. If there is no male, the females mount each other likewise and lay eggs, but nothing is produced from these. The male drives grown chicks from the nest, but mates with them before driving them out. The dove is greatly burdened in laying eggs; and if she delays laying, she is struck by the male. Doves have a peculiarity among birds: they do not raise their head when drinking, until they have had enough. Doves and turtledoves live fifteen years. There are two kinds of hawks: one kind never catches birds sitting still, but only those flying in the air; the other kind of hawk does not catch birds except when they are sitting on the ground; and doves, naturally knowing this, distinguish between the kinds of hawks and, by sitting still or by fleeing, avoid their ambushes, according to which method - sitting or flying - they know will get them caught by that kind. The chicks of doves are better and healthier in spring and autumn than at other times, and this because at these times they live mostly on grain. Pliny is the authority that fresh dove's flesh, plucked together with that of swallows, is effective against serpents. It is a peculiarity of doves, among other birds, that, having drunk, they do not tilt back their neck, but drink with a broad throat, in the manner of beasts of burden. Doves, however, seem to have a certain understanding of glory. For sometimes, sitting alone in private, admiring the colors variously arranged around its neck, it smooths its little feathers with the applause of its wings and beak, and, for the governance of flight and finer grooming, arranges its down and feathers. The sparrowhawk, seeing this, launches into flight, and, hidden in foliage, watches for it, far swifter, and seizes it as it delights in its very glory.

The carchates, as Aristotle says, is a bird that dwells by the sea, and is smaller in size than the hawk. This bird submerges itself in water and stays there, before it recovers breath in the air, for as long as a man could walk the distance of one mile.

And oh, would that those who are sometimes swallowed up by luxuries or riches would, at least after some time, breathe toward heavenly things and, with the prophet, long for the wings of flight and the rest of the wilderness.

The quail, as the Book of Properties says, is a bird which we commonly call 'quiscula.' It is called by the Greeks 'ortigia,' because birds of this kind were first seen on the island of Ortygia. It is also called 'ortygometra,' as if 'leader of the flock.'

Solinus: they have their season of arrival once summer is over. When they must cross the seas, they wait for favorable winds, and, fearing the length of the crossing, husband their strength by delaying. They never set out with the south wind, but, fearing gentler breezes, trust themselves mostly to the north winds, so that a drier and stronger wind may more easily carry their somewhat plump and therefore slower bodies. Blessed, then, are the poor in spirit, who boldly commit themselves to the gentlest breath of the south wind, so as to cross the sea, that is, the world. But unhappy are those who, weighed down by the burden of flesh and the world, entrust themselves to the blasts of the north wind, and therefore, according to the prophet Job, spend their days in good things and in a moment descend into hell.

Accordingly, about to cross, they gather in troops, then, massed together more thickly, hasten on, and their haste often brings destruction upon sailors: for it happens at night that they fall upon the sails and, their weight overloading the folds, tip the ships over. These signify certain men who, having zeal but not according to knowledge, wish to proceed with excessive severity, and therefore often become the ruin of the weaker. As these quails, then, approach land, that is, a sea harbor, hawks, watching, seize them, and for this reason it is the concern of all of them to enlist a leader of a different kind, through whom the first dangers may be avoided. For they have crows as leaders. Remember, then, faithful soul, what was said at the beginning of the world to the enemy of the human race: You shall lie in wait for his heel, that is, his end, where he must come, as it were, to the harbor of salvation or of ruin. Attend, then, to what follows: And she shall crush his head - that is, the devil's - and his head is called the suggestion of his temptation, which is most grave and most dangerous at a man's death. There, then, faithful soul, crush his head, and this with a spirit purified through contrition and hope raised up in the mercy of divine pity. So, then, enlist your leader, or rather your leaders, the holy angels, that they may protect you from the assault of the cruel hawk, the devil.

Among birds, the quail kind has very rare females. Among the kind of fish, likewise, scallops have very rare females. But among mankind, males are born fewer and rarer than females, and the reason is this: that human nature, prone to mating at indiscriminate times, mates with women more often in the evening and in the first hours of the night, namely when bodies are still full of the vapors of food and the spirits not yet purged by sleep; and if offspring is conceived then, it takes on the weaker, female sex. But those conceived at dawn, when it is the hour of blood, and bodies and spirits have been purged by the evaporation of vapors, more often obtain the male sex in conception. This alone among birds, along with man, among all the creatures of the earth, suffers the falling sickness. Their most pleasing food is the seeds of poisonous plants, for which reasons the tables of the prudent have condemned them.

The Book of Kyranides says that if its eyes are dissolved with a little water in a glass vessel for seven days, and afterward a little oil is added, and you wrap a wick in this and light it in a lamp which you place among those sitting together, they will see each other as if fiery.

The goldfinch is a small bird, taking its name, as Isidore says, from the fact that it feeds on thistles [cardui]; and it seems marvelous that this little bird should be nourished on the sharp prickles of the thistle's spines. This bird is adorned with black and saffron on its body, and with red color on its head. Of this it is commonly said that, enclosed in a cage, it draws to itself, with its beak, water placed below by a thread suspending a little vessel, and, its foot sometimes also set on the thread, when it reaches the little vessel, it quenches its thirst with drink; and this indeed is a marvel of nature, which gave such cunning to the small goldfinch, which it was unwilling to grant to the ox or the ass, great animals.

div.head: 40. De crochilo qui est rex avium dicitur

cit.quote: The wren, as Pliny says, is a bird we call, in Italy, the king of birds. It is indeed the smallest of all birds; but, as Pliny says, the smaller the body, the greater the swiftness. It has, moreover, so great a spirit that it dares to make attempts against the eagle, the queen of birds. It is fertile in chicks, rearing very many at one brood. It feeds on spiders. It deceives men, for when it offers itself nearby as if to be caught by hand, it escapes, its effort and labor vain, unprepared. In winter many gather together in a single burrow or cave, so that the warmth, which is small in such tiny bodies, may be increased, the crowd nonetheless contributing to the warmth.

Diomedian birds are those named, as Solinus says, from King Diomedes. The Greeks call them 'herodii.' They are the size of a swan. Their color is white, their eyes fiery, and their mouths toothed. They fly in flocks; the foremost leads the flock, and the last drives the column on. There is also discipline among those in the middle. With their beaks they hollow out rocks in the cliffs for their nests, then, laying twigs crosswise over these, they imitate roofs of wickerwork, that is, roofs like barrel-covers; and lest the wind by chance carry off their hut, they press it down with the dust-material they had gathered while hollowing the nests. They measure their exits and entrances by the quarters of the sky: the entrance leading to feeding is set toward the east; the one that receives them on their return faces the sunset. When they mourn with tearful cries, they signify by foreboding either a change among them or the death of their king.
Solinus and James: if a Greek approaches them, they, it is said, fawn upon him; but other nations they attack with bites.

The dariata, as Aristotle says, is an eastern bird. It lacks feet, using its chest, beak, and other parts for crawling. There is a certain kind of them that appears only after the rain that falls at the very end of summer, and appears only at this time.
