The pelican also lives on crocodile's milk, which the beast, because of the excessive abundance of its dugs, discharges in great quantity in some marshy place. Whence the pelican also gladly follows the crocodile.

The philosopher: this bird is always afflicted with leanness, and whatever it swallows it digests quickly, because its stomach has no side-pouch to hold food; for it has only a single passage of the intestine, which reaches from the entrance of the mouth to the secret parts of nature.

The Book of Kyranides: flesh-eating birds, gathered against those that do not eat flesh, wait one month, their armies divided on either bank of the river. When they engage, a clamor rises to the sky, and they fly together and fight so fiercely that much blood is shed and much plucking of feathers occurs, whence the people of Lycia stuff their beds with them; among these the pelicans especially are present in great numbers, mightily armed with their beaks.

The purple gallinule is a bird outside the custom and manner of other birds, as the philosopher John says. For it has one foot broad for swimming, and the other cloven for walking. And in this it is noted that it enjoys both elements, swimming in the water like ducks and walking on land like partridges. It has one foot like an eagle's, the other like a goose's. Spotting a fish in the water, it rises above the clouds and, descending with force, seizes the fish with one foot into the depth of the water, and thus, swimming with the other foot, carries the fish to the desired place. This bird is larger than the eagle and smaller than the swan. Some fable that the purple gallinule is the same as the pelican; but this is disproved by the opinion of most.

It is a bird of a foreign region. Pliny relates of it: this, which is contrary to the custom of all birds; for it alone, besides the parrot, the purple gallinule, taking up water with its foot as if with a hand, carries it to its beak and drinks and feeds itself in a human manner; and nature seems to have given it this as, in a sense, a punishment, because with every food, and with each single bite, it must drink; for it naturally has a weak power of appetite in drawing in and incorporating food into itself. This bird is like those who gorge themselves, who wish to drink at every bite. The most praised of purple gallinules are those with a large beak and very long legs.

The peacock is a most beautiful bird, a friend of beauty and cleanliness. It has a serpent-like head, and feathers above it like a crown, or rather a crest. It has a sapphire-colored chest, a long, extended neck, likewise sapphire in color; it has mostly reddish feathers, a long and eyed tail, a terrible voice, a simple gait. With its cry it drives away all venomous animals, which do not dare to remain in places wherever they hear the peacock's voice.

Augustine: the flesh of a dead peacock does not rot or smell foul for a whole year; the blessed Augustine, in the book On the City of God, recounts having tested this himself. This same teacher says, moreover, that it never rots at all.

James: when the peacock is looked at and praised, it spreads its tail in a circle, bends it, and shows its beauty; and this especially facing the sun, because then the colors shine more brightly. But if watched by someone silent, it hides all the feathers it delights to have admired, drawing its eyes shut.
The peacock, with its tail spread, when it sees the deformity of its feet, at once lowers its spread tail.
Pliny: it begins to display its jeweled colors from three years of age, and then gives birth. It lives twenty-five years.
As the Book of Kyranides says, a precious stone grows in the peacock's head. Peacock and goose eggs are useful for preparing a golden color.

The peacock, having lost its tail each year along with the leaves of the trees, seeks hiding places, ashamed and mourning, until it grows back. When the peacock wakes at night and cannot see itself, set in darkness, it cries out fearfully, believing it has lost its beauty. The peacock lays eggs three times a year. If its eggs are set under hens, chicks emerge. The males break the eggs from desire to be the ones brooding; for this reason the females lay in hiding. [They pursue their own chicks as if they were strangers, before the mark of the crest has grown on them. Beans lightly roasted also provoke lust.] Unless the eggs are received on soft bedding, they break at once. The brood hatches in twenty-seven days, or later, on the thirtieth.

Aristotle: the peacock, with its voice, terrifies serpents, and they do not easily dare to live nearby, where the peacock's voice is often heard. Before mating, they kiss one another. When the male grows old, he cannot mate, but kisses. The female, from desire of mating, mounts upon another female.

[a fragmentary note:] when it climbs high, it is a sign of rain. Peacock chicks must be raised most carefully: for they are easily hurt to death. Their greatest danger is when the crest begins to grow on them, and then they must be confined from running about. There are some peacocks entirely white in color, and yet that sheen, which is usual in the varied feathers of other peacocks, is in these distinguished, in a wondrous way, as a white sheen from the other white feathers, so much so that the jeweled eyes, which in other peacocks shine with gold or sapphire, shine here with a white splendor. Wild peacocks inhabit deserted places, but are in no way similar to domestic peacocks in sheen, color, or tail. Nor is it a wonder, if nature, in creating them the burden of such tails, seemed rather to have weighed down these flying creatures than to have honored, with such glory, birds unaccustomed to it.

The partridge takes its name from its voice. Whence James, Ambrose, and Isidore say that this bird is so cunning and deceitful that, stealing another's eggs, it broods them; but the deceit does not succeed: for when the chicks hear their true mother's voice, by a certain natural instinct they leave the one who brooded them and return to the one who bore them. [The partridge, moreover, has a drier brain than other birds, and consequently becomes forgetful, and so, forgetting its own nest, loses its eggs, which are seized upon by another and brooded.]

It builds its nest amid the thickest places of thorn-bushes. Dust is the covering of its eggs. When someone approaches their nests, the mothers, going out, offer themselves freely to those who come and, feigning weakness of foot or wing, as if about to be caught at once, make their steps seem slower. By this deception they occupy those in their path, until they have led them far from the nests. The chicks, when they fear being discovered, gather little clods of earth in their feet and hide beneath them, concealed. Often the mothers carry off their chicks, to deceive the males, who very often trouble them with unwelcome advances. Pliny: when the males fight over the females, the defeated ones are mounted by the victors in an unjust mating.

And, as the Experimentator says, headlong lust forgets sex. The mother flies in a circle around the hunters, until her chicks flee, and after their flight, she too flees; and then, fear removed, she calls her chicks. The flesh of partridges, above the flesh of other wild birds, is most wholesome.

When they are caught by a fowler in a net-trap, one follows another, and the wretched one that follows does not discern or draw back from the danger, deceived by the company of her already captured companions. In which is clearly shown the folly of men perishing through sins, when, by one another's example, they fall into the devil's snare, who hunts precious souls. Whence the prophet Habakkuk cries out: He has gathered everything, he says, into his net; over this he will rejoice and exult. Not without reason did he say 'everything,' because in truth almost the whole of it, the part that remains for God being smallest and, in comparison to the rest, almost nothing.

Partridges sit at night with their hindquarters turned to face each other. The females of partridges are so stirred by lust that they are said to conceive from the mere scent. For at the time of lust, their tongues extended toward each other, they burn with desire for mating. When they mate, they produce a stench in the act. The lifespan of partridges is said to last up to sixteen years. What we have said of partridges, namely that they conceive from the wind, we also assert of doves, geese, peacocks, and hens. But their offspring in this case are infertile, smaller, less pleasant in taste, and moister. Softened in vinegar, they become so tender that they can pass through rings. Pliny said that partridge gall with honey, in equal measure, is good for clarity of the eyes. The partridge does not grow fat, as Pliny attests.

[The spoonbill] is a bird, as Pliny says. Flying up to those birds that dive into the sea for prey, it seizes their heads with its bite, until it forces them to give up their catch. This same bird, if it has filled itself with shellfish, vomits them up, cooked by the heat of its stomach. Then it separates the shells; but, taking the selected and separated flesh, it swallows it into its stomach.

Plovers are birds nearly the size of a partridge. They are adorned with varied feathers, marked with saffron, white, and black. They are said to live on air alone, and yet are fat; the proof that they live on air is that, although they grow fat, nothing can ever be found in their entrails. They are caught in this way: fowlers have lead-weighted rods, and, throwing these higher into the air, frighten the birds off and force them to fly lower, then stretch nets over the ground and catch them as they flee.

The magpie is a most cunning bird. As Pliny says, when it senses that its nest has been closely observed by a man, it moves its eggs elsewhere, aided by the dexterity of its claws. Some birds lacking this dexterity place a twig through two eggs, so that, held together by some sticky binding, with the neck placed in the middle at an even balance on either side, they carry the others. The magpie is a bird marked with a variety of black and white. It builds its nest among thorny places, and takes great care to fence and fortify it, with earth on the inside and thorns most carefully arranged all around on the outside, below and above, leaving only the narrowest opening on the side, through which it enters and exits, and this in the place where the nest is least accessible.

Its chicks are said to be eaten for the sharpening of eyesight, though these do not easily submit to cooking unless first skinned. This bird too, when it knows it has been caught in a snare, is still in its whole body, and struggles only with the effort of its beak to open the snare, nor does it move the rest of its body until the utmost despair. Caught in its youth, the magpie learns words and sometimes dies, overcome by the difficulty of a word. Accordingly, unless they hear again what they had learned, memory fails those seeking to recall it. They are marvelously delighted if they hear again the word they had forgotten. They choose words deliberately in their thought, and do not conceal their intent. They have broader tongues, which imitate human speech. In antiquity, young Caesars kept birds trained in Greek and Latin speech, meditating daily and constantly saying new things.

The woodpecker is a small bird, as the Book of Properties says, which pierces trees with its beak. When they strike the bark of trees on their backs, they perceive that food is beneath. Pliny: they raise their chicks in hollow trees, and if anyone shoots an arrow or something like it into these trees, the woodpecker, applying a certain herb, at once expels it, however forcefully it was driven in.
When you have observed this herb applied to a lock, take it, for it has, as the Book of Kyranides says, the power of opening locks, if you add the proper words.

Having hooked claws, it rarely lands on rocks, lest the sharpness of its claws be blunted. Many of its kind are black, like the blackbird, saffron-colored like orioles, but those are more beautiful and larger which are reddish on the crown of the head, saffron on the chest, green around the neck, sky-blue on the wings, and shimmering on the tail. The woodpecker is said not to live in the region of Tarentum. It is peculiar to these that they go bald once every year, namely, as Pliny says, at the time when turnips are sown.
The Experimentator says that someone wrote in verse of the woodpecker: 'Small, talkative bird, I greet you, master, with my voice: if you do not see me, you will deny that I am a bird.'

The sparrow is a bird, as the Book of Properties says, gladly dwelling on the roofs of houses or on old walls. Birds of this kind fly in flocks to feed, and have the pith of barley as their most pleasing food. And this is remarkable, that they separate the grain from the chaff with such subtlety that the delay between picking and sorting is thought to be almost imperceptible. Sometimes, however, when it hurries and wishes to swallow the barley together with the chaff, it is choked by the awns of the chaff. Sitting on the ground before flying up, it strikes the ground with its foot, and then rises into the air. They are quickly roused to fury, but their discord lasts no time at all.

As the Experimentator says, sparrows are hotter than all other birds, whence they are astringent and stimulate the blood, and are exceedingly lustful. Its dung is very hot when discharged, but cools very quickly. And it signifies those who believe for a time and, in time of temptation, fall away. The sparrow digests quickly whatever it swallows. Whence it happens that the food it eats never fattens the body, but only sustains it.

Female sparrows are said to live longer than males. Aristotle says that male sparrows live only one year; females, however, live a long time. We believe this indeed of the sparrows of the East, since among us, who are in Europe, male sparrows live as long as females. And this is quite plausible, because that blackness which Aristotle says is on the male's neck is not found among us; rather, a certain white spot marked with that blackness on the cheeks is found in male sparrows among us; and these remain alive winter and summer, just like female sparrows. The age of sparrows seems to be shown by the hardness of the beak, since when a sparrow is young, it has a tender beak, saffron-colored around the jaws; but an old sparrow has a black, hard beak, large around the jaws. In certain parts of the world sparrows suffer from the falling sickness, and this, as Aristotle believes, because they eat the seed of henbane.

When a sparrow's chicks are about to fly, neighboring sparrows accompany the parents in supporting the efforts of the fledglings, so that the weak ones, if necessary, may be strengthened by the massed support of the many.

And in this the providence of prelates is noted, that when they see weaker subordinates being advanced to positions of authority requiring strength, they ought to strengthen their insufficiency with the support of prayers and exhortations, and, if anything is lacking in them, supply it, if they can. Whence the Apostle: Bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.

The reed-sparrow has an origin of this kind: from the adulterous mating of the nightingale and the sparrow, a third kind of bird is conceived and brooded. And it is called the reed-sparrow, for it sings more than the sparrow and less than the nightingale; for it has a song foreign to the nightingale's, yet good and varied. It builds its nest among growing reed-beds, and, dwelling there, took the word of its name from this.
[The nightingale] is a bird named, as the Book of Properties says, from 'philos,' which means 'love,' and 'menos,' which means 'sweet.'

The nightingale is a bird so named, as the Book of Properties says, from 'philos,' which means 'love,' and 'menos,' which means 'sweet.' For this bird gladdens its hearer with wondrous melody. It rejoices at the rising of the sun and precedes its coming with joy. It sings only in springtime, never in winter. At the start of spring it delights so much in the pleasantness of its own voice that it eats most rarely, and when it does, does so in the greatest haste. The nightingale is also said to delight so persistently and indiscriminately in singing that it would rather cast off its life through weakness and fail utterly than be deprived of the melody of its voice. Whence the nightingale is also named from 'philos,' which is 'love,' and 'menos,' which is 'failing,' as if 'failing from love.'

Pliny: for they compete with one another, and openly, and the rivalry is so spirited that, defeated, they often end their life in death, their breath failing before their song does. This is the first marvel observed in it, that so great a voice, so persistent a spirit, exists in so small a little body. Then we marvel at its perfect knowledge of music. For a modulated sound is produced, and now it is drawn out long in one continuous breath, now it is varied by a bend, now broken off short, now joined together in a trill. For sometimes, unexpectedly, it murmurs even with itself, full, deep, sharp, rapid, sustained, quivering; and sometimes middling, highest, lowest, and, to put it briefly: it presents, in so tiny a throat, all that human skill has devised with the elaborate contrivances of pipes. Younger nightingales practice and learn songs to imitate; the pupil listens with great attention and gives back the song in turn: correction is understood in the refined version, and a certain reproach in the teacher. Accordingly, from the end of spring, as the heat increases, the voice becomes altogether different, and the color too changes; and finally, in winter, it is not seen at all. And it should be noted that as soon as the nightingale begins to mate and indulge in lust with its partner, it at once loses the pleasantness of its voice and, as Pliny says, its voice becomes different, and its color changes. [This bird sometimes commits adultery with the sparrow and allows itself to be mounted by it.] The thinness of their tongues is not like that of other birds.

The parrot is a bird of India, as Solinus and James say, green in color, with a purple - that is, golden - ring around its neck, a large and broad tongue, whence it also brings forth articulate words, so that, if you did not see it, you would think a man was speaking. It greets a man, saying: 'Hail!' or 'Chere!' In its first and second year it learns more quickly and retains more tenaciously. Its beak is of such hardness that, when it plunges from a height onto a rock, it catches itself with the thrust of its beak, so that it uses this as, in a sense, a foundation beyond the ordinary measure of firmness; its head, moreover, is so strong that, when it is compelled by men to imitate human voices, it must be struck with a small iron key. It feeds itself with its foot and brings food to its mouth, as a man does with his hand. They are said to nest in the mountains of Gilboa, because it rarely or never rains there, and parrots cannot bear rain. Other kinds of water they can tolerate in any form, but they die in the rain. It guards its tail with the greatest care and diligence, and often wipes its feathers with its beak.

As Aristotle says, it gladly drinks wine, and is an excessively lustful bird. Nor is this a wonder, because it gladly drinks wine, wine in which lust dwells. It has a certain natural cry, with which it seems to greet Caesars.

Whence it happened that, as Charlemagne wandered through the wastes of Greece, parrots came to meet him, and, as if in the Greek tongue, greeted him, crying out: 'Hail, Emperor!' And the outcome fulfilled the utterance of their words like a kind of prophecy, since, though at that time Charles was only king of Gaul, in the following time he became Emperor of the Romans. It is also read in the Life of Pope Leo: for when a certain noble had a parrot trained to speak, he sent it as a gift to Pope Leo. And while it was still on the road and had men in its path, the bird cried out: 'I am going to the Pope! I am going to the Pope!' Without delay, when it entered the Pope's presence, it cried out: 'Pope Leo, hail! Pope Leo, hail!' At which the Pope, greatly delighted, often made use of the parrot's chatter for recreation after his daily labors.

The ostrich is a bird, as Isidore says, called in Greek 'assida'; it is also called 'camelon,' because it has feet like a camel's. This bird, when the time comes for it to lay eggs, raises its eyes to the sky to see whether the star called the Pleiad has risen. For it does not lay its eggs on the ground unless that star has risen. And the reason is this: in summertime, when the crops flower around the month of July, the star of the Pleiad rises in the sky, and then indeed the ostrich digs in the ground and there lays its eggs and covers them with sand. Once these are covered, it leaves the place, and, having just laid its eggs, forgets them and never returns to them again. For it is naturally forgetful. And so, in the warm season, it produces its eggs and covers them with sand in the ground, so that what it would otherwise have done by sitting and brooding, the calm of the season and the temperate air seem to provide for it.
Whence the prophet Jeremiah says of this bird: the ostrich in the sky has known its season. So, then, the eggs warmed by the sand irradiated by the sun, chicks are hatched from them.

[It may be asked] why the ostrich buries its eggs in sand and does not brood them, as other birds do, but only with its gaze? Solution: every generation of things requires a twofold origin, a material cause and an efficient cause. The material cause is the matter from which a thing draws its being; heat is the efficient cause. For heat corrupts, digests, and transforms into a new form. Matter, however, is manifold: very coarse, moderate, and fine. As the matter is, then, so must the heat be. If, then, the matter is fine, it can be transformed by weak heat, as we see in the hen's egg, which, being of a fine substance, is warmed by a light heat, so that an animal is generated from it. Whence women warm them in their lap. But the ostrich's egg has a very coarse substance, and so requires the strongest heat. The animal, moreover, on whose power it depends, has tough, indeed very tough flesh, and is a most hot-natured animal, which the effect of the thing shows, since it even digests iron. From this, then, it happens that the ostrich covers its eggs with sand, so that they may be more warmed by the heat of the sand. It, meanwhile, fixes its gaze upon them, so that, by the heat of the visible spirit, which is potentially hot in it, since it proceeds from a most hot animal, the air that surrounds them may be warmed. And by strong heat, the very coarse substance, dissolved and broken down by the movement of generation, produces from itself the animal on whose power it depends.

[The ostrich has something of the nature] of the gerfalcon and the hawk, but is slow to fly. It eats iron. These birds, as Aristotle says, are almost of the kind of beasts. For though they have feathers, they never use them in flight, since they are never raised from the ground. The formation of its wings is thin, and its down is like hair.

The Experimentator says that the ostrich has upper eyelids. The shape of its head is distinct, and is close to the neck. As it walks, it raises its wings. It eats and digests iron, because it is of a very hot nature. It naturally hates the horse and pursues it in a wondrous way. The horse, indeed, fears and hates it so much that it dares not even look at it. Beneath its wings it has a small bone with which it pricks itself in the side and stirs itself up, when provoked to anger.
And it signifies those who, provoked to anger by a light word, at the devil's instigation, burn for vengeance.

These birds run on the ground so fast that they surpass horses in speed. They have cloven hooves for gripping stones, which they hurl, in flight, against their pursuers. They are so foolish that, when they have hidden their neck in a bush, they believe the height of the rest of their body is also hidden. Their eggs are so large that, cut crosswise, they are made, because of their capacity, into vessels for drinking. The ostrich naturally goes bald, as Pliny says, and sheds its feathers so much that it remains almost naked. But it has a very tough skin, by which, featherless, it is protected from the harshness of cold. It has a large, broad breastbone on its chest, shield-shaped, and this was created in it for the protection of its great body. For it has a body nearly as large as an ass's; of moderate stature.

The screech-owl is a nocturnal bird, as Isidore says. It has its name from its voice: for when it cries out, it shrieks [stridet]. Whence Lucan: what the warm eagle-owl complains of, what the screech-owl of the night. The screech-owl is a nocturnal bird, then, and is commonly called 'amma,' from loving [amando]: for it loves its little ones. This bird alone, contrary to the custom of other birds, is said to instill a certain milk-like moisture into its chicks.

Starlings are small birds, as Pliny says, [a near-duplicate repetition follows in the source, again attributed to Pliny] small and quick for flying. They shine with a dusky color. They fly in flocks and wheel about in a kind of ball formation, with all of them heading toward the middle, and this because of the hawks that lie in wait for them. They gather at evening and murmur together in immense crowds.
Silent at night, at reddening dawn they raise a murmur; then, dividing up, they fly in troops to feed.
The turtledove is a bird, as Isidore says, named from the sound of its voice.
Aristotle attests that it is of wondrous chastity.

It loves its mate and keeps faith with it alone, so much so that, when it dies or is caught by a hawk, it does not join with another, but goes about alone, perching on the dry branches of trees, moaning and sad. On this the great Basil says: let women hear how, among irrational birds, the continence of widowhood is preferred over repeated marriages. It has a moan instead of a song. It is hostile to no bird, but is most patient against the attacks of all birds. It builds its nest from very few branches, in which it rests and broods its eggs.

The turtledove, as Ambrose says, casts squill leaves over its nest, so that no hostile animal attacks its chicks, for these are driven away by their good smell. For it knows that venomous animals are accustomed to flee leaves of this kind. [The turtledove lives on fruits. It flees the smell of sulphur.]

The Experimentator says that the turtledove lies in its feathers, in the hollows of trees, through the whole winter. It dwells in the safest and most pleasant places, and places its nest among the branches of a dense tree. The turtledove lays eggs twice in spring, and often three times, but this when one pair of eggs has spoiled or been lost by accident. Among other birds, the turtledove alone feeds its chicks at night. Its chicks, like the dove's, are born in pairs, warm and moist, which their heaviness for flight attests, but as they begin to fly they lose this very heaviness; their flesh also becomes lighter and more acceptable for digestion (for movement consumes the excess moisture, and through this the heaviness). The blood of the right wing, applied to the eyes, is medicinal.

The turtledove hides in winter, comes forth in spring. Many of them seek warm lands in winter, and many remain, as Aristotle says, if they have a place suited for resting, facing the sun. In the south wind they cannot fly well, because that wind is moist and heavy. The turtledove also sometimes becomes so naturally weak that it can be caught by hand. They also sometimes cry out while flying, and this because of the exhaustion of flight. Wood-pigeons and turtledoves often lay three eggs, yet never rear more than two.
The turtledove, as Isidore says, flees the roofs of men and dwells in the woods.

The 'trogopale' is a bird, as Solinus says, found in Ethiopia. It is larger than the eagle. It has horns like a ram's, whence it presents an armed head against all birds hostile to it, driving them off with the roughness of its horns. This bird is of a rust-colored hue. It has a head like the phoenix's, except that it presents an armed head, as we have said.

Thrushes are birds, as Pliny says, small indeed in body, but great in foresight: for, building on the tops of trees with mud, almost continuously, that is, without interruption, they breed apart from mating, and it is remarkable that ten days after mating the eggs ripen in the womb, and only then do they lay.
These birds signify those who, ready for every good, once a good intention has been conceived in the heart, at once set their hands to accomplishing it and bring forth saving fruits.

The bat is so called as if using its wing 'in the evening' [vespere]; as the Book of Properties says, for it flies only in the evening and at night. In winter it hides. Rarely or never does it go out to feed. It hangs on walls or lies in caves, like something dead. But if you bring it to the sun's warmth and clear air, it gradually stirs, and, restored to its former vigor, flies back to its sleep. There is no down on its body, no feathers on its wings.

It differs in no way in form from a mouse, since it alone among birds gives birth and suckles at teats, like a beast, except that it has a tail and wings shaped like a bird's, though these have no feathers projecting from them, but only membranes stretched out in a leathery flexibility. The flying parent embraces her twin young and carries them with her. Its blood, with thistle, is an outstanding remedy against the bites of serpents.

As the Book of Kyranides says, its blood, applied after the hairs have been plucked out, lets your hair grow back. If you place the same beneath the head of a wife without her knowledge, she will soon conceive.

As Pliny says, it finds gnats most pleasing as food. It has the outlines of feet on its tail, and some on its wings too; but it never uses these to support itself. For when it must rest, it leans on its chest, mouth, or wings. This lowly creature has this trait, that they cling to one another and hang, as it were, in the shape of a cluster of grapes from some place, and, if the outermost one lets go, they all come apart. It uses teeth, which we are not accustomed to find in other birds. In India there are bats larger than doves, having, as it were, human teeth, with which they strike men in the face, cutting off their nostrils and ears and other members.
'Vanelli' [lapwings] are birds, as the Book of Properties says, so commonly named.
[a fragmentary note:] 'simphalides'

They are quite beautiful birds, the size of a dove, with a crested head like a peacock's, a neck of a green and shining color, the rest of the body marked with variety. This bird, when it senses a man approaching its nest even from far off, at once comes out and rushes toward him with a cry, thinking, namely, that it will make the man leave by the insistence of its cry. Thus the foolish little bird, thinking to drive the man from her nest by her cry, betrays her nest by the sign of her cry. For the man, at once made quite certain that he has been noticed, and that the crying bird's nest is nearby, presses on and, having thus discovered it, strives to plunder it.

The owl [ulula] is a bird, as Isidore says, named from wailing and mourning. For when it cries out, it imitates either weeping or moaning. Whence, falsely, among augurs, it is said that if it laments, it shows sadness, but if silent, prosperity.

The hoopoe is a bird forbidden by the Law. As Isidore says, it is an unclean bird, which builds its nest in dung and dwells more gladly in filthy places. Yet it is quite a beautiful bird, and is helmeted with certain crested, standing feathers [with a seven-colored crest on its head, which opens and closes]. In winter it hides and is silent; it comes forth in spring, and is tiresome with a single repeated call, like the cuckoo.

The aging parents shed their feathers in the nest among their now-grown chicks, and are fed again by their chicks, until they recover their strength and feathers. The Physiologus says there is also another devotion in them toward their parents. For when their parents have lost their sight through old age, the chicks naturally gather a known herb, and with it anoint their parents' blinded eyes, so that, by the herb's remedy, their eyes recover their clarity; and in this the devotion of the younger Tobias is shown.
James: if anyone anoints his temples with hoopoe's blood and then goes to sleep, he will see, in his dreams, demons as if suffocating him.
The hoopoe's heart is effective for evildoers and enchanters, but the Experimentator does not write how this works.
The vulture is a large and heavy bird, as Isidore says, but quite excellent in flying, although before it rises from the ground into the air to fly, it makes three hops.

Whence it happens that it is sometimes caught by a dog, before it can raise itself, by its usual hops, into the heights of the air. The vulture's feathers, if placed in fire, drive away serpents with their glow, as Pliny says. He also says that those who carry a vulture's heart at their side are safe from the attack of wild beasts, serpents, and crawling things. Vultures, like eagles, sense carcasses across the sea; for, flying higher, all the heights of the mountains, hidden by darkness below, are seen by them from on high. Flying, it notices a smelling carcass.

Isidore: it seeks out the eye in a carcass first. It follows armies, so as to be sated on the corpses of the dead. The vulture, once it has grown up and sees its mother old and too weak for flight, kills and destroys her.

No one, as Pliny says, has ever come upon the nests of vultures: for this reason there were those who falsely thought they flew in from another part of the world; but they nest, in fact, on the highest cliffs. But if by chance some other bird, even a stronger one, wishes to plunder its chicks, it exposes itself to danger: it strikes with its wings, wounds with its claws. It nourishes its chicks until they can fly, and this until winter, when the snow falls, marking as foolish those who are overly fond, for too long, of their offspring's infancy. Then the mother, driving them from the nest, forbids them to come near the places where they were born, jealous, namely, of food, since one pair of vultures occupies much territory. They do not hunt in places near the nest, but in the most remote places; and this a friendly, peace-loving nature has taught them, lest they stir up the hatred of neighboring communities against themselves. When it hunts something, it does not carry off the prey at once, but first tests its weight, then, having tested it, carries it.

Ambrose: some vultures are said to refuse mating, and, in a certain conjugal manner, to be unwilling to mix in the filth of nuptial union; and thus to conceive without any male seed, and to breed without union, and their offspring to live to a great age and a long life; so that the span of their life is drawn out to a hundred years, and the end of a short lifespan does not easily overtake them. Vultures are accustomed to announce the death of men by certain signs, as Ambrose says. For, taught by a certain sign and by a certain instinct, when opposing ranks of men prepare for war between themselves, vultures follow in a great throng ahead of time, and by this signify that a multitude of men is about to fall in the coming battle, destined to be prey for vultures. This indeed men can gather by a certain reasoning from the manner of their behavior.

The vulture hunts from midday until night, and from the time of sunrise until midday it rests. When it grows old, its beak lengthens above, so that its curve reaches the lower lip; and so it happens that, unable to open its beak, it dies of hunger and starvation.

For it does not know how to sharpen its beak on a rock like the eagle, nor how to shake off this trouble; and so it dies. This bird, if it does not see a man, gladly walks on the ground, and this because of the weight of its body, whence it is also called by some the 'ground-walker.' [Some have said that a dying vulture swallows its own brain, out of spite, namely so that it may not benefit human use, since it is said to be effective against paralysis.] The Experimentator: the vulture is slow; for a bird of such heavy flesh cannot have a swift flight. If it sees its chicks growing fat too quickly, it grieves. For this reason it wounds them with its beak on the feet, so as to keep them lean. When the vulture is flying, if it spots a carcass, it descends to eat it, and, because it turns indifferently toward every carcass, it does not avoid dangers and snares, and so falls more easily into the hands of hunters. The vulture fights with the gerfalcon and rushes upon it. But since the gerfalcon is agile, it yields to the rushing attack, and the heavy bird, unable to check itself, kills itself. It also fights with the parrot and with other birds. What it has left over of food, it stores in the nest, so as to feed itself and its chicks from it, since it does not easily obtain food.

[Zelencid] birds are birds, as Pliny says, whose aid the inhabitants of Mount Cadmus seek from God in their prayers, when their crops are devastated by locusts. They come, then, as is most certainly believed, at God's command, and destroy the locusts. Yet it is not known whence they come or whither they go, except when the people of that land need their aid. Here ends the book on birds.

In general, concerning sea monsters: the abides, the hahune, the great sea beasts, the barchora, the crocodile, the sea-stag, the caab (why this is discussed in the book on fish, see there), the cricos, the celethy, the chilon, the sea-dogs, the ceruleum, the sea-dragon, the dolphin, and another kind of dolphin in the Nile, the sea-horse, the Nile-horse, the river-horse near Damascus, the 'exposita' beast, the helcus, the seal, the fastaleon, the galalca, the sword-fish [gladius], the hippopotamus, the kylo, the kilion, the koki, the squid, the ludolacra, [the monk of the sea, the sea-unicorn, also called monoceros], the nereids, the nautilus, the orca, [the onos], the perna, the pester, the platanist, the octopus, the saw-fish [and another sea monster], the sirens, Scylla, the scinii, the tortoises of India, the tuna of the Black Sea, the testeum, the sea-cow, seal-calves, the zedrosi, the zedrach, the zethiron, the zyfius. Here end the chapters. Here begins the sixth book, on sea monsters. And it should be noted that sea monsters and fish are different from one another.

Given to the world for wonder at God: for in this they seem the more to be marveled at, because they rarely present themselves to the sight of men. Yet it can be said that in scarcely any other things beneath the heavens has God worked so marvelously, except human nature, in which the trace of the Trinity seems to appear. For what can seem more wondrous beneath the heavens than the monster of the whale, which in size is without doubt comparable to mountains and the vastest plains? The size of full-grown whales is not usually seen among us in the Mediterranean seas, but in the Ocean, or in those seas that are not usually navigable. But besides whales there are other sea monsters, which by their diversity or size proclaim God's wonders: for the land scarcely has a quadruped animal that the sea does not have in some way resembling it, but the sea also frequently shows likenesses of birds and serpents. Nor should it be believed, as some have supposed, that monsters of this kind were generated from adulterous minglings, but that God originally created all these among the primordial creatures. Some of these crawl, others run, others leap, others even fly; but all alike swim. Most of these have scales, others very tough skins, nearly all have the small fins and tails of fish, or make use of arm-like limbs. Some recover their breath in the air, like land creatures; but most, like fish, are generally given life by the scantness of breath in water.

The 'abides' is a sea animal, as Aristotle says, which is at first aquatic, and its nourishment is in salt water. Then this animal's form changes and becomes different; and then, leaving the water, it is nourished on land (then its name also changes, and it is called 'astois'). And this is remarkable, that as the very form of its body changes, so too its very nature and habits change, so that, having first lived in water, it is then fitted for its life on land; and the reason is that, according to the disposition of its limbs and the condition of its form, its very life in habits also changes.

The 'hahune' is a sea monster, as Aristotle says. This animal is more gluttonous than all other sea beasts. It lives on prey, and whatever it eats turns into the thickness of its body. Whence it happens that its belly is stretched beyond estimation and beyond the proper measure for the size of its body. When this animal fears some danger, it hides its head within itself in this way: it gathers its limbs into itself, like a hedgehog. For it is so thick and fat an animal that, drawing in its skin and flesh, it folds and hides the extremities of its body within itself, so that they do not appear. Yet it does not always do this without harm to itself: for it fears death so greatly that, when it sees some danger threatening it, it hides its head within its body, and when it senses that the danger has not relented and that the beast lying in ambush has not withdrawn, it never draws back out the head it has hidden within, but, when afflicted by hunger, devours its own flesh, choosing rather to be consumed in part than to be entirely consumed as prey to other beasts. This is a reproach to the wretched man who, when he sees danger threatening his body or soul, through the heaviness or wantonness of his fat body, does not take pains, by consuming his own flesh through fasting and abstinence from food and drink, to avoid the world, or the flesh, or the demons who lie in wait for his salvation. For we see quite certainly that, through bodily abstinence, men often escape the danger of death, as dropsy through abstinence from drink, fevers and many other illnesses through abstinence from food. This animal lacks a stomach, and so, when it has eaten, its belly is greatly swollen, and when the belly can be stretched no further, it casts the fish back out through its mouth, and this easily, because its mouth adjoins its belly directly, since it lacks a neck like the other sea animals: for no fish has a neck.

There are sea beasts, as Pliny says, in the eastern sea of such great size that they stir up whirlwinds and storms, turn the seas from the bottom, and roll the churned-up clouds together with the waves, so that it is related in the histories that Alexander the Great led his fleet against them, in a line facing them, exactly as against an army of enemies coming to meet him.

The 'barchora,' as Aristotle says, is a sea animal, and eats small fish. This animal's mouth is stronger than the mouth of any other animal, since if it takes a stone into its mouth, it breaks it. This animal sometimes comes out onto the shore and grazes on plants. And then it must return to the water and submerge itself, lest the skin of its back be dried by the sun and it be unable to bend as needed. This animal is caught by fishermen by means of small fish, which they sew alive onto a line and throw into the sea. The small fish, unable to escape but floating together, lie open to the bites of the aforesaid animal. But the animal itself, laboring to swallow one after another, is meanwhile caught, being occupied.

The whale is the largest of all fish, as Isidore says. The sea produces this fish to a size of four acres. They have narrow openings to the mouth, whence they swallow only small fish, which, devoured by the fragrant breath of their mouth and drawn in, are sent into their stomach. For in the throat it has a certain skin like a membrane, and this, pierced with many channels, does not allow anything of great bulk to enter its stomach.

But it has a large and gaping mouth, and by this the prophet Jonah is believed to have been swallowed: indeed, a dwelling sufficient for so great a guest. In its youth it has black teeth, which in old age become white. It has an eye on its forehead.

[the fish] sometimes belch up such quantities of swallowed water in a wave that they often sink the fleet of sailors with a stormy deluge, and also sink ships with their agitations and whirlings. And so, when a storm arises at sea, they raise themselves above the waves. Whales, as Pliny says, carry their young when they are sick and weak.

And, as the Experimentator says, if the young are small, they take them into their mouth. It does the same thing when it sees a storm approaching; and after the storm it spits them out again. When whale calves are hindered by lack of water from following their mother, the mother, having taken in water in her mouth, casts it out toward the young like a river, so as to free them where they are stuck on land. They long accompany the grown ones. They mature quickly, growing for ten years. Lacking gills, they breathe through a blowhole; and few of the sea creatures do this. Some whales are so large that they seem like islands or mountains.

Isidore: these sometimes lift sand on their backs, on which, when a storm presses, sailors, thinking they have found land, rejoice, so as to rest from the waves, and cast anchor, and, sails lowered, thinking they are resting on solid ground, light fires; and when the beast senses these, suddenly and unexpectedly stirred, it plunges down, dragging with it both ships and men into the deep.

The great Basil says the same as Isidore, that the whale raises up a great quantity of sand on its back. The same: when you see whales gathered in a dense mass as they return, you would think a most swift torrent was flowing out. I have watched this myself and marveled at God's wisdom. These monsters, in the Atlantic Sea, as Ambrose says, are of such infinite size that you would think them mountains, if you saw them rising up with their peaks reaching to the sky.

The hunting of whales is said to be as follows. The whale, after it exceeds three years of age, mates with the female whale. Without delay, in this very mating, it is deprived of the power of its genital member, so that it can no longer mate; but, entering the deep sea, it grows so large that it cannot be caught by any human art. Within three years of its age, then, it can be caught, and this, as the Book of Properties says, in this way: fishermen, having marked the place where the whale is, gather there with many ships and, having made a concert of pipes and flutes, lure it as it follows them: for it delights in sounds of this kind. And when the fishermen see it, dazed near the ships and stunned by the sound of the music, they secretly throw onto the whale's back an instrument prepared for this purpose, shaped like a rake with sharpened iron teeth, and secretly flee. Without delay, if the instrument has struck a certain spot of the wound, the whale makes for the bottom of the sea and, rubbing its back against the ground, violently drives the iron deeper into its wounds, until, having pierced through the fat, it penetrates the living flesh within, and thus the salt seawater, following the iron, enters the wound and kills the wounded creature. The dead whale then floats upon the sea, until the fishermen notice it; they approach the dead body with ropes and drag it to shore with great rejoicing, being certain of an abundance of such great supplies.

The crocodile is a quadruped animal, as James, Solinus, and Pliny say, which is equally at home on land and in the river. By day it rests more often on land, and this so motionlessly that, unless you know the beast's habit beforehand, you would think it dead, luring birds with its open mouth for the sake of food. But by night it stays in the water. It has eggs like a goose's, which it lays on land, namely where the overflowing river cannot reach. In brooding their young, the male and female take turns. This beast often, as James says, grows to twenty cubits. It is armored with the greatest firmness of hide, as if with a shield. It lacks a tongue. The gape of its mouth extends to its ears. It moves its upper jaw. Its bites are horrible and tenacious. For the row of its teeth is packed together like a comb. With the gaping of its mouth, then, it lures birds for the sake of food. With its eyes closed, it pretends to sleep, its mouth wide open. But the birds, descending as if to food, it kills and swallows. And in this it signifies usurers, who invite needy and poor merchants to borrow; or princes who invite their stewards to gain and afterward, having seized the occasion, strip them inhumanely. The crocodile is armed with the fierceness of its claws. In winter it takes no food.

It is dangerous not only to animals but also to men, and yet, as the Experimentator says, when it has killed a man, it mourns him. With its heart torn out, the crocodile still lives a while afterward, which is indeed contrary to every animal that has its life from the heart.

The Saracens eat its flesh. An ointment is made from its dung, with which old and wrinkled prostitutes anoint their faces, so that the loose skin is stretched smooth and they appear more beautiful. But the disguised color does not last long. For when sweat or foul water touches the counterfeit ointment, an artificial yellowness appears on the face, and a thicker pallor overtakes the smeared skin, and would that it were always so; but the blackness conceived from the ointment, to its own harm, flees at the washing of water, and at once the usual furrows of wrinkles return to the skin. In the river Nile, as Isidore says, and in the river of Caesarea in Palestine, crocodiles are found more than elsewhere. In a certain river of Palestine, as James writes, there are crocodile beasts; and for this reason: there were two noble brothers ruling in those same regions. And when one grieved to share dominion with his brother, he had a kind of crocodile brought into the river, so that the brother, whom he feared to kill openly, might, by his habit of bathing in the river, be secretly devoured by the monsters. Time passed meanwhile, and the envious brother, forgetful of the deed, sat on the riverbank, and without delay a monster unexpectedly crept up on the shore and, seizing him as he sat, tore him apart, and the wretch fell into the very snare he had set.

This beast, Pliny says, once sated with fish and always given to sleep on the shore with its mouth full of food, is invited to open its jaws by a small bird, called there the 'trochilos,' but in Italy the 'king of birds,' for the sake of feeding: it first scrapes the mouth, then the teeth and the jaws within, and finally, like a spear thrust in, gnaws at the invited bird. But what does so small a bird bring as food to so great a beast, except only that which lay open to prey and became plunder? This crocodile indeed signifies wicked princes, whose mouth is great traitors, who bring peace with their mouth and malice in their heart; the teeth are stewards who despoil the poor; the jaws are the counselors of secrets. To all these a wretched peasant sometimes comes, who seeks a stewardship and, giving and promising something of his own to all, obtains entry. Without delay, when he thinks himself satisfied, he is stripped not only of what he seized but of all he owns. There is a race of men naturally hostile and opposed to this beast, around the banks of the river Nile, called the Tentyrites, from the island where they dwell. This people is small in stature, but bold against these beasts. For they alone dare to swim in the river Nile, where crocodiles dwell, and leap onto their backs and ride them like horses. As the beasts gape, then, their heads thrown back, the riders, right and left, hold a club as if for a bridle at the moment of gaping, and drive their captives to land and, even by voice alone, terrified, force them to vomit up the bodies they have recently devoured. Some have believed this animal, like the bear, grows continually.

The sea-stag is, as the Book of Kyranides says, called the 'polmorarius.' It raises its horned head above the waves and invites birds to perch upon it, as if to rest or eat its flesh; but it suddenly seizes and devours the resting birds it has killed.

The 'caab' is a sea animal, as Aristotle says, having small feet in proportion to its body, which is indeed large. Its feet are like a cow's feet. It has, however, one long foot, which it uses in place of a hand for everything, since through it it takes its food and brings it to its mouth, and through it digs up whatever it wants. And this foot is created cartilaginous, lacking bone. When it swims in water, it breathes in it; but breathing, it draws water with its breath into its body, and when it is filled with water, returning to the air, it expels the water and thus breathes.

The 'cricos' is a sea animal, as Aristotle says. It has two clefts at the end of its foot, which make three toes with three claws. It has a small right foot, but a large left foot; and because of this, when it walks, it carries its whole body on the left foot. Its skin is shell-like, smooth, black, and in some parts red. Whatever it clings to, it clings to with a strong grip. When the sky is clear, this animal is free and will walk about; but when the winds stir, it clings to rocks and stays still, unmoving; and this seems quite remarkable, that in clear weather this animal has power over itself, but in stormy weather it is weakened and enfeebled in body. The cricos signifies dissolute young men of the world, who have a small or no right foot, that is, the love they ought to have toward God or their parents, since, gaping after shadowy loves, they entrap girls and, clinging to them stubbornly in spirit, whatever these girls may be, would rather offend God, their parents, and their neighbors than fail to carry out their deceit. The skin, that is, the covering of the deceit they call love, is shell-like, that is, smooth, brittle, dissolute, and black, that is, foul, drawing the redness of sin. It has two clefts in its foot, which make three toes individually, that is, two evil intentions in the love of deceiving and dishonoring, by which deceived girls are despoiled in three ways: namely of chastity, that is, of the honor of the soul, and of goods, if any can meanwhile be taken from them.

The 'celethi' is a sea animal, as Aristotle says, which, unlike other monsters of sea or land, generates eggs in its own womb; and when these have been brooded in the womb for the due time, worms come out of them. When it has borne these [or: conceived them], the offspring take on their perfect form and become, with incredible speed of time after birth, like their parents. This animal sleeps heavily, so that it can be caught by hand. It has, however, a large heart in proportion to its body, and yet is a very fearful creature.

The 'chilon' is a sea animal, as Aristotle says. This animal, unlike every other kind of animal, does not graze, but is fed only by its own moisture, which comes forth from it; this moisture is viscous and thick, and the animal takes it alone as its nourishment. Whence it happens that this animal is always fasting and yet strong in body. We see that in females fasting can last longer, so that they do not eat for many days, more than in males; and this is because of the moist and viscous superfluities, which abound more in females than in males.

Sea-dogs are sea beasts, as Pliny says, terrible in breath and hostility. For they are enemies to every living thing that falls before their blows. They have most robust gills, shaped like nails. [Its hide puts land dogs to flight.] They hunt through the sea, like dogs hunting wild game on land, in great numbers and packs of fish, except that they cannot bark, but instead of barking have a horrible breath. Pursuing, then, the schools of fish, they drive them into narrow places and there rage with cruel death upon the trapped fish. Fishermen, noting the places where the fish, hidden, lurk in flight, catch them, hemmed in, with nets. These beasts can be killed only with difficulty, with many tridents.

The 'ceruleum,' as Solinus says, is a sea monster, in name and in color, which the river Ganges produces. This beast has two arms, each no less than six cubits long; this monster is so strong in power that it seizes, with its bites and arms, the most monstrous beasts coming to the port, and drags them down into the depths.

The sea-dragon is a monster horrid in cruelty. Like a land dragon, it is extended in length, but lacks wings. It has a twisting tail, a head small in proportion to its body, but a horrible gaping mouth. It has scales and a tough skin. It is deadly to fish and other sea creatures; for the fish or animal it bites dies. If it ever wounds a man himself, he will not escape either. It has fins in place of wings, which it uses in swimming. It crosses great stretches of sea in a single burst, and this more by the strength of its power than by the oaring of its fins. The sea-dragon, once caught, as Pliny says, and cast onto the sand, digs a burrow for itself with its snout with wondrous agility. The ash of its bones heals toothache.

Dolphins too are in the sea, as James and Solinus say, beasts of manifold form. Nothing among beasts is swifter than these in the deep sea. And unless its mouth were beneath its snout, nearly in the middle of its belly, no fish could escape its speed. But nature has provided a delay in this, since, unless they turn over on their backs, they cannot seize or hold anything. The tenth month releases the birth. The males, however, devour the young when the females give birth; and the mothers hide with their offspring. For they love them most tenderly and lead them behind them for a long time, and the young follow their mother beneath the water. But when the young reach the strength of maturity, unless they are strong, even their mothers pursue them.

The young of dolphins, as Aristotle says, grow quickly and keep growing until ten years. These young, once ten months are complete, enter into mating and are made pregnant. Dolphins give birth only in summertime, never in winter. They nourish their young at the breast. Meanwhile they take the tender young into their jaws. Their mouths, however, are not in the place other beasts have them, but in their bellies, and, contrary to the nature of water creatures, they alone move their tongues. They have spiny dorsal fins, which bristle upright when the beasts grow angry; but when they are calm, they are covered by certain receptacles. They are said not to breathe in water, and to recover the vital air only in the upper air. Instead of a voice they have a moan, similar to a human one; and this because they have a lung, and a windpipe; and their tongue is not free, nor do their lips extend enough to articulate a voice. They have no ears, but an opening in place of ears. Dolphins have no trace of smell, and yet they smell most keenly. They sleep on the surface of the water, so that they can be heard snoring.
They live for very many years, indeed up to a hundred and forty years, and this the Experimentator says, judging from their severed tails.

They are said to hear more keenly with the north wind blowing; when the south wind blows, their hearing is blocked. They are soothed by music, delight in the songs of pipes, and, wherever they hear these, come in schools. Arion, a man skilled in the art of the lyre, when sailors at sea were preparing to kill him, obtained from them that he might first sing to the lyre. At his song, schools of dolphins gathered, and when he threw himself into the sea, one of them received him and carried him to shore. The dolphin alone, as Aristotle says, lacks gall.

Small dolphins are always together, as it were in schools, and have two large dolphins as guardians. And if one of them dies, the others carry it on their shoulders and guard it, until it is cast up by the sea's storm onto the shore. They guard their dead, lest it be eaten by other fish. For they love one another in a wondrous way. Whence, on Pliny's testimony, it is told that, when a dolphin was captured by the king of Caria, a huge multitude of the others gathered at the port, where the dolphin was held bound. As these lamented, as if pleading for mercy, the king ordered it released.

If anyone eats dolphin flesh, as the Experimentator says, and falls into the sea, if he is found by dolphins, they devour him at once. But if he has not eaten it, they lift him up on their snouts and drag him to land and defend him from other fish. How it happens that they can recognize in a man the eating of dolphin flesh, I cannot see, unless this too is a secret of nature, in which, as in many others, God is proclaimed wondrous. A multitude of other fish follows dolphins, which fishermen, knowing this, take advantage of, fishing where the dolphins have passed. Under the emperor Augustus, a boy in Campania first lured a dolphin with scraps of bread, then trusted himself to its care by hand; afterward, as the boy grew bolder, leaping onto the dolphin's back, he was carried by it. This at first seemed wondrous to onlookers, but at last, through such constant repetition of the spectacle, it grew so familiar that it ceased to be a marvel. But after many years, when the boy had died, the dolphin, seeing that he did not return to their usual ride, and waiting at the accustomed place, and he not coming, died of grief before the eyes of the common people. Maecenas, Fabianus, and Solinus record this in their writings. At the city of Hippo in Africa, near the sea, a dolphin was fed by the people of Hippo, and let itself be handled, and often carried those placed upon it. The proconsul of Africa, Flavianus, too, when he had anointed it with perfumes, was, by the novelty of the scent, lulled to sleep and was tossed about by the waves as if dead.

At the city of Iasus in Babylonia, a dolphin grew fond of a certain boy, and when, after their usual play together, it followed him too eagerly as he withdrew, it was carried onto the sand and stuck fast. Likewise, near the same city, when a stormier wave killed another boy, named Herianus, who similarly sat upon it in the sea, the dolphin carried him to land and, as if confessing its guilt, punished its penitence with death.

There is another kind of dolphin, in the river Nile, whose backs have serrated crests. These dolphins cunningly entice crocodiles to swim, and, swimming beneath the waves, deceive and kill them with treacherous cunning. For they cut and kill the crocodiles' tender bellies with their serrated crests. Crocodiles, moreover, see more dimly in the water, but most sharply on land.

The sea-horse is a large and very strong monster. This monster is the strongest against nearly all other sea monsters, and can do nothing outside the water, as Aristotle says; but as soon as it lacks the element of water, it will also lack life. It has partly the form of a horse, and this in its upper parts. Its hind part, however, ends in the nature of a fish. It lives on the flesh of other fish. In battle it is cruel; but it fears man and dreads doing battle against him.

The Nile-horse, as Michael says, is a huge and most fierce monster in the river Nile, dwelling in the river Nile. It has legs, feet, and claws like a crocodile's, but much larger. It is most greedy for human deaths. For when a ship comes upon it in the harbor, fixing one foot on the ground, it seizes the ship with the other from the front and most easily splits it apart, or sometimes tips it over and sinks it. Whence it happens that, in the places where it dwells, it destroys a monstrous multitude of men. But this good is granted to the world, that this beast is very rarely found. It could be caught by no instruments, except only an iron net made of chains, which is fashioned among the people of Damascus with wondrous skill for this purpose. Once caught, it is killed only with iron hammers. Its hide is said to be a cubit thick, and of such hardness that it cannot be pierced by any spear or armor.

The river-horse, as Aristotle says, is a monster in the eastern regions, of wondrous form. It can live equally on land and in water. It has a mane like a horse's; its feet are cloven, and it has hoof-soles like a cow's, and has a lofty face, and a tail like a pig's, and neighs like a horse. Its hide is very thick, and its internal organs are like a horse's. Its size, however, is like an ass's.

The 'exposita' beast is found in that part of the sea which, flowing past Judea, breaks against the town of Joppa. One of these beasts, as Pliny writes, was brought to Rome among the other wonders of the world, which Scaurus, the elder of the Romans, displayed most lavishly in his aedileship. In this beast were found the largest and longest teeth; its fat, too, measured five cubits.

By this, then, can rightly be signified not only kings, I would say, but the plunderers of the whole earth, who, with as it were the most monstrous teeth, gnaw and devour the poor peoples far and wide; and, gorged on their spoils, become food for him who, according to the prophet, devoured all the tenderness of Babylon.
The 'helcus' is a sea animal, as the Book of Properties says, called namely the 'seal': it has a hairy skin marked with white and black spots.

Of this animal, moreover, this marvelous thing is told: that, once dead and skinned, the hair on its pelt, by a certain natural instinct, takes on the state of the sea, whatever that state may be. For if the sea rises stormy into waves, the hair likewise rises up bristling. But if the sea is calm, the hair lies flat: thus the state of the sea is detected in this insensate and dead thing. Pliny: this creature gives birth on land, in the manner of beasts of burden. It never bears more than twins, and rears its young, suckling them at the breast, and does not lead them into the sea before twelve days. They are killed only with difficulty, unless the head is crushed. They have a bellow instead of a voice. No animal is weighed down by heavier sleep. Whence they say that its right fins, which it uses in the sea, have a sleep-inducing power, when placed under the head in sleep.
The seal [focha], the sea-ox, as the Experimentator says, is a most powerful animal in its kind. It does not easily change its place, but always stays where nature established it.

It is a spirited and irascible animal, yet not toward other creatures, but toward its own kind. Aristotle: for it always fights with its female, until it kills her; and, once killed, it casts her from the place and brings in another. Nor does it cease bringing in females this way, until it happens either that it dies its own natural death, or is overcome and killed by its own female. Its rival offspring live by plunder because of this destructiveness.
The seal, as the Book of Kyranides says, has hands like a man's and a face like a calf's.

The 'fastaleon' is a sea monster, as Aristotle says, but has nothing monstrous in its habits; for while all the sea animals are hostile to one another and devour one another, the fastaleon alone is free of this cruelty. And the reason is this: the fastaleon does not eat flesh at all, but lives on plants and the other foods on which other animals live, except flesh, which it naturally abhors.

The 'galalca' is a sea monster, as Aristotle says, which has a habit beyond the custom of all other animals. This animal, when it senses that its young are alive in its belly, draws them out from its womb, not waiting for the due time of giving birth. But when it has drawn out the young, if it finds them mature enough for life, it leaves them outside. But if not, it places them back into the womb and returns them to itself, to brood them further.

The 'gamanez' is a monster, as Aristotle says, which dwells in river waters. The male of this monster has the greatest concern for its young: the female, however, neglects them and withdraws and wanders through the waters. Then the male, moved by natural devotion, stays beside his young, until they grow and have the power to flee hostile fish. Meanwhile the father builds around the young a certain structure, by which they are protected in the time of their youth. And so that enemies may be frightened off, he cries out loudly; and he is watchful over them at all times. And if it happens at that time that he by chance falls into a net, he tears the nets apart with his very strong teeth and escapes more by boldness, in that time of watchfulness, than by strength, since he is roused to unaccustomed vigor by desire for his young.
The sword-fish is a sea monster, as Pliny and Isidore say, taking its name from the fact itself, in that it has a beak as sharp as a sword, with which it pierces and sinks ships.

The hippopotamus, as Pliny says, likewise dwells in the river Nile. It is born on land. It is equally capable in water and on land. It is, moreover, generally larger than elephants. It has an upturned snout, cloven hooves, a twisted tail, teeth that itch and curve like a boar's tusks; but its back and neighing are like a horse's. By night it grazes on crops, to which it goes as if walking backward, so that, its tracks deceiving, no ambush is prepared for its return. When this beast is distended with too great a fullness, it most eagerly seeks out freshly cut reeds or the points of thorns, and rolls among them for a long time, until a certain vein in its leg is wounded by their cuts, so that it is relieved by the loss of blood. It gladly receives wounds in its feet more than in the other parts of its body. It carefully tends the wound, until it is healed into a scar. They are found especially in the regions of India.
On the back it is impenetrable, except when wet with water. Spears are made from its hide. Scaurus brought this beast, together with five crocodiles, to the Roman games, as Pliny says.

The 'koki' is a sea animal, as Aristotle says. It stays on land as well as in the sea. It cannot breathe in water. It sleeps near the sea, on land, and there is the greater part of its dwelling. There it gives birth to its young; it bears two or three. In birth, the afterbirth comes out with the young, and its labor proceeds in every way like a human's. On the twelfth day after birth, the young follow their mother to the sea, and this many times in a day, and for this reason: so that the young may grow accustomed to the sea waters. This animal has breasts, from which it suckles its young. It has a cartilaginous body like the cuttlefish, and its bones are less robust than they should be, whence it happens that, its legs weakened, it can sometimes scarcely walk or support itself on its feet. Its walking, moreover, comes more from vigor of spirit and lightness of body than from strength. It can be killed only with difficulty, except with hammers. Its voice is like a bull's voice, and this especially when it is being killed. The female koki's nature is like a woman's nature, and in her belly is found a member shaped for mating. It has very sharp teeth, a small tail like a stag's, kidneys like a cow's. In its belly there is no blood; and the reason is this: two veins, which branch out beneath the kidneys, do not reach as far as the belly; and so this animal's belly lacks blood. The rest of its bodily organs, however, have blood, which never freezes. This animal has four feet, and they have joints, five toes on each foot, and the shape of the foot is the shape of a fish's tail.

The 'kylion' is a sea animal quite marvelous, as Aristotle says, in which nature is believed either to have erred, or to have changed the order of its own usual practice. But far be it that nature should be believed to have erred: for it has arranged all things well, and created for each thing what is right and just. In truth, though it has placed the liver on the right and the spleen on the left in all land creatures, both small and great, in the kylion, nevertheless, it placed the spleen on the right and the liver on the left.

The 'karabo' is a monster of the great sea, called the 'gabari.' As Aristotle says, monsters of this kind fight most fiercely among themselves like rams, and the opposing sides fortify themselves with a multitude of allies. Whence they have often been seen going about like flocks, waging war upon one another. Wars occur among living creatures for four reasons. The first cause is natural pride, which rules in every creature. The second cause for which they fight is food; the third, mating; the fourth, offspring. For the sake of offspring different kinds of animals fight among themselves, as the hen with the kite, and geese with the crow. The karabo is defiled in its food; it lives on dung and mud, and so is a heavy animal, and when its belly is split open, much mud is found in it. The karabo has a broad tail, whence it happens that, when it fights, it turns itself easily.

The squid is a sea monster, as Aldhelm says, so marvelous that you would surely believe nature had played a game in this, having created a creature to be preferred to almost all other sea beasts: for this animal, with a scaly skin, searches the depths of the sea with schools of fish. But when it tires of the sea's waters, it raises itself up with feathered wings, which nature gave it for this purpose, and rises into the sky with the birds. Yet, once raised into the air, this monster cannot withstand the blast of the winds, but after a little while, when buffeted by opposing winds, it is forced to return to the water and slips back into the depths.

The 'ludolacra' is a sea animal of very marvelous nature and form, as Aristotle says; it has four wings arranged thus: two on its face and two on its back, with which it strives, with wondrous speed, from place to place, wherever its will drives it.

'Monks of the sea' are sea monsters named from the fact itself. Animals of this kind dwell in the British Sea. They have the form of a fish in their lower parts, but in their upper parts partly a human appearance; they have a head shaped like the head of a recently tonsured monk: a shaved and white crown above, and a black circle around the head, over the place of the ears, in the shape of the circle of hair left on the head of a monk or cleric, spread out to a great breadth. This monster gladly lures men walking along the seashore and plays before them and approaches with leaps. And if it sees a man delighting in its play, it rejoices, and plays all the more on the surface of the water. But if it sees a man drawn near in wonder, it too approaches, and, if given the opportunity, seizes the man and drags him into the depths, and thus is sated on his flesh. Its face is not entirely like a man's, since it has a nose like a fish's, and a mouth continuous with the nose.

div.head: 34. De monoceros quod est unicornus maris

cit.quote: The 'monoceros,' or sea-unicorn, is a sea monster, as the Book of Properties says, which can take its name from the fact itself: for 'monos' means 'one,' and 'ceros' 'horn.' Whence the monoceros is called a beast of a single horn (just as the scriptures speak of the fierce land beast, the unicorn), and, horrid to see, it has a very great horn on its forehead, with which it can indeed pierce and destroy ships in its path and destroy a multitude of men. But in this the mercy of the Creator has provided for mankind, since, this animal being created slow in proportion to its cruelty, ships, once the monster is sighted, can flee.

Nereids likewise are sea beasts, as Pliny says. These are shaggy over their whole body with bristling hair, and have some form resembling a human. When one of these, imitating the human condition, must die, its moaning and lamentation is heard from afar by those who dwell nearby, and its sadness confesses that the necessity of death is bitter for mortal creatures.

By this we would say a wretched soul is signified, which bore a feigned semblance of reason together with man, but, bristling with the shagginess of its shameful deeds, is compelled by demons to depart at the end of its life. And there is no doubt that, sad and fearful, it cries out and laments, but in vain, destined for everlasting fires.

The nautilus is a sea monster, as Pliny says, a marvel outstanding among sea creatures. It rises to the surface of the sea and there, releasing all the water within it through a tube, lightens itself of its ballast so that it can swim easily. Afterward, folding back its two front arms, it stretches between them a membrane of wondrous thinness, which, this membrane acting as a sail, carries it toward the open air, and, rowing with its remaining arms, it steers itself with its tail in the middle, as with a rudder. But if any troubling fear arises, it takes in water and sinks itself.

The 'onos' is a sea-ass, as the Book of Kyranides says, eight feet in length; some call it the 'pultum.' Burn its flesh in a new pot, and, mixing the powder with its blood kept for this purpose, anoint frenzied patients in the bath and they are healed; the same is effective for those with stones, so much so that they urinate out the stone without injury.

The orca is a sea monster, as Pliny says, whose form can be described in no other way than as an immense mass of flesh. These beasts pursue whales, that is, cetaceans, with grievous hatred. With their teeth they savagely break into the secret parts of whales, or their calves, or even nursing or pregnant female whales, and tear them apart with their bite. The whales, however, unable to bend to fight back, sluggish in resistance, and burdened by their own weight, with weak fins, know only one remedy: to flee into the deep sea and defend themselves with the whole ocean. The orcas, on the other hand, persistent in their malice, strive to meet the fleeing whales and block their path, and to slaughter the unwary in narrow straits, driving them into shallows, dashing them against rocks.

By whales, indeed, we believe innocent and simple souls are signified, equally inexperienced in good and evil, who, when they have reached the company of the good and begun to lead a separate and, as it were, secluded life away from the world, and to grow heavy with the offspring of good works conceived from the fear of God, at once the orca of that infernal, dread abyss, the devil, that monster, sets out to pursue them with various assaults of temptation, and now strives to press them into the straits of poverty, now to drive them into the shallows of lust, now to dash them against the rocky danger, which is hardness of heart. But these, inexperienced in misery, not knowing how to resist through prayers and fasting or through confession with frequent cleansing of the heart, broken by despair, flee to the great and fearsome sea, and, making void their first pledge of chastity betrothed to Christ, become all the more freely prey to that ancient wickedness's most cruel monster.

The 'perna' is a sea animal, a monstrous and large animal, as Aldhelm says, and is born, in the manner of oysters, among shells, which shells have a sky-blue color.
