This monster is clothed, among these very shells, with a most noble fleece, exceedingly tawny and reddish, from which precious garments are made for the adornment and decoration of men and women. Head-veils are made from these, which serve the adornment and luxury of women. Thus the fleece of this animal is put to a double use, and serves the purposes of both sexes.

The 'pistris' is a huge sea beast, as Pliny says, in that part of the ocean facing Gaul. It is of such great height that, raising itself above the waves, it presents the likeness of an enormous column, and, taller than the sails of ships, belching forth a kind of deluge, terrifies those tossed on the waves.

This beast, I would truly say most fittingly of the most blessed Augustine, who, rightly a most strong and lofty column in the house of God, towers above other expositors and, belching forth in overflowing abundance the streams of his teachings, has watered the whole Church, and refuted the wave-tossed heretics with insistent and frequent disputations.

The 'platanistae' are sea beasts, on Pliny's testimony, which are born in the river Ganges of India. They have a dolphin's snout and tail. They are sixteen cubits in length. Allied with these are beasts called 'statiae,' with two arms each. These are said to have such great strength that they attack, with their bites, elephants coming to drink and tear off their trunks.

The octopus is a fish, as Pliny says, which uses its feet and arms like hands. It has such power in its arms that it sometimes seizes by force a sailor standing carelessly on his ship and drags him into the sea and is sated on his flesh: for it gladly feeds on flesh. In the sea near Venice they are most numerous. It has a two-pronged tail and a sharp tube on its back, by which it crosses the sea, directing it now to the right, now to the left, as it wishes. It swims obliquely, head-first, its head being very hard. Lying on their backs, they cling to rocks so that they cannot be torn away. Alone among fish they come out onto dry land. Octopuses mate in winter, give birth in spring. They lay eggs in such abundance that they cannot be contained even in the skull of a slain man; these are carried off by wanderers and hatched. Octopuses mate with the head turned toward land. Octopuses sit upon their eggs and, brooding, form a kind of chamber with their arms as if latticed. The octopus cannot be torn from the rocks; but if something foul-smelling is brought near it, it recoils at once from the smell. They feed on the flesh of shellfish, which they crush in their embrace. Thus, by the shells and husks lying about, their lair is discovered. By this trick they also deceive shellfish: shellfish lack sight and sense, except that they sense food and flee dangers. And so, while the shellfish open themselves, the octopuses lie in wait.
Having taken a rock, they make a shade for themselves against fish, as Pliny, Ambrose, and the great Basil say, to which [fish] cling fast
[a fragmentary listing:] fish, octopus, shellfish - Pliny, Ambrose, the great Basil

The great saw-fish is a sea beast, as Isidore says, huge in body, having very broad fins and monstrous wings. This beast, when it sees a ship sailing on the open sea, raises its wings above the water and strives to sail against the ship's course. And when it has attempted this for thirty or even forty stadia and has not prevailed, at last, unable to bear the effort, it gives out, and, folding its fins, draws them back to itself. The waves then carry it back, exhausted, to its original place in the depths of the sea.

There is also another monster called the 'serra' [saw], as Isidore and Pliny say. It takes its name from the fact itself, in that it has a serrated crest. This beast, swimming secretly beneath ships, cuts them from below, so that, as water enters, it may sink the men through treacherous cunning and be sated on their corpses.

Sirens are vocal creatures, as the Physiologus says, which from the head to the navel have the form of a tall woman, with a horrifying face and very long, scaly hair on the head. They appear, moreover, with their young, whom they carry in their arms: for they suckle their young at the breasts, which they have large on their chest. Sailors, when they see sirens, are greatly afraid, and then throw an empty jug to them, so that, while they play with the jug, the ship may meanwhile pass by.
[a fragmentary listing, attributed to Aldhelm:] eagle, siren, fish-beasts

Isidore describes these sirens as not truly beasts, but certain prostitutes, who led passing travelers to destitution. They had wings and claws, because love flies and wounds. They dwell in rivers, that is, in the flow of lust. Most, however - indeed nearly all philosophers, and even some holy expositors - hold a view contrary to Isidore, [saying that we believe the sirens are, in truth, sea monsters] but irrational ones: their song, indeed, is to be believed not articulate, so as to be distinguished into syllables and words, but rather indistinct in articulation, like the song of birds.

Scylla is a sea monster, like the sirens. This monster indeed truly dwells, as the philosopher Aldhelm says, in that sea which lies between Italy and Sicily. It is hostile to sailors and to every man, and delights in their blood and flesh. It has a head and chest shaped like a maiden's, like the sirens; and it has gaping jaws, an open mouth with horrible teeth, a beast-like belly, and a tail like a dolphin's.
They are of wondrous strength and are not easily overcome in the water; but on land they are less strong and nearly unwarlike.
Aldhelm: they have voices somewhat musical, and these beasts too take wondrous delight in song.

'Scinnocs' too are most numerous around the Nile, as Isidore says; they are beasts similar to crocodiles, but of much smaller and narrower form. Drinks poisoned with their flesh lose their venomous power. These beasts, moreover, foresee storms, and, blocking the burrows where the wind enters, open doors on the other side. Their bushy tail serves them as a covering.

The Indian Sea has tortoises, from whose shells men make roomy dwellings for themselves, and sail between the islands of the Red Sea in these as boats, as Pliny says; these tortoises are caught in wondrous ways, but especially when, floating upright at the surface of the open sea at midday, they lie on their whole back through the calm waters, and the pleasure of breathing freely so deceives them, forgetful of themselves, that, their shell dried by the sun's heat, they cannot dive, and float unwillingly, ready for the hands of hunters. They say too that, having gone out to feed at night and eagerly filled themselves, they grow weary, and, once they return in the morning, fall asleep at the surface of the water. Then three swimmers approach lightly together: by two of them it is turned onto its back, and by the third a noose is cast around it as it lies helpless, and thus it is dragged to land by several men together. This monster has no teeth, but sharp edges to its beak, and the upper part is closed by the lower like a small box. Its mouth is of such hardness that it can even crush stones. They mate in the manner of beasts of burden. The females, however, do not easily or lightly submit to mating, until the male, having turned her over, places a stick in her mouth. Having come onto land, they lay eggs like goose eggs, up to a hundred in number, and, having buried them, brood them at night with their chest, outside the water. They rear their young over the span of a year. Some say that these creatures brood their eggs by gazing at them with their eyes alone; and this is quite marvelous, but the matter is hidden from us.
The tuna is a sea monster, as Solinus says. It has a tail two cubits wide. It breeds in the sea and never elsewhere. It comes onto land to graze.

They enter on the right side, and leave on the left; and this is thought to happen because they see better with the right eye, though dim-sighted in both. When the north wind blows, they more readily leave the shores. Pliny: they follow ships out of curiosity to see the sails moved by the wind; and they are so affected by this stupor that they are not even moved by fear when a trident is cast at them. In wintertime they hide in the deep pools. They grow so fat that their life is longest, up to three years. In Ethiopia there are tuna-beasts, dark in color, which suckle their young with twin breasts on the chest, as Solinus says.

The tuna breeds in the Black Sea, as Solinus says. For it breeds nowhere else, and this because of the sweeter waters there. It enters rivers on its right side, but leaves on the left. This is believed to be because it sees more sharply with its right eyes than with its left.
The tuna [tunnus] is a sea fish. Dissolve its eyes or lung in a glass vial with seawater, and whatever you write with this will glow at night like a flame.

The 'testeum' is a sea creature, which can take its name from the fact itself: for it has a shell-like skin, Aristotle says. It is born in the Arabian Sea. This animal grows sick from the fact that the heat within its body cannot find a breathing-vent through the pores, because the thickness and hardness of its skin prevents this; when it grows sick, I say, it seeks fresh waters and drinks from them for some time, and by the change to fresh water its skin is made fine, and it sweats out through the narrow pores and recovers. The healed animal, then, returns to the salt waters and returns to its original condition. It is evident, moreover, that there is fresh water within the sea; and this can be proven thus: take a wax vessel and seal it on every side, and cast it, empty, into the sea for the space of a day and a night, and afterward you will find that same vessel full of fresh water. This animal is largest in the Red Sea.

The sea-tortoise is a huge and exceedingly strong monster. It is shaped like a land tortoise, but exceeds its size immensely: for it is eight cubits in length and four in width. It has a triangular shield, like an ordinary shield, but much larger, indeed five cubits. It has long legs, large claws, and toes on its feet larger than a lion's. It is wondrously vigorous in strength and boldness, since it does not fear to attack three men. Its strength is foiled if you can turn it onto its back on the ground. For it rises with difficulty once turned onto its back, and this because of the breadth of the shield by which so great a beast is enclosed on its back: it is covered by this shield against missiles; the shield, moreover, is triangular.

The sea-cow, as Aristotle says, is a large, strong monster, and irascible toward injuries. This animal does not lay eggs, but bears live young; at most it bears two, but more often one. It grows to its full size over ten years. The mother feeds it for a long time and leads it with her wherever she goes, because she loves it tenderly. And it should be noted that the mother is pregnant for ten months. This animal lives a hundred and thirty years; and this has been proven from their severed tails.

Seal-calves are fish, as Pliny says; these breathe and sleep on land. This animal is shaggy with fur. It gives birth on land, producing fertile offspring in the manner of beasts of burden; with a single mounting, like dogs; it never bears more than twins, and rears its young at the breast. It does not lead them into the sea before the twelfth day, gradually accustoming them from then on to the vast waters. They are killed only with difficulty, unless the head is crushed. They have a bellow instead of a voice, whence they take the name of 'calf.' No animal is weighed down by heavier sleep. For this reason they say its right fins have a sleep-inducing power, and entice sleep when placed beneath the head. With the fins they use in the sea, they also crawl on land in place of feet. Their skins too, even removed from the body, are said to retain a sense of the sea's condition.

Sea-beasts likewise, on Pliny's testimony, inhabit Arabia. The bones of these beasts are so large that doors for houses and palaces, and beams or other necessities of construction, are conveniently cut from them. For they are found to be forty cubits in length.
These beasts signify, in the Church, the saints, by whose bones, that is, virtues, the holy universal Church is adorned, strengthened, and built up.

The 'zydrach' is a sea monster, as the Book of Properties says, of very marvelous form, and which presents malice in its shape, and yet is harmless. It has a head shaped like a horse's, though of smaller form; its body, however, is in every way most similar to a dragon's. It has a long tail, in proportion to its body, slender and twisting like a snake's. Its whole body is variously colored. In place of wings it has fins like a fish's, and it moves from place to place like swimming creatures.

The 'zytiron' is a sea monster, which the common people call the 'soldier of the sea,' as the Book of Properties says, and it is huge and most strong. It is said to have a disposition of this kind: in its front part it presents, as it were, the form of an armed soldier, and a head as if helmeted with a casque of wrinkled, tough, and exceedingly firm skin. From its neck hangs a long, broad, and great shield, hollow within, so that the monster can be protected in it against the blows of its attackers, after the manner of a fighter. Certain very strong veins and sinews extend from its neck and from its vertebrae into its shoulder, and by these the aforesaid shield hangs from its shoulder-blade. This shield, moreover, is triangular in form, of such hardness and firmness that it can scarcely ever be pierced by a spear. It has exceedingly strong arms, and in place of a hand something like a cloven hand, with which it strikes so powerfully that a man would try in vain to withstand its blows without the greatest peril. Whence it happens that it can be caught only with the greatest difficulty by man. And if it is caught, it can be killed only with difficulty, and only with hammers. This animal's kind seems to imitate the discord of the human race, in that it stirs up wars among itself; and they cause such great disturbance of the sea in fighting that a kind of storm seems to arise in the place of their contest. These monsters are found in the British Sea.

The 'zyfius,' as the great Basil says in the book of the Hexameron, is exceedingly fearsome. It is a sea beast which, exceeding human estimation, is so great that provident nature, mother of all things, is believed to have played a game in creating this monster. For it resembles neither the form of other fish, nor sea monsters, nor land beasts, nor the birds of the sky, but has an appearance and form in which this beast alone can glory, so as to render a worthy spectacle to those who see it, and from this, praise of every kind to the Creator, through those who have seen it. If you saw its head, it would seem altogether monstrous; if the abyss of its mouth, you would flee as from the maw of death; if its eyes, you would shudder; if the rest of its body, you would confess that you had never seen anything like it among created things.
[a fragmentary closing note:] of this whale-beast

In general, concerning fish: the eel, the alphoraz, the astaraz, herring, the albirez, the sea-ram, the golden fleece, the abarenon, the sturgeon [accipender], the amius, the aforus, the australis, the sea-spider, the flounder [bothe], the burbot [borbothe], the fish of Babylon, the whale [cete], the crab, the claucius, congers, shellfish, the carpera, the capitatus [and sea gudgeons], sea-ravens, snails, the day-fish [dies piscis], dolphin-fish, the dentrix, the sea-urchin, the pike [ezox], the ericius, the exochius [and the sea exochius], the eracliodes [and the fundula], the conger, the granus, the flying fish [irundo maris], the kalaas, the kylok, the squid, the sea-locust, the sea-hare [and the Indian sea-hare], the pike [lucius], lampreys, the mullet [mugilus], pearl-oysters, the octopus [multipes], the murex, the sea-mouse, the mule-fish [mulus], the red mullet [mullus], the milago, oysters, purple-fish, the pinna, the stickleback [pungitivus], scallops, the sea-pig, the sea-peacock, the turbot [rumbus], the frogfish [rana maris], salmon, the sturgeon [sturio], sponges, centipede-fish [scolopendre], the starfish, the catfish [sylurus], the solaris, the ray [scuatina], the salpa, the cuttlefish, the sea-scorpion, the sparcus, the scaurus, the torpedo-fish, the trebius, the trout [truithe], the trimallus, sea-foxes, the vergiliales [and the uranoscopus], sea-vipers, the venth fish. Here end the chapters. Here begins the seventh book, on fish of the sea or of rivers.

No fish, as Aristotle says, has a neck, a male member, testicles, or breasts. From these, however, we except the dolphin, the whale, and the other sea monsters, and this because they generate their like. For they have breasts, at which they suckle their young, though not above, but near the joints; and these breasts do not project, but are like two channels, from which milk comes out, and the young follow their mothers. This indeed can be seen with the eyes, as a proof of its truth, wherever sea monsters give birth. Every fish, and every soft-shelled animal, sleeps little. This cannot be judged, however, by the closing of eyelids, since they have no eyelids, but by the fact that they are caught by hand and struck with an iron trident while asleep; and it should be noted that they do not move while sleeping, except in the tail, and this but little.

Augustine seems to hold that fish have souls. For he says they have memory. He says, indeed, that there is a spring in the region of Bulla full of fish, which, as men walk above, swim in schools, coming and going, and stand still when the men stand, waiting for something to be thrown to them, because they have grown accustomed to this.

A certain Gloss says that fish depart by a certain instinct, when the country in which they were accustomed to dwell is about to be devastated. Nor is this a wonder, since, if the men to whom God gave fish for use are not present, the effect will justly cease when the cause ceases.

[fish have] a sense of hearing; whence silence is enjoined on fishermen. A fish will never be seen mating with fish of another kind, but they keep to nature's order, both in sex and in kind. Let unhappy man blush, who transgresses even the bounds of nature and, more irrational than all beasts, treats right and wrong alike, and, a shameless violator, holds his own sex and order in contempt. All the fish of the sea eat one another, except a certain animal which Aristotle calls the fastaleon. And the reason for this is that this animal does not eat flesh at all. No sea animal eats its own young, except once they are fully grown and have taken on a form like their parents'. The flesh of fish dwelling near the shore is firmer and healthier; but the flesh of those dwelling in the depths is moister and less wholesome. All fish that have stones are fat. And every school of fish has a leader. Every fish living on prey does not swim socially, like the pike and its like. Every fish that has a covering has gills on its head. No fish has ever been seen to mate with a fish of another kind.

bibl.author: Consolatio Philosophie Boethii Boethius Anicius Manlius Severinus

cit.quote: Let man, then, most unhappy of all brute creatures, blush, who oversteps the bounds set by the Creator, and, an enemy of nature, mates against nature's laws with unclean beasts. Whence, in the book of Boethius's Consolation, not without reason, figured Wisdom is seen to lament, in that part where her torn garment bore the painted image of man.

[concerning fish] that a great, indeed the greater, part of the eggs which fish lay perishes through many chance occasions; nor is this a wonder, since if they all survived, they would multiply excessively. All fish that swim broadly - like the flounder and scallops - are fattened by a south wind blowing. But fish that are stretched out long - like the pike - are certainly fattened by a north wind blowing. Male fish have channels full of seed, so that the seed often seems to flow out externally. Small fish breed where there is little water, and this especially around the roots of willows or other trees.

There are certain fish, as Pliny says, that are naturally so light that, unless their heads made up the greatest portion of their body, they could not sink in the water. Female fish are larger than males. Fish are caught better before sunrise, because then the fish's sight is most easily deceived. They see equally well by night as by day. They die from a taste of oil.

The greater part of the eggs perishes in fish, when the female lays while wandering about. And this applies against those religious who, curiously wandering about, lose the offspring of their good works. Unhappy, then, are those whose profession or office does not require this, who by wandering outside often lose their virtue of spirit.

Certain fish are generated of themselves, without any mating, and some from the slime of other fish, and some simply from the earth, and some from putrefaction and corruption, which appears to float on the water's surface like oil. Before the time of birth or mating, male and female fish wander and swim together in schools; but at the time of mating and giving birth, each pairs off with its own mate. Certain fish, when they breed, grow weak, and for this reason are generally caught more at this time than at another. Dryness harms fish; and the greater part of fish are fattened in rainy weather, since rain benefits them as it does the plants of the earth. Whence they seem to swim up and play in the falling rain. Every fish that naturally has a stone in its head is more harmed in winter than one that does not; and the reason is this, that the stone in the brain chills the brain. For this reason, as cold approaches, fish of this kind seek the depths. Every sea monster, and every kind of fish that walks, breathes accordingly. The flesh of fish that gladly swim in deep water is moister and less wholesome to eat. In the depths and bottom of the sea there is a multitude of fish and many kinds, which scarcely or never come within sight of men. The growth of all the eggs of sea fish is quick and swift.

Some fish, as Pliny says, have multiple gills, others simple, others double. These expel through the mouth the water they have taken in. Old age is shown by the hardness of the scales, which are not alike in all. If wood is rubbed with the lung of a sea fish, it will appear to burn, as does oil. Whence it is also customary to make oil from the lungs of certain sea fish.

As the Experimentator says, some fish do not touch the vessel used to catch them unless it is new. For some have a sense of touch and some do not, as Aristotle says, and these are caught more quickly. Female fish are longer than males and have firmer flesh. The flesh of fish is firmer on the back and front than in the rest of the body. Eggs are found only in fish that mate. The greater part breed on riverbanks, if these are available to them, and this because there is no wind in that place, and it is warm, having in itself many fresh waters. Marsh fish become pregnant mostly after five months; and after one year all fish generally breed. [Fish always strive to return to the place of their birth, however far they have gone downstream or up; and for this reason they often fall into danger.] Some fish become pregnant with a south wind, some with a north wind.

There is a method of fishing, as the Experimentator says, in which a ditch is dug beside a river, so that the river's water enters the ditch, and wood is placed there, and then fish come from the river and hide there for the sake of calm; and this especially in winter.

The great Basil says: see how each kind of fish holds to its own allotted region, and none encroaches on another's boundaries, but each is content with its own dwelling. Certainly no surveyor has distributed dwellings to them, nor marked them off with an enclosure of walls, nor set boundaries to be observed; but usefulness has been granted to all in common. But we are not like this: for we boldly exceed the boundaries of our elders and trespass on our neighbors' groves, and join house to house and field to field.

The eel is a fish, as Jerome says, similar to a serpent, whence it takes its name from 'anguis' [snake]. The more firmly you grip it, the more quickly it slips away. It is skinned only with difficulty. They say it is born from the slime of other fish.

Pliny says of these that there is no male or female sex in eels, nor indeed are eggs found in them. They also frequently rub themselves against rocks; these scrapings come to life, and there is no other way they are produced.
Eels killed in wine, as Isidore says, if drunk from, cause a distaste for wine in those who drink it.

They are stirred by the sound of thunder. They delight in clear river waters. They are predatory toward certain lesser fish, especially, however, when found in spawning season. Eels, as Aristotle and Pliny say, live many years, and can survive six days without water, and this with the north wind blowing; but when the south wind blows, they live fewer days without water. In winter they cannot live in shallow water, nor do they easily tolerate murky waters. And so, at the setting of the Pleiades, since the water is then disturbed by opposing winds, namely around the time of the Pleiades, they are caught most. They feed at night. Dead fish do not float in sunlight, except when, putrefied, they dissolve in the water.

As the Experimentator says, eel fat heals the ears. It has a most stubborn death, so that, even skinned, it still lives. It requires more cooking than other fish; otherwise its food is harmful. Roasted at the fire it is more suitable, because its harmful quality evaporates. In the river Ganges there are eels thirty cubits long.

The 'alphoraz' is a fish, as Aristotle says. It is not born, but is created from heat and moisture, and this in a muddy place, which sometimes lacks water. It grows, then, from the putrefaction of that mud, when the pool has no water, and is formed in the shape of a little worm, and afterward, when the water rises, that worm grows into a fish. It lasts, however, only a short time and quickly dissolves. Sailors have reported that if this fish dissolves until only its head and eyes remain of it, it will be reborn from these and last a long time again.

The 'astaraz' is a fish, as Aristotle says, which is generated in autumn and at the start of spring. For fish of this kind are seen to bubble up in the foam of rain near the banks, when it has thickened, just as maggot-worms of the beetle bubble up in horse dung in summertime. Others, however, have said that it is generated from the slime of the earth and nourished by the slime of rain. When the weather is cold, they cannot easily be caught, since they hide in whirlpools and hollows; but if the day is clear, they climb up onto the banks and seek warmth. The brightness of the sun, however, is quite contrary and harmful to them, and so they seek the shade of trees, under which they are protected from the sun. But when the year is rainy and warm, an abundance of this kind is found.

Herring are sea fish, as the Book of Properties says, in the western sea that lies between Great Britain and Germany. The season in which herring are usually caught is said to be the best time for almost every kind of sea fish. For each kind of sea fish has almost its own season, and is not good at another time. The best catch of herring is around the month of August or around September. Its season lasts until December, but this rarely, because of the shortness of the time. This fish is quite small, but when freshly caught, it provides a more delicate food. Salted, it can keep sound longer than other fish for human use. [There is a sweetness in its head, which is scarcely ever spoiled by the bitterness of salt.] This fish, almost alone among all fish, lives on water alone and can live only in water, and dies as soon as it touches the clear air, and there is no delay between contact with the air and its death. Its eyes shine in the sea at night like a light, but their power dies with the fish itself. Wherever they see a light over the water in the sea, they gather in schools, and by this trick are lured into nets. At the stated seasons they are led, as if ready for the taking, into the use of men, by divine gift. In wintertime, however, they hide in the secret depths of the sea until the due season, and this around Germany. [The best herring are in the region of Scotland, the worst toward Germany.]

The 'albirez' is a sea fish, as Aristotle says, of the kind of fish called 'rugana.' This fish, the albirez, has a very thick skin, so firm and hard that soldiers use this very skin for helmets. For it has a naturally implanted power, so that it can withstand strong blows. Soldiers, then, are accustomed to shape this skin like a cap and place it beneath iron helmets, and if some blow of a sword or other weapon strikes it, it causes no pain.

The sea-ram is a sea fish, as Pliny says, which, like a bandit, lurks hidden in the shadow of large ships standing at anchor, and, if the pleasure of swimming entices anyone, waits, and, its head raised above the water, watches unseen, until it drowns the swimmers.

The sea also nourishes a golden fleece, as Ambrose attests, and the shores produce wool of that recalled metallic hue. No one, however skilled in art, who dyes fleeces with various dyes, has yet been able to imitate its color.

It is believed, from the kind of fleece, that this was the fleece for which countless thousands of men, cities burned, and homelands laid waste, in the regions of the Trojans, as the most ancient History of the Greeks relates.

The 'abarenon' is a fecund fish, as Aristotle says, with many eggs. It does not have the nature of other fish, in that it lays its conceived eggs by movement in contact with the sea; this fish, then, about to lay, by a certain natural instinct, rubs its belly against the sand, which is rough to the touch and salty to the taste, and thus lays its conceived eggs and, after the due time, brings forth its young.
The sturgeon is a fish, as Pliny says, most noble among the ancients. This fish alone, contrary to the custom of all other fish, has scales over its whole body turned toward its mouth.

This fish signifies jurists and lawyer-clerics, who turn all the protection of the ecclesiastical body, whose members are the faithful, generally into a contest of words, taking no care to notice that there is no end to words. And while most of them do not trouble to keep the scruple of conscience and God before their eyes, they strive to allege falsehood as truth, or truth wrapped in the falsehood of quibbles: Woe to the misery of such men, and woe again, and a third time! [The 'woes' are the miseries of guilt and of punishment.]

The 'amius' is a sea fish. It is a rock-dwelling fish, as Isidore says, that is, it bears a stone within it. This fish is quite beautiful, for on each side it has, as it were, little bars of a continuous crimson color. In the rest of its body, moreover, it is entirely varied with different and pleasing colors, like a silk cloth.

The 'haniger' is a sea fish nearly similar in color to the amius, but different in form. For it holds a shape nearly like an eel's, but is shorter. It has, in place of a mouth, a long cartilaginous snout, entirely red like a stork's, with long streaks of varied colors on its side. Its flesh provides a more delicate food for the wealthy.
The 'aforus' is a tiny fish, as Isidore says, which, because of its smallness, cannot be caught with a hook.

Blessed, then, and truly blessed is humble smallness, and small humility, which the ingrained malice of shameless gluttony cannot deceive, nor can the enemy of the human race entangle it in his snares. For humility knows no fall.
The 'australis' is a fish, as Isidore says, either because it takes the wave of the waters into its mouth, or because this fish is born at the time when the Pleiades begin to set.
The 'aranea' [weever] is a kind of sea fish, as Isidore says, which, having stings in its ear, strikes those who come near it with its ear.

And it signifies those who, having an itching of the ears to hear evil reports about their neighbors, often lending their ears to these, strike themselves with a grievous wound. And so it is said: Hedge your ears about with thorns.

Flounders are river fish, which swim only by the breadth of their body. For they are very thin fish and quite broad; they have fins around the circumference of their broad body. When hunted by fishermen, seeking the bottom of the water, it stirs up the water above itself, so that it cannot be seen, especially since, its body flattened, clinging to the ground, it closely resembles the earth on its back, having red spots on its back. It breeds in certain river waters, but not in all; in ponds, however, scarcely and very rarely. Flounders, as Aristotle says, become pregnant with a south wind.

Burbots are river fish, so commonly called in Gaul. They seem to have a similarity to the eel: for they are slippery; and they are skinned just as eels are. They have a black skin, and their flesh is sweet to eat, especially the liver, which is the best and most delicate of all fish. It has a large head in proportion to its body, a wide and very broad mouth. When it exceeds twelve years of age, it grows to a large body; and then its name changes, and it is called the 'solaris,' of which more is to be said below. Burbots are called 'lotte' in French, or 'quappe' in German, according to the different languages.

There are fish which Theophrastus describes as marvelous around Babylon, namely in places where rivers, falling, have caverns holding water. From these places, or caverns, monstrous fish come out to feed, moving on their little fins and by the frequent motion of their tail. They have heads like a sea-frog's, the rest of their body like that of gudgeons; gills like other fish.

[a near-duplicate of the whale chapter from Book 6, repeated here in the source with only minor wording variants:] The whale is the largest of all fish, as Isidore says. The sea produces this fish to a size of four acres. They have narrow openings to the mouth, whence they swallow only small fish, which, devoured by the fragrant breath of their mouth and drawn in, are sent into their stomach. For in the throat it has a certain skin like a membrane, and this, pierced with many channels, does not allow anything of great bulk to enter its stomach.
But it has a large and gaping mouth, and by this the prophet Jonah is believed to have been swallowed: indeed, a dwelling sufficient for so great a guest.

In its youth it has black teeth, which in old age become white. It has an eye on its forehead. These fish sometimes belch up such quantities of swallowed water in a wave that they often sink the fleet of sailors with a stormy deluge, and also sink ships with their agitations and whirlings. And so, when a storm arises at sea, they raise themselves above the waves. Whales, as Pliny says, carry their young when they are sick and weak.

And, as the Experimentator says, if the young are small, they take them into their mouth. It does the same thing when it sees a storm approaching; and after the storm it spits them out again. When whale calves are hindered by lack of water from following their mother, the mother, having taken in water in her mouth, casts it out toward the young like a river, so as to free them where they are stuck on land.

They long accompany the grown ones, mature quickly, growing for ten years. Lacking gills, they breathe through a blowhole; and few of the sea creatures do this. Some whales are so large that they seem like islands or mountains. Isidore: these sometimes lift sand on their backs, on which, when a storm presses, sailors, thinking they have found land, rejoice, so as to rest from the waves, and cast anchor, and, sails lowered, thinking they are resting on solid ground, light fires; and when the beast senses these, suddenly and unexpectedly stirred, it plunges down, dragging with it both ships and men into the deep.

The great Basil says the same as Isidore, that the whale raises up a great quantity of sand on its back. The same: when you see whales gathered in a dense mass as they return, you would think a most swift torrent was flowing out. I have watched this myself and marveled at God's wisdom.
[these] monsters, in the Atlantic Sea, as Ambrose says, are of such infinite size that you would think them mountains, if you saw them rising up with their peaks reaching to the sky.

The hunting of whales is said to be as follows. The whale, after it exceeds three years of age, mates with the female whale. Without delay, in this very mating, it is deprived of the power of its genital member, so that it can no longer mate; but, entering the deep sea, it grows so large that it cannot be caught by any human art. Within three years of its age, then, it can be caught, and this, as the Book of Properties says, in this way: fishermen, having marked the place where the whale is, gather there with many ships and, having made a concert of pipes and flutes, lure it as it follows them: for it delights in sounds of this kind. And when the fishermen see it, dazed near the ships and stunned by the sound of the music, they secretly throw onto the whale's back an instrument prepared for this purpose, shaped like a rake with sharpened iron teeth, and secretly flee. Without delay, if the instrument has struck a certain spot of the wound, the whale makes for the bottom of the sea and, rubbing its back against the ground, violently drives the iron deeper into its wounds, until, having pierced through the fat, it penetrates the living flesh within, and thus the salt seawater, following the iron, enters the wound and kills the wounded creature. The dead whale then floats upon the sea. When the fishermen notice this, they approach the dead body with ropes and drag it to shore with great rejoicing, being certain of an abundance of such great supplies.
Some reckon crabs among the fish, as the Book of Properties says.

They have feet and arms, eight in number, and pincers in place of hands, with which they mostly crawl. It moves backward, and never, as Aldhelm says, knows how to walk forward. But understand that the crab does this only in fear and flight. For, fearing or fleeing, its tail drawn in, moving backward, it strives to hide itself in the mud, or in a cave, and then it occupies a very small space. Naturally, however, when it is without fear, it walks forward, and moves ahead with its arms extended. When they grow old, two stones of white color, mixed with redness, are found in their heads. Some say that these little stones are of such power that, given in a drink, they heal the pangs of the heart.

And indeed this is quite believable, since, as Galen says in the Anatomy, the heart is greatly strengthened by hard, stony substances, such as crab-stones, pearls, sapphires, hyacinth-stones, and the like. The crab changes color when cooked, for it turns red; yet while alive it is suffused with a greenish or blackish hue.

Ambrose relates something marvelous about crabs; for he says that the crab naturally delights in the flesh of the oyster, but just as it craves this feast, so too, in seizing it, it avoids danger to itself. For the hunting of the oyster is dangerous to it: for the oyster has certain hard and strong cases, in which it is enclosed; and the crab, indeed, if it rashly attacked these very cases, could well be crushed and killed by the closing of the shells. To guard against this, the crab devises a trap by a cunning trick. And so, since every kind of animal is soothed by delight, the crab watches to see whether that oyster, in places remote from every wind, opens its double shell to the sun's rays and unlocks the fastenings of its shells, so as to take its pleasure in the free air in turn. And then, secretly inserting a pebble, it prevents the oyster's closing, and thus, finding the fastenings open, safely thrusts itself into the shells and feeds on the inner organs.

There are many kinds of crabs, as Aristotle says. One of these is in Judea and is called the 'soldier,' because it is a most swift animal, and when it is split open, no flesh or superfluity is found in it; and the reason is that it does not feed on food: for if it used food, it would have superfluities.

In the western sea, as Solinus says, there are crabs that seize men and drown them; they have backs as hard as a crocodile's. Crabs hide for five months in winter. In springtime, like a snake, they shed their old age. In winter crabs seek sunny shores, in summer they retreat in schools to shady places. They are harmed in winter, and grow fat in autumn and spring, but more so at the full moon. Crabs have a long life. The female's first leg is doubled, in the sea single. The right claw is nearly always larger than the other. Males have two spines between the belly and the tail, which females lack, since they have their eggs in the belly. They are effective as remedies against the bites of serpents. While the sun passes through the sign of Cancer, they fight among themselves with their little horns. When the male wishes to mate with his female, he mounts her from the back; but she, sensing the male's motion behind her wishing to mate, leans over on her side and turns toward him, and thus the mating is completed. A crab, given milk to drink, can live many days without water.
The 'clautius,' which is called the 'sheat-fish' [glanis], as Pliny says, bites baited hooks from behind and does not swallow them, but ravages them by stripping the bait.

This fish signifies those who, though they flee the open vice of fornication, lest they be caught by the telltale sign of resulting offspring, are nevertheless most shamelessly defiled by the very circumstances surrounding fornication, such as kisses, illicit conversation, and most wicked caresses.
Sea congers are fish of a long form, like the moray eel, as Pliny says; but they have a much larger body. Their flesh is most sweet to eat. They become pregnant when a strong wind blows.

By these fish are signified those who, possessing patience of hope, are also mature in virtue. They become a delightful food for Christ, doing his Father's will. And so, when the wind of the Holy Spirit blows, which rushed violently upon the apostles, they become pregnant, out of fear of God, with the fruit of good works.

Shellfish in the sea are keeled like ships, as Pliny says, with a curved stern and a beaked prow. In this is housed the 'nauplius,' which is a tiny creature similar to the cuttlefish, kept only for the sake of playful company. And this is remarkable, that the shellfish opens its valves for this and permits the play, well aware that it will not be deceived by any trick from the guest let inside.

The carp, or 'carpera,' as the Book of Properties says, is said to take its name from the fact itself: for it can be called 'carpera' as if 'she who bears by plucking' [carpens parit]. It is a fish with, as it were, golden and broad scales, of ponds or rivers. This fish, when, nature dictating, she senses her eggs in her belly ready to be laid, approaches the male fish and, with her mouth, signals with a light nudge that he should help her to lay. Then the male, understanding her movement, discharges milt in place of seed. The female, receiving this discharge with her mouth, at once lays eggs destined for future offspring. For the female cannot lay eggs unless she has first received seed in her mouth. This seed she then receives seems to help not only the laying, but also the conceiving and forming of the eggs from which offspring is hoped for in the following year. Sometimes, in the first year of its birth, a black little worm grows near the ear of the young carp, and this most often after August; and it dies of this wasting; the remedy for it is fresh, running water. Carp offspring thrive in shallow waters. It is the common belief that if small ditches, nine or ten cubits long, are newly or recently made, and a pair of carp - that is, a male and a female - are placed in each ditch, their offspring will be produced there. And it should be noted that carp should not be placed in these ditches except just before spawning. But after they have spawned, they are removed. The offspring, however, once strengthened over three or four months, are taken out and placed back in the ditches, where they grow along with the mature ones. The carp's brain is said to grow and shrink according to the waxing and waning of the moon; and though this is true in every fish, it is more so in the carp, just as some have said of the wolf and the dog among quadrupeds. The carp has many tricks to escape being caught in nets. For when it has entered a net, it goes around seeking an opening; and if it does not find one, it strives to leap over the net into the open air, so as to fall outside. If it cannot do this, it seeks an escape beneath the net; and, foiled in this trick too, it holds a plant in its mouth at the bottom of the water, so that the approaching net is deflected. Nor, failing even in this, does it stop there: coming with force from above, it fixes its head firmly in the mud below, so that the net, passing over its tail, fails to catch it. There are, then, five ways in which this cunning fish tries to escape.

It signifies the fivefold cunning of malicious men, by which they indeed seek escapes, lest they be caught in the nets of the divine word. Their explanation, indeed, we leave for the learned reader to unravel.

The 'capito' [gudgeon or bullhead] is a fish, as the Book of Properties says, quite small, rarely growing so large as half a foot. And this indeed takes its name from the fact itself: for it has a large head, nearly the size of the rest of its body. This fish, dwelling in rivers, gladly hides beneath stones and among rocks. It has a wide mouth and a round head.
[these] fish signify those who, with a perfect and excellent heart, hearing (and receiving with an eager desire) the word of God, hold fast to it and bring forth fruit with patience.

'Capitones' of the sea are likewise a fish, nearly three cubits long. They have large heads, but very small and narrow tails, in this signifying those who, once they have received the Spirit, are consumed by the flesh. The flesh of these fish is quite edible, but very indigestible; whence it also causes fevers. They have red spots, and very sharp fins on their back.
Sea-ravens are named from their voice, as Isidore says: for they grunt in the chest, and are caught, betrayed by their own voice.

They signify certain impatient men, who, though they conceal their impatience outwardly in their actions, nevertheless murmur inwardly in their hearts, and through this are often caught in the devil's snares.

The 'capa' is a sea animal of the snail kind. Its shell is nearly a cubit long, somewhat oblong; its outer surface, filed and polished, is transparent like a pearl, and drinking vessels are made from it. The animal of these shells has, on one side, a reddish wool-like substance, which, applied to the ear, draws out and removes matter from sores. In Greece an abundance of these shells is found.

Snails, both aquatic and terrestrial, coming out of their dwellings, extend two horns and, drawing them in, move them to help themselves. They lack eyes, but nature has restored to them limbs in place of the sight they lack. And so, with their horns, they feel out their path ahead and are not deceived, wherever they wish to go. Snails and oysters and every kind of them grow and shrink according to the moon. For, as physicians say, when the moon is waxing, it increases moisture; but when it is waning, moisture diminishes.

The 'day-fish' [dies] is a sea fish, as Aristotle says, which, after reaching maturity, lives only for a single day. And it is therefore called 'day,' in which its full rising and its sudden setting appear. And in this nature is quite marvelous, [which forces a creature created only for life to leave life so suddenly. Here the diligence of the Creator is noted:] for this animal has two wings and two feet, and lacks blood.
But to what purpose are feet or wings given for so brief a service? Truly, a sufficient reason is that God may be proclaimed wondrous in his creatures.

There is another kind of dolphin, but of smaller form, as Isidore says, than dolphin-beasts, which, appearing at the surface of the waters as a storm approaches, play there. By this sign sailors know beforehand that a storm is coming. They are so vigorous in the agility of their bodies that they even leap over ships.
The 'dentrix,' or sea-bream, as Isidore says, takes its name from the fact itself, in that it has hard teeth, large and numerous, with which it ravages oysters or harmless fish.

These fish signify those who, ruling with cruelty, have many fierce ministers, by whose service they ravage the strongholds of the poor as if they were oysters, and those who lead an innocent life by their own labor.

div.head: 33. De echino notatur mirabile quid de pisce isto

cit.quote: The 'echinus' [remora] is a fish, as Isidore and James say, half a foot long, of such power that, by clinging, it holds a ship fast.

Let the winds rush, the storms rage, the waves rise: the ship is held not so much by this little fish restraining it as by clinging to it. This has indeed seemed incredible to many; but there is such great authority in this, and such great agreement, that no one is left any room to doubt it. First in this agreement is the blessed Ambrose; second, James, bishop of Acre; third, Aristotle; fourth, the blessed Isidore; fifth, the great Basil too. We have set down the authorities for this matter in careful order, since it is indeed a marvel, and marvelous beyond estimation, that a half-foot-long little fish, by no force but by clinging alone, holds fast a two-hundred-foot ship with its cargo within, so that it cannot be moved even a fraction.

Where are the foolish and stupid men - I do not say philosophers, but unclean heretics - who reject the honest faith of the Christians because they find its articles beyond nature and human power? Tell me, most wicked serpent, which would seem more incredible: that a virgin should conceive and give birth without male seed, or that a half-foot-long little fish should be able to hold, by clinging alone, so great a mass as a ship, immobile against the strongest blasts of the winds? I believe reason will tell you that a virgin could more plausibly give birth than that the remora fish could hold a ship fast.

For it is certain, on the blessed Ambrose's testimony, that mares, cats, partridges, and vultures, and also many other animals, conceive and bear offspring without any mingling of seed and without the mating of males, from breath and scent alone, and indeed both are marvels as regards nature and human power.

But the Virgin's giving birth surpasses this with elegance: for Christ is truly almighty God, who could be born in this way because he willed to be born in this way. But there is no other explanation for the astonishing wonder of the remora fish, except that God is proclaimed wondrous in his creatures, and by this the foolishness of heretics is confounded, since they are unwilling to believe anything beyond the common course of nature.

Among the kind of crabs, as Pliny says, are sea urchins, which similarly have spines in place of feet. They are born white around the crown. Their eggs are bitter, five in number. Their mouth is in the middle of the body, glassy in color, nearly in the shape of a scorpion. In place of teeth they have heavy spines in the mouth. Many men use this fish to harm their enemies. This fish cannot be eaten, however, because, eaten, it brings death, dissolving a man from the state of his constitution. This fish has wings beneath its belly, which resemble feet.

As the blessed Ambrose and Pliny and the great Basil write: the sea urchin is often a sign of a coming storm or of calm, and in these matters it is usually a messenger to sailors. Finally, when it senses a coming storm, it seizes a heavy pebble and carries it as ballast and drags it like an anchor, so as not to be tossed about by the waves. And so it does not free itself by its own strength, but steadies and guides itself by another's weight. Seeing this, sailors take note, and, following the example of the sea urchin, steady their ships by casting anchors.

This is against those who are unwilling to be subject to another's guidance and risk peril under the governance of their own will. Christ, on the contrary, said: I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father.

The 'ezoz' is the largest fish of the Danube, which the Swabians call 'husem.' This fish is smooth over its whole body and has nothing rough in its body or its habits, but is a most gentle and fearful animal, since it cannot even defend itself from the smallest little fish. Whence it is chased off in flight by the stickleback. The sturgeon fish most gladly rubs itself against this fish in play, and the ezoz, as soon as it senses this, flees to the hiding places it is accustomed to dig for its safety along the shores; but sometimes in vain, because the insistent sturgeon drives it out of hiding. The ezoz flees, then, and the sturgeon follows, and since both are large and cannot even hide in the deepest waters, moving about and stirring up the water ahead of them, they are often caught together by fishermen. This fish, once caught, is given the strongest wine or milk to drink, and this because, once made drunk with much wine, it can live for many days, and this so that it may be carried to distant lands for food. It drinks, before becoming drunk, four sextarii of wine. It is so large that it can scarcely be pulled on a cart by three or four horses. Its flesh is most sweet, very similar in taste and appearance to pork. The ezoz has a single intestine, few and small bones, and these more cartilaginous than solid. In the head, however, it has many solid bones. And in this are noted those who are great in the affection of their heart, with a purpose of virtue, but lack the effect of action.

The 'ericius' [sea-hedgehog] is a sea fish, having its head and mouth below, as Aristotle says, and the passage for its waste above; and this is contrary to other animals. It uses spines in place of feet. Its front parts are separate, its hind parts continuous. It is a horror to the other fish of the sea, because it is bristling with spines; whence it does not easily become prey to any fish.
Its flesh is intensely red, similar to the color of vermilion, as Pliny says.
The 'ezochius' is a fish found in Arcadia, as Pliny says. It comes out onto dry land because of sleep, and cannot live without sleep.

By these fish can be signified those who, fleeing the sea of the world, scorn its abundance of delights and, like Elijah fleeing Jezebel's luxury and the tumult of the world's vanity, rest, as if in sleep, in the secret place of intimate contemplation, in the dry land of poverty as if in a desert.

There is also another 'ezochius,' a sea fish, commonly called the 'esui.' This grows to nearly seventy cubits in length, and fourteen feet in height or breadth. In its lower jaw there are two bones like beams; in these are forty-two very large teeth; in the upper jaw, however, there are no teeth, but in the bones of the upper jaw there are certain hollows, matching the number of teeth, into which the teeth of the lower jaw, when it closes upon the upper, fit like the closing of little boxes. On its forehead, beyond the ordinary provision of nature, it has an eye four feet wide. Its mouth is so wide open that it can close, with the gape of its mouth, a boat holding twelve men. It has such a multitude of intestines that they exceed, in bulk, the entrails of forty oxen. It is a creature remarkable for its bulk. It is caught in this way: it comes out of the sea into fresh waters. When fishermen notice it, they pursue it with crossbows and bows. And when, fleeing, it comes into waters so narrow that it cannot go further up nor turn back because of the persistence of its pursuers, it draws in water like the whirlpool of Scylla and unexpectedly floods its attackers with such an inundation that it drowns most of them, engulfed as if by waves. When this attempt fails, it tries another. It puts its tail to its head and strikes those nearby so powerfully that scarcely anyone it touches escapes without mortal danger. But after this, if it is caught and overcome, when it has received a fatal wound, it lets out a cry of such horrible wailing that it seems as if one of the demons had cried out, above every sound of beasts or men.

There are fish around Heraclea in Pontus, as Theophrastus writes. This kind pursues the farthest waters of rivers, digging through the lands that lie between the rivers. And this is remarkable, that it undertakes such great labor to change from one water to another. It also makes caverns for itself in the earth, so as to live there even with the alternating rivers.

The 'fundula' is a small river fish. It takes its name from the fact itself: for it always seeks the bottom [fundum]. Whence it is rarely or never seen at the surface of the water. It provides sweet food, but quite indigestible. It is varied in color, longer than its thickness would suggest.

The conger is indeed a large and strong fish. This fish, as Pliny says, has such enmity with the moray eel and other fish that they cut off each other's tails. It is so strong, moreover, that it tears apart the octopus with the strength of its teeth.

The gudgeon is a small little fish, as the Book of Properties says, and though small, yet where it has sandy waters with small stones for nourishment, it provides indeed a more suitable food. Some say that this little fish, in the hot days of summer, has certain small white worms inside its belly, and is spoiled by their foulness. This little fish has a nearly round shape, with small scales similar to silver.

The 'granus' is a sea fish. As the philosopher says, contrary to the nature of all animals, it has a single eye on the very top of its head: with this eye always watching above, it guards against ambushes.

By this fish are signified those whose eyes are always toward the Lord, so that, in the mirror of divine contemplation, they see more clearly whatever adversity, whatever danger, may occur, so that they have a single eye of intention toward God, by which they are rendered watchful both before and behind.

The flying fish [sea-swallow] is a fish, as Pliny says, indeed most similar to the flying bird, the swallow. This fish, besides the squid and another sea fish, has a habit contrary to all other fish: for it stays in the water like a fish, and yet, having wings, rises to the realms of the upper air.

These fish most fittingly signify those who, though sometimes involved by duty in worldly business, nevertheless, when the time and place allow them to return to themselves and remember heavenly sweetness, are eagerly raised up to the contemplation of spiritual things.

The 'kalaoz' is a sea fish, as Aristotle says, of manifold appearance, found in the regions of the East. This fish has a nature contrary to all other kinds of fish, in that the rain of heaven, which is usually a remedy for life and an aid to fattening for other fish, is given to this fish as its ruin, since, if there is much rain, it is blinded in its eyes, and consequently, unable to seek food, dies of hunger and starvation.

The 'kylos' is a sea fish, as Aristotle says, and clings to rocks. The shell in which it hides is like the shell of a vessel, and is very rough. The formation of its body is like the formation of flesh. This kind of fish senses whatever approaches it. It attaches itself to rocks with its hind feet, but with its front feet, which it uses almost as hands, it preys upon whatever fish pass by it. But if something passes that it believes it cannot overcome, it swells up and contracts itself and clings more firmly to the rock to which it is attached. Its mouth-opening is in the middle of its body. There are two kinds in this class of fish: one is small in body and is eaten, and for this reason men hunt it in winter and eat it in summer: for, salted, they keep for a long time. The other kind is large and marked with white; but it is so pestilential that if anyone touches it, its condition dissolves and worsens in the time of heat.

Squid are sea fish, as Pliny says. They are caught at five cubits. Their life rarely exceeds two years. They fly out of the water, launching themselves like an arrow. The squid has two feet, with which it brings food to its mouth. There is a certain kind of them that is most fierce, so much so that, about to fight, they form ranks and steady themselves as if fortifying themselves. They have their head between their feet and their belly. Near Mauritania, in the ocean, not far from the river Lixus, so great a multitude of squid fly up out of the water that they sometimes even sink ships.

The Book of Kyranides says: it is a fish without scales, which violently raises itself above the waves in time of storm, and it happens that it is seized by a strong wind and thrown onto mountains, and is dashed to pieces. It has a forked tongue like a horse's tail.

The sea-locust is a fish, as Pliny writes, four cubits long. They are protected by a fragile shell, in that kind which lacks blood. They hide for five months. In springtime they shed their old age, in the manner of snakes. Sea-locusts float about like crawling creatures. If no fear presses, they swim on a straight course, their horns - which are naturally shaped round - extended to the sides; but when raised up in fear, they proceed sideways, obliquely. They fight one another with their horns. This is the only one of these animals that, unless boiled alive in hot water, has no firmness in its flesh, which remains fluid. They live in rocky places. They are harmed in winter, and grow fat in autumn and spring, more so at the full moon. It fears the octopus so much that a sea-locust placed near one dies.

The sea-hare is most venomous, as Pliny says. In the Indian Sea it is so harmful that its mere touch immediately causes vomiting and dissolution of the stomach; but in our sea it is shapeless, hare-colored, similar in size to the land hare, with coarser fur. This fish, and others, has an adversary in the stingray, most pestilent, which pierces them as if with the iron of poison. Fish fleeing it, so as not to be struck by it, fix themselves among the roots of trees. But if anyone is bitten by this same fish, its ash is a remedy.

div.head: 49. De lepore maris illi alio genere

cit.quote: There is also another fish besides the aforesaid sea-hare, as Pliny and Isidore say, which, taking its name from the fact itself, has a head like a land hare's; in the rest of its body it is a fish.

The pike is a fish, as the Book of Properties says, also called the 'water-wolf.' If it has fresh river waters and sufficient food for life, it grows, over the course of time, to a very great length. Its food is fish and whatever crawls in the manner of frogs. It devours a fish nearly its own size in this way. For once it has overcome its prey, it first devours the head with its mouth; once this is digested, it gradually approaches what follows, until it has consumed the whole. It refuses to spare even its own kind, either from natural cruelty or because it is jealous and impatient of sharing food and plunder. It even pursues its own offspring, once they have taken the form of a fish. It carries in its brain a stone like crystal, but this only once it has lived a long span of years.

Pikes become pregnant, as Aristotle says, when the north wind blows; likewise fish that grow long in shape. The pike has less cunning in deep water. The pregnant female pike swims as far upstream as she can from the place where she is accustomed to dwell, and there lays her eggs, so that her young are not an obstacle to her prey; and this because of her natural cruelty, since she is jealous and impatient of sharing food and plunder. Others have said that she goes upstream for sweeter water, since water is always sweeter the closer it is to its spring. It is a fish having sharp scales and sharp fins. If the water-wolf seizes it by the head, it quickly swallows it; but if by the tail end, it can in no way do so, because the rough scales stiffen in the opposite direction.

They say moray eels are only of the female sex, and conceive from a serpent, and for this reason come out onto dry land to mate. Whence they are called out by fishermen as if by a serpent's hiss. Ambrose says that the serpent, coming to mate with the moray eel, first vomits out all its venom. In this is signified how great the kindness of a husband ought to be toward his wife, since indeed they have come together for this, that the two should be one flesh. They are killed with difficulty by clubs and hammers; struck on the head, they can scarcely be killed, but struck on the tail, they are killed at once.

The moray eel lays eggs every month, whereas other fish lay at a set time. Its eggs grow very quickly. Aristotle calls the male that breeds the 'myrus,' and does not say that these conceive from a serpent; he also says there is a difference between them, in that the females are varied and shapeless; the myrus is of a single color and robust; it has teeth projecting outside its mouth. Pliny: in northern Gaul, all moray eels have seven spots on the right jaw, which shine, resembling the shape of the constellation of the North, though only with a certain vigor, but these die out together with the creature's life. They say that a taste of vinegar drives them into a rage.

Aristotle: it is dangerous to eat moray eels, unless they are first very well and very long cooked in wine and carefully seasoned with aromatic spices, and especially pepper: for they are attested to abound in a venomous humor, and for this reason do not easily yield to cooking.

Moray eels, as Pliny says, gladly keep themselves among reeds and branches, so that, if by chance enclosed, they may escape the net by manifold twisting. Moray eels have a venomous bite, but the bite is healed by the ash of their own head.

The mullet, as Pliny says, is a naturally careless fish. For its foolishness is mocked, since, in fear, with its head hidden, it believes its whole body is hidden and safe. The mullet is a most swift fish in river waters. The mullet has enmity with the pike only in winter, but in summer they are at peace; and this is believed to be because in winter food is scarce, over which they fight, but in summer it is abundant, and for this reason they are at peace in summer.

By this fish are signified those who, saying they guard their heart, which is the head of the soul, believe their body safe amid worldly dangers, not heeding that many, presuming on their own strength, have perished miserably, like Samson and David and many other great men.

Pearls, as Solinus says, are made in this way: the shellfish in which they are found approach the shore at nighttime and conceive pearls from the dew of heaven; if what they receive is pure, the gems are white; if turbid, they either languish pale or are clouded with a reddish hue. Indeed, as often as they receive the seed of the morning air, the pearl becomes clearer; as often as the evening air, it becomes darker; and the more dew it has drawn in, the greater the size of the stone becomes. If, the shells being open, a sudden flash of lightning shines, they are struck with untimely fear and, closing in sudden dread, either miscarry or produce small gems. Such feeling do these shellfish have, that they fear their offspring being stained. When the sun sends forth its burning and blazing orb, lest the stones be darkened by too much heat, the shellfish sink into the depths. Two are never found in one shell: whence they are called by many 'uniones' [single pearls]. When hail falls, the stones in the shells turn yellow. They fear the ambushes of fishermen, and for this reason hide more often among the rocks. They swim in schools, and the one among them that is more experienced leads the school, and when she is caught, the others scatter. The pearl is soft in the water, but once removed, hardens into stone. They are not found larger than half an ounce. They are said to wax and wane with the moon, while they live within the shell.

There is great difference in their whiteness. The highest praise of color is when they shine white like alum. There are some that are found in oblong shells shaped accordingly. It is the glory of women to hang two or three of these pearl gems from their fingers or ears. Placed in vinegar, they dissolve quickly. Whence let us recall that saying of Pliny: there were two very great single pearls which Cleopatra, the last of the queens of Egypt, possessed, given to her by the kings of the East. When, then, her husband Antony was daily gorged with exquisite feasts, the harlot queen, with an insolent expression, began to mock his feasts, declaring that she would consume, in a single dinner, six hundred thousand sesterces - that is, a hundred times what he consumed in his feasts. At this the king marveled. Wagers, then, having been made, the table set, Cleopatra sat, and, a vessel with vinegar alone being brought before her, took one pearl from her ears. And when she had thrown it into the vinegar, the queen swallowed it, dissolved into decay. At once she reached her hand toward the other, but Plancus, the judge of the royal wager, unwilling to let that singular work of nature perish, quickly declared Antony defeated. This stone, crushed and prepared in the proper measure, is effective against weakness of the stomach. It has, they say, also the power of concord, and confers health of mind and body - of mind, indeed, because it makes the one who wears it chaste.

The 'megaris' fish is a sea fish, as the Book of Properties says. It is two hand-spans long. It is held cheap in the regions where it is caught, but, brought to more distant places, salted, its rarity raises its price. Freshly caught and unsalted, however, it makes a more delicate food for those who eat it.

This fish signifies those who, though held cheap among their own people - for no prophet is accepted in his own homeland - obtain honors and high positions when they come among strangers. They can also signify those who, though base in reputation and merit, are nevertheless raised up by base men, their like, either because these wished to have a partner in crime, or because they found no one more fit for the honors.
Whence the French proverb: for lack of a good man, a fool is placed on the seat.

The 'multipes' [octopus], as Pliny says, is a sea fish, taking its name from the fact itself. For just as the many-footed land creature has many feet, so too does this one. Its feet extend from its side. This fish mates in winter, and, among other fish, builds itself a nest from small twigs.
The great Basil says that it warms the egg placed in the nest in the water, and produces offspring from it.

It lays eggs over two months, and this only a single egg, small, the size of a nut. But once the female has laid the egg, she sits for forty nights and broods it, and in the time that follows, countless fish come from it. And it is necessary that they produce many offspring, because, were this not so, their kind would be greatly diminished, since they consume one another, and it is an animal of great appetite. It is, however, a very weak animal and spoils quickly, perhaps because of too much food. Aristotle: the male's head is longer than the female's. The female, when she lays eggs, becomes very weak because of the excessive sitting and because she does not feed at that time nor is sated with food. The octopus overcomes the karabo sea monster, which is nevertheless strong and robust; and it overcomes it more by cunning than by strength; and this is the sign that it overcomes it, that sometimes, when they are found together caught in a net, the karabo is often found dead or mortally wounded. And in this it is given to understand that wisdom avails more than strength, and that victory is given not by might, but from heaven.

[a fragmentary note on] the octopus, which is naturally cunning, in that, so that the shell of its back may be hard and able to withstand the salt waters of the sea and the harshness of the rocks, it swims at the surface of the water and places the shell of its back toward the sun, so that it may be dried and become harder.

Murex shells, as Pliny says, are sea shellfish that hide before the rising of the Dog Star and come out at the appointed time. They also have a precious liquid, useful for dyeing garments. But in murex shells the color is found only in a single white vein: the rest of the body is barren of it. This color is drawn from them alive, since with life they vomit forth the substance. Mucianus is the authority, Pliny relating it, that when moray eels clung to a ship full of wind - as was said of the remora - the ship stood still that was carrying noble boys to King Periander, to be castrated. It does not have a spherical or round mouth, nor one projecting into a point, but is closed on both sides like a shell.

The sea-mouse, coming out onto land and digging a pit in the earth, lays eggs, and covers them again with earth; but, returning after the thirtieth day, opens the pit again and leads its offspring into the water. Their offspring, at first, lack sight, as generally do the offspring of all water creatures.

The 'mulus' [mullet, red fish] is a sea fish, as Pliny says, which has a grace of nobility beyond other fish, given as food only to the noble. For it is most rare. This fish is not raised in abundance in fishponds and pools, but only the northern ocean, in the nearest part of the West, produces it. There are, moreover, several kinds of them, which feed on seaweed and oysters and mud, and on the flesh of other fish. But the nobler ones are marked by a twin barbel on the lower lip, and their food is what has grown near the shore in the clear air. Men of eminent rank say that a noble mullet, as it dies, is of varied color and is admired for its numerous variety.

We would say these two kinds of fish signify two kinds of worldly power among princes. Of these, those that are baser and fall into demonic use live off the plunder of the poor as if it were flesh and seaweed, that is, superfluous vanity. But the others, who are nobler and live in the calm of conscience on their own income granted by divine generosity, are honored, with their twin barbel as if with a twin grace of virtue, before God and men, and after death, marked with the merits of their various virtues and surrounded with variety, are presented at the table of the heavenly King as choice food for the Lord, by the angels.

The 'mullus' [red mullet] is a fish, as Isidore says, taking its name from the fact itself, in that it is soft and most tender. Its consumption diminishes lust, dulls the sharpness of the eyes, and those who often eat it smell of fish. A mullus killed in wine, those who drink from it afterward develop a distaste for wine.

The 'mulago' is a sea fish which, as Isidore says, flies up above the waters, and this whenever the storm is seen to be changing; as a sign of the joy that it has ceased, it flies over the waves. This is unlike other fish and sea monsters, which seem to play upon the waters as a storm is rising.

Oysters, as Pliny says, are a species of shellfish or snail, on whose flesh crabs live by a wondrous cunning. For since they cannot open their shells by force, they lie in ambush, and when the oysters open their shells, throw in stones, and thus, the closing hindered by the inserted stones, gnaw at their flesh.

Purple-shells too are similarly sea shellfish, as Pliny says, which live for very many years, up to seven. They hide for thirty days around the rising of the Dog Star. They gather in springtime and spit out, from their mouth, the worn liquid. They have this liquid in the middle of their throat. Purple-shells reach their full size within a year. But if they exceed this while still growing, the shells lose the power of desire and can no longer mate or conceive, so as to produce the precious liquid in season. Whence the greatest care is taken to remove or crush purple-shells in their first year, lest they grow further. With this liquid, garments called 'purple' are usually dyed. This color glows faintly with the hue of a darkening rose. Purple-shells, when returned to the sea half-dead, revive. Purple-shells are caught by foul-smelling bait.

The 'pina' is likewise of the shellfish kind, as Pliny says. It has a round body. Male and female walk together as companions. The pina opens its shells to the moon and offers itself, as if dead, to small fish. These, rejoicing at once, once their licensed boldness has grown, fill the pina's shells. Soon the pina, sensing itself full, kills whatever it has enclosed by seizing it, and gives part to its companion. This clearly shows that sense exists in water creatures.

Of fish, the stickleback is nearly the smallest of all fish, taking its name from the fact itself: for it pricks with certain spines. The male among them is red around the throat, the female lacks this redness. Both are mottled with spots. The common people believe these grow in the water without seed and, more marvelously, that other fish are propagated from their seed; whence they also call this fish the 'mother of fish.' To this they add proofs; for they say that if a new pond is made and no fish placed in it, these little fish are found in it in the first year, but in the second year fish of a different kind are propagated from these same little fish.

Scallops are in the sea, as Pliny says. They hide in great cold and great heat. For this fish must have temperate air to live, since it cannot bear the extremes of the elements. This fish's claws - for it is armed with claws - shine in the dark like fire.

The sea-pig is an edible fish. It largely holds the appearance of the land pig. It has an almost identical head, limbs on its body, and ribs arranged in the manner of a pig. Nearly all its flesh turns to fat and passes into thickness. Its tongue is loose like a pig's, but they differ in voice. On its back there are certain spines with a most potent venom; but their gall is a remedy for the sting of these same spines. Their agony, however, is great. As Pliny is the authority, they seek food at the bottom of the sea and dig, in the manner of pigs. They have their mouth-opening around the throat.
The sea-peacock is a sea fish, as Isidore says, so named from the peacock bird, in that it resembles it in colors. As Isidore says: They are painted on the back and neck with varied colors.

They signify those who, with manifold virtue and modesty, bear the burdens of their neighbors, as the Apostle commands: Bear one another's burdens. They also have a neck colored with varied hues, since, from the manifold merit of their virtues, they raise their hope patiently toward heavenly things.
