The sea-frog, which Pliny calls the 'fisher,' itself pursues fish in this way: it has projecting horns beneath its eyes, with which, having stirred up the mud, it displays them for the sake of plunder. Then unwary little fish, rushing at the stirred-up mud and not seeing the plunderer lurking within it, gather round, until, coming too close, they are suddenly torn apart by their enemy.

Oh, how many, following this example, gaping too eagerly after temporal gains as if at stirred-up mud, have been suddenly swallowed and torn apart by the enemy of mankind! Of this mud the prophet says: Why do you heap up thick mud against yourself?

The turbot preys in a similar manner. The turbot is a large and strong fish, but slow. Also hidden in stirred-up mud, it moves its extended fins, and without delay, when it sees fish approaching, seizes and devours them. Proof of its cunning is that, although it is the slowest of all fish, it is nevertheless very often found to have the mullet, a most swift fish, in its stomach.
And this is what is said by the Lord in the Gospel, that the children of darkness are more prudent than the children of light in their generation.

Skates - or 'rais' or 'rochen,' as the common people call them in various tongues - are sea fish, as the Book of Properties has it. Among noble fish it is reckoned quite base, and this where there is an abundance of fish. But where fish are scarce, there its rarity raises its price. In breadth and length, which are nearly equal, it measures two or three cubits. It is nearly round in shape. It has horrible eyes, a mouth hideous in its deformity, and this not in the place other fish have it, but in the place of the belly; where the head and eyes are, it has no mouth. It has a long tail like a snake's, with certain very sharp little spines on it. These fish sometimes have a stone in the head, and we do not believe nature created this without purpose. Their flesh is as indigestible as beef.
These fish become pregnant, as Aristotle says, when the south wind blows.

Salmon, as the Book of Properties says, are fish which barbarians call 'lastas.' They grow to great breadth and length. They are strong in power, and all the agility they have comes more from the power of their strength than from lightness of body. For they are heavy and weighty.
The salmon, as Pliny says, was in antiquity preferred above all river fish, and especially, as he also says, in Aquitaine.

These breed young and cannot live long in the fresh waters of ponds, unless they have free passage to the fresh waters of rivers; indeed, even where in passing it finds a hedge or such an obstacle, joining head to tail with its body bent, it leaps across to the water it seeks. It does this same thing when it senses itself caught in a net. [They do the same when they wish to cross to the salt waters of the sea. For they grow most easily and quickly where the sea's waters rise and fall, meeting fresh waters. Whence in river waters the smallest salmon are found, the length of a finger. But salmon a foot long are very rarely found in fresh waters, because, after a year has passed, they are accustomed to cross to the salt waters of the sea, mixed however with fresh water, where, growing to their due strength, they return again to the place of their birth.] Its flesh is red, and though sweet and quite pleasing, it quickly brings on satiety in those who eat it.

The sturgeon is a large fish, which barbarians call 'stora.' It dwells in river waters, and this in those that are great and broad. It cannot live long in ponds, unless it has passage to the fresh waters of rivers. It takes little or no food into its body, since the calm clear air alone is sufficient food for its nourishment. For this reason it happens that it has a small belly, but is nearly solid in the place of the belly as in the rest of its body. For it has intestines, though very small in proportion to its body, but a liver quite large, and this liver so sweet that it can scarcely be eaten without disgusting the stomach. Whence its gall, which lies next to it, is usually mixed in when the liver is prepared, so that the excess of sweetness in the liver is more carefully tempered by the excess of bitterness in the gall. It lacks a mouth in the place that occupied the mouth in other animals; it has only a small opening beneath the throat, closed when it wishes, but open to the calm air. In the south wind they fatten more quickly; but when the north wind blows, they sink into the depths. A sturgeon placed in milk lives as long as in water. [This fish, freshly caught and eaten, passes almost entirely into nourishment for the body. At the sound of thunder its flesh suddenly spoils and grows foul. There is also another fish, called the 'dannus,' which, if hung on a beam, trembles at the sound of thunder. This fish, too, is nearly always harmful and especially induces fevers.]

Sponges, as Pliny says, are born in the sea, on rocks and in the crags of cliffs. They are nourished by shellfish, or fish, or mud. That there is understanding in them appears from the fact that, when they sense they are being torn away, they contract and are much more difficult to pull off; they do the same at the pulsing of the current. They also say that, once torn away, they grow again from the roots left behind. They rot in sunny places, and so live best in deep pools.

Centipede-fish, as Pliny says, are similar to the land creatures called centipedes. Having swallowed a hook, they vomit out everything into the earth, until they expel the hook; then they swallow it all back again.

By these fish are signified those who, sensing earthly riches to be a danger to themselves, cast them aside, vowing a common life in a monastery. But when they have lived there for some time and are unwilling to be content with the common allowance, they gather private possessions again for themselves and become worse in this, that, like dogs returning to their vomit, their money remains with them for their ruin.

The starfish is in the western sea, its shape like a star. It has flesh within, but a very hard callus outside. Aristotle and Pliny relate that it has a fiery heat within it, so that it burns whatever it touches in the sea. When it has eaten some creature, that creature is soon found in its belly, hard, like twice-baked bread.

The catfish, as Pliny says, is a fish with a wondrous concern for its young. For when the female gives birth within three days, the male guards the laid eggs for fifty days, so that they are not taken by others. This fish, indeed, ravages wherever it is, an animal eager to overcome everything it can.

The 'solaris' is a fish taking its name from the fact itself: for it gladly lies in the sun on riverbanks. It has a large head, a broad mouth-opening, black and slippery skin, like that of snakes. Its liver is most sweet and especially edible. It grows to a vast size and very great length, but this only once it has lived a long span of years. For it grows more slowly than other fish.

The ray [scuatina] is a sea fish, on Pliny's testimony. It is five feet in length, with a tail a foot long. Hidden in the mud, it suddenly seizes fish. It has such a rough skin on its body that wood and ivory are most effectively polished with it. The bristles of this same skin are short and black, similar to the awns of the fuller's herb, but much shorter. The providence of nature made this creature so hard that it can scarcely be cut even by the edge of iron or steel.
This fish holds the likeness of the impious, by whose cruelty the patience of the blessed is proven, so that, well polished, they may be more gloriously placed in the building of the Lord.

The 'salpa' [saupe], as Pliny says, is a foul and base fish. It presents, contrary to nature, a marvel to those who wonder at it, in that it can never be cooked through unless first beaten hard with a club or a rod.

This fish signifies certain sinners, foul in life, who can never be cooked through by the fire of the Holy Spirit or of charity, so as to become a chosen food of the divine will, unless first chastised by the saving scourge of some infirmity or tribulation.

The cuttlefish, as Pliny says, is a fish of whose kind the males are varied and darker and of greater constancy. When the females are struck by a trident, the males come to their aid; but on the contrary, when the male is struck, the female flees and does not return the favor. Both, however, when they sense themselves discovered, hide in the water darkened by the ink they discharge, which serves them in place of blood. This ink, moreover, has such power that, placed in a lamp, once the first light is removed, it makes Ethiopians visible in the dark. It conceives through the mouth, as the viper does. Cuttlefish do not swim in the sea except in pairs, male and female. Cuttlefish lay eggs at every season and complete their eggs in forty nights. When the female lays, the male follows her and breathes upon the eggs, so that the seed is given life. Her eggs are hard.

The sea-scorpion is a sea fish, as Isidore says, which harms the hand of the one who lifts it. It is related by philosophers that if ten sea-crabs are tied up with a bundle of oregano and thrown into a certain place in the sea, all the scorpions there will gather in that one place.

The sea-scorpion, as Aristotle says, lays eggs in spring and again in autumn, fittingly signifying those whose good works are always found, not only in time of prosperity, but also in time of adversity.

The 'sparus' takes its name from the throwing-spear, because it has that shape. Land instruments of work were invented before those of the sea, and this in name, not in creation. For the 'sparus' is a rustic missile weapon, named from 'scattering' [spargendo]. There is a fish of this name and this shape, as Isidore says.

The 'scaurus' is a fish whose flesh is quite delightful to eat. This fish, alone among all kinds of fish, as Ambrose says, is said to ruminate: for it does not have sharp, closely set teeth in its mouth, as all other kinds of fish have. These, first brought from foreign lands to Rome and thrown into the Tiber, multiplied there.

Isidore says of the scaurus that it is so clever that, when it sees itself enclosed in a fish-trap, it does not try to break out headfirst, nor does it thrust its head, harmed, against the wicker-work, but, turning around, loosens the gaps with repeated blows of its tail, and thus tries to make its way back out; and if by chance another scaurus outside sees this struggle, seizing its tail in its teeth, it helps the effort of the one trying to break free. The scaurus does this same thing when caught in nets; for it tries to get out backward.

The torpedo fish, too, knows its own power, without itself being numbed, as Pliny says; for, sunk in the mud, it hides itself, and suddenly attacks and seizes fish that, swimming above unaware, have grown numb. No liver is preferred in tenderness to this fish's.

From far off and at a distance, if anyone touches the torpedo with a spear or a rod, at once the arms of the one touching it, however strong, grow numb and paralyzed, and, though he who touched it may be swiftest in running, he is at once, by its touch, bound fast at the feet. So great is its power, moreover, that even the air around its body infects the human body. This Pliny and Isidore say of the torpedo.

The 'trebius' is a black fish, as Pliny says; it is a foot long, and, small as it is, this fish is nevertheless five fingers thick. Pliny relates that it has this power: that a piece of it, kept in salt, when brought near, draws out gold that has fallen into the deepest wells and makes it float. They change from white in winter to blacker in summer. Among all fish, the trebius alone builds a nest from seaweed and lays its eggs in the nest. There is a trebius in the ocean which, with the hard beak it has, pierces ships, but those found in the ocean are the very largest.

Trout are fish, as Isidore says. They dwell in fresh rivers, and this in those rivers that run with great force from the mountains. It has scales like the salmon's, and very similar flesh, but much more edible, and this only in summer, from the month of July until November. In winter, however, its flesh is white like other fish, and of lesser flavor. It has saffron and blood-red spots on its back.

The grayling [tymallus] takes its name from a flower: for thyme is called a flower. This fish is a sea fish, as Isidore says, and though pleasing in appearance and delightful in taste, it nevertheless, like a flower, has a fragrance and breathes out scents.
Sea-foxes, as Pliny says, in danger swallow the hook, and, once it is drawn up to the weaker part of the line, easily bite it through.

These fish signify certain faithful in the Church, who, when they see themselves being lured by the enemy's cunning toward some flattering pleasure, at once, in the danger seen amid the offered sweetness, reject it and bite it through with the mind of a gnawing conscience.
The 'uranoscopus' [star-gazer] is a sea fish, named from its one eye: for it has a single eye on the crown of its head, and this so sharp of sight that no ambush can lie hidden from it.
It signifies the very sun of singular foresight and providence, God, whose eyes, brighter than the sun, gaze upon the good and the wicked.

Sea-vipers are sea fish, quite small, a little more than a cubit long. On the head, above the eyes, they bear a small horn, sharp and deadly. For whomever this horn wounds, it infects with poison. Guarding against this, fishermen, once the fish is caught, cut off its head. The rest of the body, however, serves human use: for it is quite edible.

The 'venth' is a fish so commonly named, which in Latin is called 'aristosus,' not without reason, because of the countless bones [aristae] it has. It is the basest of all edible fish. It dwells often in fresh waters, yet in those that are made brackish by the ebb and flow of the sea. This fish's flesh is armed within with many, indeed innumerable, bones, so that it can be eaten only with difficulty. Its flesh is base and full of unpleasantness. Whence it happens that it becomes food for the poor and lowly. It is caught in this way: nets are stretched lengthwise or crosswise across the water, and before the nets, over the water, an instrument shaped like a bow is placed, so that it floats on the waves. On the upper part of this instrument a bell is hung. Hearing its sound, the fish come in schools, foolishly following the ringing of the bell. For this reason, falling into the nets, they are caught in great numbers. This shows clearly that they have a sense of hearing.

By this fish are signified those who, though unwilling to join in the dances of the mad and the revelers, either because they are old, or because they do not know how, or because they are ashamed, nevertheless gladly listen to obscene and shameful talk, and, wherever the ringing of the devil's bell is - which holds the likeness of the dancers - eagerly gather. Let them beware, then, lest they fall into the devil's nets and, filled in conscience with the bones of remorse, become food for the most base demons, who are the fishermen of the sea of this world. Of these fish and those who fish for them, the prophet Habakkuk says: Men, he says, are like the fish of the sea; and shortly after: He has drawn up everything with his hook, he says, has dragged it into his net, and gathered it into his fishing-net; over this he will rejoice and exult - as if the prophet were saying: of such men he will make his feast, and so that fisherman, the devil, will exult and rejoice.

The 'vergiliales' fish can take their name from the fact itself, for, as Pliny says, there are two lakes in Italy at the foot of the Alps, called Lake Larius and Lake Verbanus. In these are the aforesaid fish, which appear to men every year only at the rising of the Pleiades. At other times, however, they are hidden. These are conspicuous for their dense and very sharp scales, shaped like nails. Their form resembles a kind of boot, except that they have a head like fish. At the head, that is at their front end, they are small and narrow like the top of a boot, but toward what follows they widen out greatly.

By these are signified certain wicked men, who in time of peace are not seen and do not appear to men as they truly are. But when, at the time of the Pleiades, in which [sudden floods sometimes occur, and] the time of tribulation arrives, their cruelty appears as if toothed; and if before, that is at their beginning, they seemed small, that is humble, afterward, nevertheless, in time of tribulation, they expand in wickedness. Whence Solomon says: There is one who wickedly humbles himself, and his inward parts are full of deceit. Here ends the book on fish.

In general, concerning serpents: the asp, the amphisbaena, the basilisk, the boa, the berus, horned serpents, the chameleon, the cerastes, the blind-worm [cecula], the centipede-serpent, the chelydrus, the cenchris; against the three kinds of serpents that ravaged the sons of Israel a bronze serpent was raised up by Moses, and these serpents were the dipsas, the dracontopede, the emorroid [and the river hydra], the javelin-snake [iaculus], the ipnapis, the hydra [and likewise the river hydra], the lizard [lacerta], sea-serpents, the water-snake [natrix], the naderos, the pester, the pharias, the rutela, the salamander, the scorpion, the situla, the scalpiga, the stellio-lizard [and another stellio-serpent], the scaura, the situla, siren-serpents, the serps, the serpents of India, the tortoise, the tarans, the tysus, the tyrus, or 'tir,' from which theriac is made, the tyliacus, the viper. Here end the chapters. Here begins the eighth book, on serpents.

In general, first, something must be said of serpents. Aristotle: no serpent has testicles, but passages, as a fish does, and its womb is long; in its other internal organs it is like a small lizard. A serpent's tongue is fine, long, black, and forked, and for this reason it seems to project far out of its mouth. Its heart is behind its neck and resembles a kidney. Large serpents have their gall above the liver, but small ones have it above the intestine. If a serpent is blinded, it regains its sight again, like the swallow. But if its tail is cut off, it grows back again naturally, like small lizards. A serpent has thirty ribs. Serpents join to one another so closely in mating that they seem to be one body with two heads. Every serpent indifferently eats both flesh and plants. It is, however, an animal that drinks little. A serpent greatly desires wine; whence those who hunt serpents are accustomed to lure them with wine. Though serpents drink, they nevertheless have no outlet for urine, and this because they have no bladder. What they drink and its surplus are consumed by the natural heat, which is very great in them. They have, however, a place through which their waste exits, though this is small in proportion to their body.

The earth, once a man has been struck by a serpent, as Pliny says, no longer receives it, but it suffers the penalty, destined to die shortly after. A serpent cannot kill more than one creature at a time, except the salamander alone. Serpents brood their covered eggs in the earth and hatch their young the following year. Venom, as Pliny says, is nothing other than the gall of serpents, and it travels from there to the veins beneath the spine and afterward to the mouth, or to the tail, as in scorpions. A serpent's tongue is very fine, three-forked, quivering, of a dark color, and, if you draw it out, quite long. Serpents hide in winter in the earth, or in rocks, or in the hollows of trees, and endure without food. In springtime, however, they come forth. In Ireland no serpent can live, nor indeed anything venomous, and not only can it not live there, but wherever earth brought from Ireland is thrown upon a venomous creature, it dies at once. Whence it happened that there was a dispute between the Irish and the Scots over a certain island; and when the Irish sought a judgment that serpents be brought to the island, this to be a sign of the outcome, that if serpents brought to the island died at once, the island would go to Ireland: without delay, the serpents brought there died, and the island went to Ireland. In Syria snakes do no harm, for which reason the Syrians do not kill them. Aristotle, on the contrary, relates that on Mount Latmus, in Caria, guests are not harmed by scorpions; but they kill the natives.

James and Isidore: serpents are, by nature, hot creatures, whence they do little or no harm once they have grown cold. By night, moreover, they harm less than by day, since they grow cold in the night dew. In the cold of winter they coil into knots, but in summer they loosen. One infected with venom first grows stiff; but once warmed, the venom kills the man through dryness. They say, however, that it cannot harm unless it touches a man's blood. It is also said that serpents flee a naked man and do not dare to trouble him.

Ambrose relates that the spittle of a fasting man kills a serpent. For if a serpent is touched by it, even a little, it dies at once. See, O man, how great is the power of fasting, that man kills an earthly serpent even with his spittle, and, still more fittingly, a spiritual one. No bone is found in the belly of any animal.
As the Experimentator says, there are as many poisons as there are kinds of serpents, as many forms of destruction as there are species, as many kinds of pain as they have colors.

A serpent rendered weak cannot move, because wherever a blow falls upon it, it breaks the spine through which the movements of the ribs, feet, and body were carried out. It is rightly believed to happen that, just as death comes to man through the serpent, so death comes to the serpent through man. Its spleen is small and round. Serpents, like swallows, recover lost sight. Serpents have this peculiarity, that they can move the head without the body, which no other animal can do. Serpents have spines in their flesh like a fish's. The tracks of serpents, as Isidore says, are such that, though they seem to lack feet, they crawl by the effort of their ribs and scales, which are arranged in equal order from the top of the throat to the bottom of the belly; they rely on their scales as if they were claws, and their ribs as if they were legs. A serpent, hiding its head, exposes its whole body to the one striking it; for even if its head escapes, it still lives, having lost its body. About to enter the water, it lays aside its venom, but once it has left the water, it takes up the venom again; and if by some chance it cannot find the venom it has lost, it dashes its head against the ground repeatedly and dies of grief. It lives a long time; for once it has grown old, it consumes its own flesh by fasting, until, its skin loosened by leanness, it passes through the opening of a rock, where, casting off its old skin, it recovers its youth and is renewed. It is helped in this by the juice of fennel, and it does not repeat this remedy more often than once a day and night. It sheds its skin first from the head. The same creature, its sight darkened in its winter hiding-place, is told to recover by rubbing itself against the herb rue, restoring its eyes. It flees a good smell, and by this it is often killed. Serpents are said to be generated from the marrow of men, and this especially in the spine.

The asp is a serpent of a sky-blue color. By its bite it injects and spreads venom, whence it also takes its name: for 'aspis,' as James says, means 'venom' in Greek; and hence 'aspis,' because it kills with a venomous bite. It is charmed by the power of certain words, by some men, so that it does not kill with its venom - or, as some say, so that, calmed, it can be caught and the precious stone that grows naturally in it can be taken from its forehead. But it is naturally wary against the charmer; for when it perceives the incantations of the wise sorcerer, it plugs one ear with its tail, and presses the other to the ground, so as not to hear the charmer's voice.

The asp, as Solinus says, has life only with its mate; and from this it happens that, when one is killed, the other pursues vengeance with incredible care: it follows the killer and, however great the crowd of people, harasses him; it breaks through every obstacle, crosses every distance, and does not let the killer of its mate live, unless kept off by rivers or by the swiftest flight.

As the Experimentator says, the asp does not harm the Africans or the Syrians; whence they expose children born to them to serpents, and if these harm them, they cast them out as if born of adultery; but if not, they raise them as their own. When an asp, coming to the table of a certain rich man in Egypt, was constantly fed there, it gave birth to young, one of whom killed the host's son. And when the mother returned to her usual feeding and understood the crime, she killed that young one and never again entered that dwelling. The asp's teeth are exceedingly long, so that they appear outside the mouth, as in the boar.

The amphisbaena is a serpent having two heads, one in its proper place, the other at its tail. This makes it possible for the serpent, with either head, to move in circling paths; Solinus, in his book, calls this the 'amphin.'

But Aristotle too relates of the serpents of the East that have two heads; but he says this occurs from a monstrous birth. These serpents have two heads and one body. Both heads take food and pass it into the one body; they also crawl toward their enemies with both heads. Aristotle relates, however, the cause of this monstrosity: that if two seeds are joined together in one womb and no partition separates them, then a monstrous serpent will be generated. This, however, rarely happens in serpents, since the womb of serpents is very well arranged for distinct offspring.
The amphisbaena, as Pliny says, is the only serpent that ventures into cold, coming forth before all others, and before the cuckoo's call.
Its eyes shine like fire, as Isidore says.

The basilisk, as James says, is a serpent said to be the king of serpents. Whence 'basiliscus' in Greek is the same as 'regulus' [little king] in Latin. The basilisk, then, is a singular evil upon the earth; half a foot long, marked on the head with white spots like a kind of diadem; by its breath alone it splits rocks. Other serpents fear and flee this serpent, because it kills them by breath alone. Men, however, it kills by sight alone. For if it sees a man first, the man dies first; but if a man sees the serpent first, the serpent is destroyed, as James of Acre says.

Pliny seems to suggest the same thing, where, having spoken earlier of the catoblepas animal, that it kills men by sight, he adds: The same power, he says, is in the basilisk serpent; and afterward, in book 29: By sight, he says, it kills a man.

How this can be, the Experimentator gives a reason in his book. For he says that the rays of the basilisk's eyes corrupt the visible spirit of a man, and once this is corrupted, the other spirits, which descend from the brain and the life of the heart, are corrupted too; and thus the man dies. Basilisks, like scorpions, seek out dry places; and once they reach water, they cause dropsy and derangement.

Nor is the basilisk given only for the destruction of man or other creatures, but also for the earth, which it defiles fatally and scorches wherever it finds a lair for its savagery. Finally, it kills grasses and scorches even the trees it breathes upon, kills bushes, breaks rocks; it even corrupts the air so much that no bird flies through it, infected as it is with pestilential breath, without harm. When it moves, it crawls with the middle part of its body. Other serpents dread even its hiss and, when they perceive it, flee wherever they can. Whatever it kills with its bite, no wild beast grazes on nor any bird touches. It is overcome, however, by weasels, which men bring into the caverns where it hides.

When these are killed, as Pliny says, the weasels die too, and nature's battle is thus completed. For nature has pleased to have nothing without its match, that is, nothing that could not naturally be overcome by some adversary. Its power, moreover, does not fail even in death. For wherever its ash is smeared, spiders cannot spin their webs, nor can any venomous creature approach. They said there was a temple in Greece smeared with this ash. This is said to happen in whatever building a part of its body is kept. Silver, indeed, smeared with its ash, is said to take on a golden color. [There is a certain kind of basilisk that flies, but does not exceed the bounds of its own region, which divine ordinance has set for them so that they do not turn to devastate the world. There is also another kind of basilisk, and for that seek in the book On Birds, in the chapter On the Cock.]

The boa is a snake in Calabria, as Solinus says, which grows to an immense bulk in this way: it first attacks herds of buffalo (or cows) and those rich in milk, and entangles itself around their udders, and, fattened by continuous suckling and nourished by such satiety for a long time, at last swells up so much that no strength can withstand its size; and finally, once it has depopulated the animals, it drives the regions it has infested to devastation.

This serpent, ravaging Dalmatia, as Jerome writes, was, at the request of the blessed Hilarion, compelled by the word of divine power to climb a pile of wood, and, the pile set alight beneath it, the huge beast was burned up.
Pliny, and the History of the Holy Fathers, describe a kind of dragon so vast in size that they swallow stags and whole oxen.
That snake which Regulus, leader of the Romans - as the Roman history itself records - killed in Africa, a hundred and twenty feet long, whose skin, stripped off, was brought to Rome as a spectacle.

Its jaws, too, were hung up at Rome for wonder. Pliny writes of this serpent that, when it was caught, it was necessary to bring in catapults and various siege engines, as in the storming of a fortress.

The 'berus' is a most wicked kind of serpent, as the Experimentator says, and more cunning than all other serpents. This serpent calls the sea moray eel with a hiss to the seashore and flatters it, so as to entice it to mating. The sea moray eel, gentle in spirit, submits to the mating, but sometimes to its own ruin. For, intercepted by the ambush of its enemy, it is killed before it can return to the water, and pays the penalty for its own destruction.

Horned serpents, as Solinus says, are so named because they have horns with which they attack those who approach. Besides this, they also have a harmful venom, by which they kill men they strike, unless theriac comes to their aid.
We read that the Holy Fathers destroyed these serpents in Egypt.
The chameleon is an animal named from the fact itself: for it is, in part, similar to the camel, though a small animal: it is scarcely found to exceed two cubits. Solinus: it is a quadruped animal,
which some call the 'lion of the earth.'
It has the appearance of a lizard, or, as Aristotle says, a face between the face of a pig and the face of an ape.

Pliny: it has straight and rather long legs, close to the belly. It has a high back like a camel's, and humped. It has a long and twisting tail, tapering to fineness. Its claws are curved and hooked. Its body has a rough skin, like that of crocodiles.

Solinus: its gait is sluggish, like a tortoise's. Its eyes are sunken, in a hollow recess turned inward, which never close, but rotate around. Its body is nearly, like the lioness's, empty within of any sign of nourishment: for it lives on the intake of air alone.

Its liver is on the left side, and this contrary to all other animals. In the arrangement of its internal organs there is great variety compared to other animals. As Aristotle says, it is very lean; and the reason is that it has little blood; and for this reason too it is a fearful animal, since the heat that incites boldness is diminished in it. The fear of this animal, moreover, is the cause of its color being variable and changeable from moment to moment, so that, whatever it joins itself to, it takes on the same color. But the better reason is that this animal has a very airy body, and for this reason most easily takes on changes of various colors from what it rests upon.

Ambrose, however, says that there are two colors this animal cannot imitate: white and red. Its body is nearly without flesh, and only a small clot of blood is found, and this in the heart. It is without a spleen. It hides in winter, comes forth in spring. It is vulnerable to the raven, by which, once killed, it kills its own killer in turn, being killed. For if the bird eats even a little of it, it dies at once. But the raven has a remedy, nature extending a hand for its healing. For when it senses itself afflicted, it takes laurel leaf and recovers its health. In Asia there is a great abundance of these.

The cerastes is a serpent, as Solinus says, having eight horns on its head, similar to rams' horns. This one hides its whole head in the sand, leaving only the horns outside. When flying sparrows or other birds land on these, for the sake of resting, the venomous serpent tears the killed birds apart with its venom. This serpent, moreover, is more sinuous than other serpents, and this because it does not seem to have a spine to stiffen it. Its horn, placed on the tables of the rich, betrays venom by sweating. From these horns handles for knives are made, and these knives were placed on the tables of emperors before every meal, so that they would show, by sweating, if any food set before them had been poisoned.
The 'cecula' [blind-worm] is a quite small serpent. Though it has no eyes, it nevertheless has the power to harm through the strength of its venom.
The centipede is a serpent, as Isidore says, having many feet.

The 'chelydrus' is a serpent, as Isidore says, that dwells in water and on land. It takes its name from the fact itself, for 'chiron' in Greek means 'land,' and 'idros' means 'water.' The ground over which this serpent moves is made to smoke, whence Macer says: whether its steamy back exhales venom, or the ground smokes where the serpent glides along. It always moves in a straight line; for if it twists itself while moving, it bursts at once.
The 'cenchris' is a serpent that moves without bending, as Isidore says, always taking a straight path. Whence Lucan: and the cenchris, always gliding on a straight track.

div.head: 14. De tribus generibus serpentium qui vastaverunt filios Israël

cit.quote: Against the three kinds of serpents, as James says, that troubled the sons of Israel in the desert, a bronze serpent was raised up, by the Lord's command, on a pole by Moses, the giver of the Law. These are said to have been: dipsads, situlas, and scorpions.

The dipsas is a serpent, as James and Solinus say, which is said to be so fine that, striking almost invisibly, it is not seen when trodden upon. This serpent, on Solinus's testimony, kills by thirst. For through this it brings on swelling and inflation, and thus, infected with this venom, one dies (and it signifies pride).
As the Experimentator says, the dipsas kills in such a way that the face of the one overtaken by death shows no sign of sadness at dying.
The proud are indeed broken only with difficulty, which is evident in the devil, who is damned by pride alone: for he will never deign to ask for pardon and confess himself guilty of crime.

The dragon is the largest of all land animals, as James and Augustine say. It has no venom. It is crested on the head, has, in proportion to its body's size, a small mouth, and narrow windpipes. It puts out its tongue toward its prey, and gapes with its mouth, but does no harm with its teeth.

Its bite, however, though small, is most severe, as the Experimentator says, since it eats venomous creatures. But if its tail binds someone, it kills; and from this not even the elephant is safe, for all the size of its body.

The dragon feels nausea in springtime, as Pliny says, a malady it checks with the juice of wild lettuce. Its dwelling is most often in caves, which it gladly chooses in rocky cliffs because of the excessive essential heat of its body, and this especially when it has flown, and because of the accidental heat of the sun, which is greatest in the regions of the East. For they are rarely found except in the warmer parts of the world: around the Tower of Babel, and in the Tower of Babel itself, and in the deserts of that ancient Babylon and its ruins, the largest dragons are said to dwell, whose voice and roaring terrify men. Growing to twenty cubits and more, it often reaches full size.

Its gaze is unbearable to men, so that they are sometimes even terrified to death by the sight of it alone. And, reaching old age and their due size, they live a long time without food, as Aristotle says. But once it has eaten, it is not easily satisfied. [This is because it is a most cold-natured animal, and the small heat within it cannot consume the thick humors of its body.]

How that dragon can still live, and must live until the end of the world, without bodily food - the one which the blessed Pope Sylvester, on a certain mountain at Rome, at the command of the blessed apostle Peter, is recorded to have shut up - I indeed cannot see according to nature, but we believe it to be a divine miracle.
It is read, however, in the Histories of the Britons, that two very great dragons were found living beneath the earth.

In the depths of the earth, as Augustine says, a dragon sometimes dwells, and, when it senses in the air a coming storm of winds or rain, comes forth and is carried above the air with the great oaring of its wings, stirring and driving the air, its wings extending in a leathery flexibility and spreading widely in proportion to the size of its body.

There is a kind of these that crawls on its chest over the ground. There is another kind of them that has feet; but this is more rarely found. From its brain, as Aldhelm says, the 'draguntia' stone is cut out, but they say it is precious only if extracted while the creature is alive. For, taken unawares by a single blow to the head while they rest in the heat, the stone is extracted while they still throb in the fullness of their vigor.

The tongue and gall of the dragon, boiled in wine, are a remedy for those troubled by incubus demons, when their bodies are anointed with this. [The book that contains the sayings of the ancients relates that the dragon is edible, especially for the Ethiopians; its flesh is most cold. The dragon grows very hot in flight, and then desires to be refreshed with elephant's blood, which is indeed most cold in its effect. The dragon is hunted in this way: it is charmed with certain ancient incantations, so that it does no harm, and, both hunter and dragon filled with wind, it is beaten before itself with coral rods, so that, terrified by their sound, it does not move and submits to the hunter's force, and this because it is done in imitation of thunder. For it fears the crashes and lightning of thunder above all other creatures; and so, when it hears thunder, it flees into caves and caverns of the earth. Nor is this a wonder, nature extending it protection through a kind of understanding: for it is said that, among all animals, the nature of dragons is struck by lightning more quickly, just as it is written, on Pliny's testimony, to the contrary, that the eagle among birds and the laurel among trees are never struck by lightning. But when hunters have terrified them with the sound of inflated skins, they have themselves bound onto the dragons, so that within a few hours they are carried to the most distant regions. They are sometimes deceived over the longest stretches of the sea and, exhausted beyond their strength, sink with their riders into the depths of the sea.] [There is also another way of hunting the dragon: a calf is taken and disemboweled, and its belly is filled with quicklime, and, propped up on stakes, it is placed where the dragon is accustomed to frequent; the dragon, coming, swallows the calf whole in one gulp. Without delay, the quicklime, beginning to be dissolved by the moisture within, sets the dragon on fire inside, and it, seeking a spring at once, the more it drinks, the more it burns; and thus the land is freed from its ravager.]
Dracontopedes are serpents, as the philosopher Aldhelm relates, which the Greeks call thus, large and powerful; these have maiden-like faces, similar to human faces, but end in the body of a dragon.

Of this kind of serpent it can be believed was the serpent by which our first mother Eve was deceived, to her own harm and ours: for Bede says that the serpent the devil used to deceive our first parents had a maiden's face.

The devil took on the body of a serpent not as a soul takes on a body, but as a man takes on a garment: for the devil and the serpent were not one being. He took it up, I say, by joining, or rather attaching himself to it, and showed the serpent's maiden face only to the woman, so that she might be enticed by a similar form: for every animal, as the wise man says, loves its like. But he concealed the rest of the serpent's body, similar to the rest of serpents, with the foliage of trees. How the devil could have made the serpent form articulate words, we indeed do not see; but perhaps he formed the words from outside, and not through the serpent's own throat, by an artificial vibration of the air. The saints say, however, that the devil was able to speak through the serpent's body, just as he once spoke through oracles and mediums to deceive the pagans. But, saving the reverence due to the expositors, it makes a great difference whether the devil speaks through a serpent, which has no throat or organs for forming articulate words, or as he spoke through frenzied oracles, who were indeed rational men - unless perhaps we wish to say that, just as the serpent had a human face, so too it had a throat and organs arranged to produce, if taught, human sounds, just as we see birds imitate human speech.

The 'emorrois' [hemorrhage-serpent] is a serpent, as Solinus says, which draws blood from its bite, and, the channels of the veins undone, drawing out all the blood, calls forth whatever belongs to the soul, the blood being drained from its seat.

Javelin-serpents, as Solinus says, are so named from the deadliness of their most savage attack. These, flying on wings, come to rest in trees, in which they hide. From these, hurled down with the greatest force, they pierce whatever creature fortune has placed in their path.
[a fragmentary note:] this serpent is called, in the Psalm, 'the flying arrow.'

The serpent 'ipnapis' is, as Solinus says, a kind descended from the asp, which kills, by sleep, those it bites. For it induces sleep through its venom, which never leaves the infected one through any effort. Cleopatra applied this serpent to her left arm, placing herself in the tomb beside her Antony, so that, touched by it, she might be dissolved into sleep and end her life with a quiet death.
Solinus [calls] this the 'hypnale'
[a fragmentary note, attributed to Jerome and the Roman History:] the asp

The hydra, as Isidore says, is a serpent in the river Nile. When it sees a crocodile sleeping with open mouth on the banks of the Nile, it rolls itself in muddy slime, so as to slip more easily into the crocodile's jaws. The crocodile, dulled with sleep, then swallows the creature that has slipped in. Soon, having torn apart its entrails, it comes out alive.

Of snakes, as Pliny writes, the hydra is the most beautiful in the whole world. Their liver is kept as a remedy for those bitten. Men bitten by this serpent, then, swell up, a disease they call 'boa,' because it is remedied with cow dung.

div.head: [L B V22. De ydro serpente fluviali

cit.quote: The river hydra is a serpent, and also one that dwells in marshes, as the Book of Kyranides says. This one raises its chest above the water. It carries a stone in its head, which, skinned or fumigated, it vomits up alive. It has also been seen to vomit up the stone when adjured by the living God, Lord of heaven and earth. I myself have tested the power of this stone: I applied the stone, bound around, to a woman suffering from dropsy, and I measured her belly daily, and it went down as much as three fingers, until it returned to its proper size. I then removed the stone, lest the natural moisture be dried up too much. It is likewise effective against every catarrh, every flux of the eyes, and every rheumatic limb.

The lizard, as Solinus says, the ancients call rather a worm than a serpent, since it strikes more mildly. Yet it hisses like a serpent and has a similar tail; it moves on feet. If one of a pair is caught, the other becomes fierce with grief.

There is also, of their kind, a little creature similar in form but different in color, which has a black tail. This one feeds on wild spiders. The lizard, as Pliny says, does not brood, forgetting the place where it gave birth, since this animal has no memory. And, Pliny writes, its young hatch by themselves, eleven in number. Some say the young are devoured by the mothers, except one left, the cleverest, which places itself upon its own mother's haunches. This one, left behind, avenges its siblings and kills its parents as their avenger. In India there are lizards twenty-four feet long, of a shining color. The lizard has a forked and hairy tongue.

Sea-serpents have very many young, and none of them have feet, but crawl in the manner of eels in the depths of the sea and swim, when necessary, since they have fins. They are similar to land serpents except in the head, since their head is very hard and rough. They are often more malicious than land serpents. And it should be noted that they do not stay in the deep places, but in the depths near the shore and around the sea's rocks.
The water-snake is a serpent, as Isidore says, that infects water with venom. For in whatever spring it is found, it mixes venom into it. Whence Lucan: and the water-snake, defiler of the water.

The 'nadera' is a snake found in the regions of Germany, the thickness of a human arm, golden in color on the belly, greenish on the back. Its breath is said to be so harmful that if you hold a freshly cut branch to its mouth, its breath makes the bark blister as if with gall-bladders. And if you hold a shining sword to its mouth, its tongue alone, touching the sword at the base, infects it with venom, and, spreading up to the tip of the sword, discolors it with a foul, sky-blue hue, as if seized by a violent flame. A man infected with this venom dies, unless theriac comes to his aid. The manner of this venom, moreover, is such that, once it has struck a man in the foot, the venom moves by degrees to the other limbs, and this because of the excessive heat, of the same nature as fire, which always rises. This venom, then, always rises, until it touches the heart, and then the man collapses and dies. The remedy, however, is that the man struck in the foot be hung up high by the feet, head down, and thus the venom cannot rise to the heart, but, reaching the top of the foot, remains there and cannot descend further; and thus the infected place is cut out and healed with medicines. If anyone wishes to walk unharmed, that is safely, in a place where these serpents dwell, let him rub his feet and hands - the limbs, namely, that lie open to danger - with rue and wormwood, and thus the serpent will flee and, the limbs protected by the remedy of these herbs, will not dare to touch them.

[The 'prester' -] is a serpent, as James and Solinus say, always running with its mouth open and steaming. It is said to descend from the kind of the asp; whence the poet: and the greedy prester, its steaming mouth stretched wide. This serpent, then, whomever it strikes, swells to an enormous bulk, as if suffering from dropsy, and thus dies: for putrefaction follows the swelling, as can be observed in ulcers.
The 'pharias' is a serpent, as Isidore says, which, always moving on its tail, seems to make a furrow. Whence Lucan: content to furrow its path with its tail, the pharias.

The 'rutela' is a serpent of the East, created usefully for many remedies, as Aristotle says. This kind of serpent is caught by apothecaries and kept in captivity. In this it should be noted that it lives a long time without any nourishment of food. But indeed every kind of serpent can live a long time without food, though especially the rutela.

The salamander, as James says, is called 'stellio' in Greek. The salamander is called 'stellio' in Greek. It is a kind of serpent found nowhere except in places where there is a constant natural heat of fire. It is large, a quadruped animal, horrid in appearance, and fearsome to all animals.

For it endures unharmed even in the destruction of fire, however strong. In the mountains of Sicily, and in parts of the world where there is a perpetual fire, the salamander is born and lives. It is caught in this way: the place on the mountain where it is accustomed to dwell amid the flames is marked. A fire is then made by the men who wish to catch it, and that fire is extended in a long trail from the mountain. The salamander, then, seeing the brighter fire's splendor and delighted, enters the kindled fire and, following the trail to its end, the fire behind it is extinguished, and so, before it can return to the mountain, it is caught by the hunters. Some say that it lives only in fire. Most authors, however, in various places and writings, more fittingly contradict this.
Some call the chameleon, that is, the 'lion of the earth,' as Pliny and Aldhelm say.
It is, he says, a quadruped having the face of a lizard;
or, as Aristotle says, it has a face between the face of a pig and the face of an ape.

Pliny: it has straight legs, longer behind, close to the belly; it has a long and twisting tail, tapering to fineness; its claws are hooked with a fine curve; its body has a rough skin, like that found in crocodiles.
Isidore mentions a certain pale wool, from which a woven belt cannot be burned.
This animal itself, as Augustine, Aldhelm, and Isidore say, lives in fire, and not only is it not burned, but it even extinguishes the fire.
Its gait is sluggish, as Solinus says, like the motion of tortoises. Its eyes are sunken in a hollow recess turned backward, which never close.

Pliny indicates that its eyes rotate fully around. It is the largest in bodily size, but empty within of any sign of nourishment. Its liver is on the left side, and this contrary to all other animals. In the arrangement of its internal organs there is great variety compared to other animals. The gape of its mouth never closes, since it does not use it for the service of food or drink, because it lives on the intake of dew or air alone.

As Aristotle says, it is very lean, and the reason is that it has little blood; and for this reason too it is a fearful animal, since the heat that incites boldness is diminished in it. The fear of this animal, moreover, is the cause of its color being variable and changeable from moment to moment, so that, whatever it joins itself to, that becomes the cause of its color.

As Ambrose says, there are two colors, however, that it cannot imitate: white and red. Its body is nearly without flesh, and only a small clot of blood is found, and this in the heart. It is without a spleen. It hides in winter, but comes forth in spring. It is vulnerable to the raven, by which, once killed, it kills its own killer in turn, being killed: for if the bird eats even a little of it, it will die at once; but the raven has a remedy, nature extending a hand for its healing: for when it senses itself afflicted, it takes laurel leaf and recovers its health.

For the salamander endures unharmed even in the destruction of fire, however strong. In the mountains of Sicily, and in other parts of the world where there is a perpetual fire, the salamander is born and lives. It is caught in this way: the place on the mountain where it is accustomed to dwell amid the flames is marked. A fire is then made by the men who wish to catch it, and that fire is extended in a long trail from the mountain. The salamander, then, seeing the brighter fire's splendor and delighted, enters the kindled fire and, following the trail to its end, the fire behind it is extinguished, and so, before it can return to the mountain, it is caught by the hunters. Some say that it lives only in fire. Most authors, however, in various places and writings, more fittingly contradict this.

Among all venomous animals, as Isidore says, the salamander has the greatest power to harm. For the others kill one at a time, but this one kills many at once. For if it crawls onto a tree, it infects its fruit with venom, so that whoever eats of it dies. But if it falls into a well, the strength of its venom kills those who drink from it.
There is a very great abundance of these beasts in Asia, Solinus [says].

The salamander, or chameleon, whichever you prefer, produces eggs like a hen and brings forth young from them. It should accordingly be noted, however, as Pliny says, that the salamander has no male or female, but all of them give birth.
The Book of Kyranides says that the salamander's heart most effectively extinguishes the fire of fevers and of lust, when carried near the knee.

It is also told that Pope Alexander had a garment made from the wool of this animal, which, whenever it needed cleaning, was washed with no other water than being thrown into the fire, and through the fire it became white again. I myself, too, have seen a belt woven from the wool of this animal, which, to test the truth of this, I threw with my own hand into a most powerful fire, and, after a long space, took back that same belt, glowing like iron from the fire, and, once cooled and handled after an hour, could not find that even a single hair of it had been consumed.

Aldhelm, in the book of Riddles, wrote in verse, speaking in the person of the salamander: Living in the midst of fires, I do not feel their flames, but I make of them the mockery of the pyre's harm. I do not burn with the crackling pyre nor the sparking ember, but grow warm with the flaming dew of the flame.
The 'salpiga' is a serpent that is not easily seen because of its smallness, and yet has the greatest power to harm.

It signifies the vice of hidden rancor, which infects many even without their noticing, and, while the fault is not released from the heart toward one's neighbor, gradually sprouting into hatred, the evil of vengeance is sought out, without heeding what has been said by the Lord: Unless you forgive men their sins from your hearts, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins.

The stellio-lizard, as Isidore says, has its name given from its color; for its back is painted with shining spots like little stars. It is so opposed to scorpions that, once seen, it brings them fear and paralysis.

It signifies those who, endowed with the beauty of natural goods, or with the power of heavenly grace, are a terror to those who do evil. Whence, wherever the sons of Israel were, there was light; and it is well known that, when they arrived, the darkness fled.

The stellio is a serpent, as Pliny says. Its venom is deadly. But a remedy is made against it from the crushed flesh of a scorpion. For nature has always implanted an opposite for its created evils. Wine in which a stellio has been drowned and died causes blotches on the face. The gall of stellios, crushed in water, is said, by some hidden instinct, to gather weasels together. The stellio is most opposed to scorpions, and they pursue one another with a natural hatred. But since the stellio is larger and stronger, the scorpion fears it in a wondrous way, so much so that, at the sight of it, it is drenched in a cold sweat.

The 'scaura' is a serpent, as James and Solinus say, which, when it grows old, becomes blind in its eyes; deprived of sight, it then enters an opening in a wall facing the sunrise, so that, as the sun rises, it may turn its eyes toward the sun and thus recover its sight.

So too those who lack the light of the Scriptures, turning their hearts toward the Sun of justice, raise themselves up in contemplation, so that what practice or the letter denied them, divine inspiration may instruct, and what the negligence of their old life wore away, the holy exercise of a new life may restore.

The 'sytula,' as James and Solinus say, is a malicious and small serpent, which kills a man by thirst. This serpent, then, shines with such variety that it delays onlookers by its beauty, and, since nature made it slower in crawling, it holds those it cannot catch spellbound by wonder. It is, moreover, of such heat that it sheds its skin in winter. If anyone is touched by its bite, seized by a fiery burning, he is set aflame.

Siren-serpents exist, just as sirens are sea monsters. As the Experimentator says, they dwell in the regions of Arabia and are stronger in running than horses. Some of them have wings and can fly. Their venom is so strong and so effective in bringing death that the bite is followed by death before pain.

They signify those who, with grievous pain and the remorse of conscience, commit sins, and yet are so wretched and worm-like that they let themselves be overcome by wicked temptation. Their sins, according to the Apostle, already go before them to judgment. The worm of their conscience begins to gnaw at them here, and will not cease for eternity. Whence Isaiah: their worm does not die, and the fire is not extinguished.

The scorpion is a serpent, as Solinus says, said to have a soft and, as it were, maidenly countenance. But it has, in its knotted tail, a venomous sting, with which it pricks and infects those who approach it. It strikes, moreover, with a sideways and curved blow, and never for a moment ceases to seek opportunities to strike. Those infected with its venom draw out death over three days. It is said that some have twin stingers, and that the males are the most savage. These are distinguished by their slenderness and length. Apollodorus indeed says that some have wings. The Psylli people, for their own profit, since by sucking venom from men's limbs they draw it out, have filled Italy with foreign evils. Whence they also tried to bring these creatures into Italy, but they could not live in that region. They are nevertheless sometimes seen in Italy, but most are harmless. For a man struck by a scorpion, its own ash, drunk in wine, is thought to be a remedy.
The Book of Kyranides says of the scorpion that, roasted, an ordinary scorpion, given secretly in food, breaks a stone in the bladder and allows painless urination.

[a fragmentary account of] little worm-like eggs. When the father wishes to devour these, those that place themselves on their mother's haunches are safe. The scorpion alone among insects has a tail, and arms, and a sting in its tail. The scorpion lays eggs in spring, and likewise in autumn. The scorpion, as Aristotle says, has two stingers. The scorpion lives on land.

As the Experimentator says, a black pig, if stung by a scorpion, dies without doubt; but a pig of another color sometimes escapes, though not always. [If you submerge a scorpion in oil, and pour vinegar over it in the sun, it revives at once. Oil blocks the pores, vinegar opens them.]
The scorpion, as Jerome says, strikes with a curved wound (that is, triangular).
[a fragmentary note:] scorpion
The 'serps' is a serpent, as Solinus says, small in body, but great and harmful in malice. Whomever it strikes, it consumes flesh and bone together with its venom, as if seized by a devouring flame.

There are, as James and Solinus say, in many parts of the East, but especially in India, serpents so vast that they are said to devour stags and to cross the ocean itself. There are also other serpents that eat white pepper; these are said to have precious stones in their heads. They fight among themselves every year and for the most part kill one another. There are also other serpents in the East which, having horns like rams', strike men by fanning them.

Some wish the tortoise to be of the kind of serpents. It is, however, an animal with two feet. It is covered with two very hard shields, like shells, and is so armored with these that it can be killed only with difficulty, even by the strongest blows. It has a head like a toad's, a tail like a scorpion's, a weak voice. It lays eggs like a hen, but its eggs are harmful to eat. It lacks venom in life, but by no means after death.
For, as Ambrose says, if anyone treads with a bare foot on its kidneys after death, he is at once infected with venom.

The female tortoise, as Aristotle says, has only one passage for the excretion of waste, though it has a bladder; and this is contrary to all animals having a bladder: for animals that have a bladder have two passages for the excretion of waste. It has, then, a bladder contrary to the nature of all animals that have feathers, or scales, or a shell, since all these lack a bladder.

The 'tarans' is a serpent, as Pliny says, of the scorpion kind. It is small, has wings, is capable of flight, and is deadly. For whomever it stings dies, unless theriac or medical remedies come to his aid. Italy often has these, but most often harmless; the East, however, has many, but always venomous. It lives most often twenty days or more without food. Killed and left to putrefy in oil, that same oil becomes a remedy against poisons and the stings of the tarans.

The 'tysus' is a serpent in the mountains of Padua, six or seven feet in length, yet very slender, and thicker in its hind parts than in its front. It has a small, sharp tail, a hand's-breadth long. It moves on its belly, having ribs which, visibly moved, it uses like feet in running. Its running is most swift, its leap beyond estimation. When it runs or moves, it holds its head and neck, down to the belly, and its ribs, raised upright and high. It harms no one, unless gravely provoked. It has two red lines on its back. Its flesh, left to putrefy, is given as food and drink against leprosy, and often proves a most effective remedy.

div.head: 43. De tyro serpente unde tyriaca conficitur

cit.quote: The 'tyrus,' as James and the Book of Properties say, is a serpent in the regions of Jericho, around the wildernesses of the Jordan. It is a serpent hostile to birds and animals, and especially to birds' eggs, which it eats and swallows along with the birds themselves. Its flesh, prepared like an electuary with certain ingredients mixed in, expels and roots out every poison. This preparation is called theriac.

Some relate that before Christ's passion this serpent had no remedy and was most hostile to men, but that on the very day Christ was hung upon the cross, one of these serpents, most hostile, was caught around the region of Jerusalem and hung on the cross at Christ's side; and from that day the whole kind of this serpent received, through the shedding of Christ's blood, the power of a most effective remedy against every poison.

Aristotle: there is a kind of dragon in that land where the tyrus serpents are, in the land of Ethiopia, and from it comes a kind of poison called 'tychicon,' which is an incurable evil. For though theriac is effective against every poison, against the venom of the tyrus itself, called tychicon, it is of no use. The tyrus is a serpent which, worn out with age, sheds its skin in this way: it first strips the skin that is between its eyes, so that, if you did not know better, you would think the beast blind. Then it removes the skin of its head, and this in a single night and day. Once the head is stripped, the rest of the body is easily stripped. Once it is stripped, it has the manner and appearance of an embryo. There is a certain small kind of the tyrus, a cubit long, bristling with hair over its whole body, whose bite putrefies the wound around it and then kills. The tyrus of India is exceedingly dangerous. The tyrus lays eggs within itself, and, before it comes forth, becomes a living creature, and thus generates its like.

The 'tyliacus' is a snake-like worm, as the Book of Properties says, often seen in many parts of the world. This worm is called 'tyliacus' from the linden tree ['tylia'], because it is born within, in the pith of the tree. Once born there, it feeds first on the pith, then on the wood itself around and within it, until, the tree consumed within, it brings it down in ruin. This snake, then, is said to grow to an immense size and to lie in wait for livestock.

It signifies the remorse of mortal sin, even when the judgment of the sin is in doubt. Let no one, then, commit himself to danger in doubt, but, setting doubt aside, let him more confidently rely on what is certain. For in accepting the scruple of doubt, one runs into the certainty of danger, just as the prophet coming from Judea to Bethel to reprove King Jeroboam, having accepted in doubt the suggestion of a false prophet, thereby incurred, by divine judgment, the certainty of death through a lion. Such men, then, sometimes lingering in doubts, gradually, through carelessness, begin to fear danger less and less, and, while not guarding against uncertain evils, fall into certain dangers, and the strength of mind that could have stood secure in certain matters is destroyed by the contempt of doubtful ones.

The viper, as James and Isidore say, is a serpent so named because it gives birth 'by force' [vi pariat]. Its nature is told thus: the father dies at conception, the mother is killed in giving birth; for the female, driven, as it were, into madness by the pleasure of lust, seizes the male's head in her mouth and cuts it off. When her belly has swollen for birth, the young, not waiting for the mature release of nature, gnawing through her sides, burst forth by force, with their mother's death. They have only cavities in place of ears, and only three teeth. Its bite is said to be incurable. It also brings on swelling and inflation.
This indeed was known to those who escaped the sea with Paul, and, when the viper attacked Paul's hand, believed he would swell up and suddenly fall down and die.
The great Basil and Ambrose relate that if anyone incautiously treads on the kidneys of a dead viper, it is said to cause harm worse than the venom itself, and an incurable wound to spread.
Its entrails are effective against the bites of all serpents, as Pliny says.
The Experimentator says that the viper's coat - that is, the skin it casts off when renewed - cooked in wine, heals the teeth and eyes. Its fat, however, removes clouding of the eyes.

The Physiologus says that the viper has a human face down to the navel, but from the navel to the tail the form of a crocodile. Its digestive passage is said to be like the eye of a needle, and so it cannot conceive in the manner of other beasts, but only through the mouth.

Pliny seems to speak much more truly and credibly, as being deeper in reasoning. For he relates of the viper, saying that the pregnant mother, when the time of giving birth arrives, expels one offspring each day, and, since there are many offspring - indeed twenty in number - the rest, which cannot be expelled and remain beyond the due time, impatient of the delay, burst through her sides, their parent killed. The viper hides itself in the earth in winter.

This serpent, though it is nearly the cruelest among all kinds of serpents, is nevertheless gentle toward its own female, as the great Basil and Ambrose say. For the viper seeks out its absent female, calls to her when absent, and cries out with a soft hiss; and when it senses its mate approaching, it vomits out its venom, showing reverence to its wife, respectful (and honoring) the grace of marriage.

But you, O man, capable of reason, repudiate your wife and think she should often be changed, and, if she is absent one day, you suspect her of adultery and at once, the cause unknown, pursue the wrong as if it were known: lay aside harshness of manner, when your devoted wife comes to meet you; drive away indignation: you are not a master but a husband; you have obtained not a slave but a wife. Here ends the book on serpents.

In general, concerning worms: bees, the spider, the adlacta, the toad, the horned toad, cockroaches, the silkworm, the locust [brucus] [and the stag-beetle], the glow-worm, the dog-fly, gnats, the mosquito, blister-beetles [cantharides], hornets, the bed-bug, the cicada, the caterpillar, the 'engulas,' the ant, the ant-lion, also called 'mirmicaleon,' the ants of India, locusts, the wool-worm, the millipede, the fly, the 'opimacus,' butterflies, spiders [phalangia], fleas, lice, the common frog, the toad, a kind of frog, the little frog, the running frog, the star-shaped worm, the despoiler of the snake, the 'setha,' the buprestis-beetle, the leech, the 'tamur,' called Solomon's worm, the 'tappula,' the tortoise-beetle [testudo], the moth, wood-worms [teredines], the 'tharmus,' the 'uria,' wasps, worms born from the earth, celandine-worms. Here end the chapters. Here begins the ninth book, on worms.

In general, first, something must be said of worms. No insect - that is, no worm - as Pliny says, has blood, except in a small quantity. 'Insect,' moreover, is the name given to every proliferation of worms. Some worms are without feet, yet have bones within, like serpents; these crawl along the ground. Others, however, have no bones in their body and no feet, and these instead draw themselves along by certain very fine wrinkles stretched in their skin, by which they move or crawl. Others have two feet or four; these run and have some small amount of blood. Others, however, have more than four feet and also run, but are entirely without blood; and this is because the blood passes into nourishment for the many feet, or because the movement of the many feet reduces to nothing the small amount of blood that is in other worms with few feet. Every kind of worm has a humor, like matter, in place of blood. There is also another kind of worm which has feet and walks, and yet, having wings, or rather membranes, is raised in flight to the sky. This kind of worm lives mostly on the leaves of trees and gnaws them with its teeth. Some worms of the flying kind, however, do not gnaw, but live instead on moisture. Many kinds of worms begin with summer and end with summer, since they are born more from corruption than from seed. There is also another kind of worm, which indeed begins with summer, and, once it has laid its seed on trees or in dwellings, ends with summer, and the seeds remain, once the parents have died, through the winter, and, as spring approaches, with the clear air and the sun's warmth, are brought to life. There is also another kind of worm, which hides in winter and lies as if dead, and, when summer comes, is renewed to life. Worms generally take on colors or powers according to the nourishment of the elements, so that those that have much of the element of fire seek the air above, those that have much of air run more swiftly; those that do not have much of earth or water are slower: for earth and water press down and weigh heavy, while fire and air lift up and stir. According to these principles the order of all creatures is arranged.

Bees, as Aristotle, the great Basil, and Ambrose relate, have, among every kind of living creature, offspring in common; they all inhabit one dwelling, are enclosed within the boundary of one homeland. Labor is shared by all, food shared, work shared, use and enjoyment shared, flight shared. What more? Generation is shared by all, and virginal bodily integrity is shared by all, and birth too, since they mingle in no mutual coupling with one another, nor are they dissolved in lust, nor are they shaken by the pains of childbirth, and yet they suddenly produce the greatest swarm of offspring. They appoint a king for themselves, they create peoples: and though they are placed under a king, they are nevertheless free. For they hold the prerogative of judgment and the affection of faithful devotion, since they both love him as if he were established by themselves and honor him with so great a swarm that no controversy or discord is ever stirred up against him. Nor is this a wonder, since a certain kindness of the king toward his people, and a certain obedience of the people toward the king, is always preserved.

Pliny: for this reason, among all the animals of the flying, insect kind, admiration is rightly greatest for bees. They gather honey, a most sweet, most refined, and most wholesome nectar, and fashion honeycombs and wax, produced for a thousand uses of life, enduring labor; they hold private councils and fly in schools behind their leaders, and are of a nature neither tame nor wild. Let us further consider their intelligence: in winter they hide away, in summer no day is lost to idleness, whenever the sky allows it. They harm no fruits, nor even withered flowers. [They take the nourishment of honey not only from fragrant but even from foul-smelling plants; yet they always wish to be among flowers, and delight more in good smells than bad: for they naturally flee foul odors, but sometimes usefully linger among them for the sake of honey's nourishment.] They work within sixty paces, and, once the flowers nearby are used up, send out scouts to more distant pastures. Caught out at night on an expedition, they keep watch lying on their backs, so as to protect their wings from dew and rain. Bees make a buzzing noise in flight because of the air trapped between their wings and body. The common people of bees are divided into three groups. There are kings, and, as it were, princes among bees. For in one hive only one rules with the insignia of command. This one is always more distinguished in form and twice as large as the rest, its wings shorter, its legs upright, its bearing loftier, and, marked on the forehead with a certain spot like a kind of diadem, it also differs from the common bees by much greater brightness. It is agreed among authorities that the emperor of bees has no sting, armed only with majesty. And since nature denied it a sting, the emperor of the human kingdom likewise, by a similar reasoning, lacks this. The first group, then, of those bees are the mothers and the retired ones, and they are lesser than the rest. The second group is that of the younger bees, which, performing their tasks with great vigor, are subject to the mothers as if by a kind of discipline and do nothing without the command of their elders. The third group is that of those bees called drones: these are without a sting, like imperfect bees; these are, as it were, dependents and servants of the first and true bees; the first bees drive these out, and, when they are slow at their work, kill them without mercy; not only do they help with the work, but also with the brood, the crowd contributing to the warmth. When the honey begins to ripen, they drive them away. When some wish to leave, many, going out one by one, kill them. Then the mothers drive out the middle group of bees, as sufficiently trained and able to fend for themselves, and these, once driven out, seek a place for themselves, since they are to provide for themselves. Once raised, they immediately work under a certain discipline together with some of the mothers, whom they have as teachers, and accompany their young emperor with attentive reverence.

As Palladius says, the keeper of bees ought to be watchful, because at that time the young bees are restless in spirit, so that, unless watched, they will escape you. Two or three days beforehand they grow more agitated and murmur loudly. Then, the king first going out, the whole people follows. And it should be noted that, if they settle in one place or on one branch of a tree, and hang suspended from a single cluster, you will know that there is one king for them all, or that, all having been reconciled, harmony remains. But if they divide into two or more clusters, you will know they are discordant, and that there are as many kings as clusters you find. Then, with a hand smeared with honey, you will separate the bees among the clusters and, having caught the kings, whom you will recognize by their size, keep the better one and crush the rest.

They arrange the work of their dwellings after the manner of a military camp: the first roughly three rows are built empty, so that there is nothing readily visible to invite one standing outside. The last rows are filled most fully with honey.

Ambrose: what architect taught them to construct those arrangements of cells with an undistinguished equality of sides, and to hang thin partitions of wax between the chambers, and to pack in honey and stretch out storehouses woven with flowers with a certain nectar? At first, honey is diluted like water, and in the first days it ferments like new wine and purges itself; on the twentieth day it thickens, and is soon covered with a thin membrane, which forms from the foam of its own fermentation. This is the arrangement of bees: they have rest in the morning, until one rouses them with a double or triple trumpet-call. If the coming day is to be mild - for they foresee rain and winds - then they all fly out; but if the day is to be stormy, then they keep themselves within their roofs. When, then, the column has gone out to work, some gather flowers with their feet, others droplets with their mouth and water with the down of their whole body. Ambrose: you would see them all competing for their task, some watching over the search for provisions, others anxious about the camp and keeping guard, others foreseeing coming rains and watching the movements of the stars. Those of an age for it go out to the tasks and bring back the aforesaid things; the older ones work within. Those that gather flowers load their thighs with their front feet, and return wholly laden, the burden hanging; three or four others receive them and unload them. For there are various offices within: some build, some polish, some carry, some distribute food from what has been brought in; for they do not feed separately, lest there be an inequality of work, food, and time.

Pliny: their observance of work is remarkable: they note the idleness of the lazy, correct it, and soon punish it even with death. Their cleanliness is remarkable: they remove everything filthy to the middle, no refuse lies among their works; indeed, they even place the excrement of the workers within, so that it does not need to be carried far, so that, gathered in one place, they may carry it out, collected, on stormy days when work is idle. As evening approaches, the buzzing in the hive grows less and less, until one flies around, ordering rest with the same trumpet-call by which it roused them, and this in the manner of a military camp. Then suddenly all fall silent. They build the dwellings of the common bees first, then those of the kings. If a more abundant yield is expected, they add further chambers. They build palaces for future emperors on one side of the hive, spacious, magnificent, separate, and more prominent than the rest. Several emperors are begun in one work and offspring come afterward, but once they have begun to mature, all, by unanimous consent, kill the inferior ones, lest they divide the swarm and stir up rebellions.
