Let the irrationality of human peoples be put to shame here, who often create for themselves worse prelates or judges, and, on the other hand, in some manner kill the worthy and necessary ones as regards due authority by rendering them useless, seeing, by contrast, that bees, the tiniest of creatures and without the experience of reason, by natural instinct, with unanimous consent, kill the inferior ones, lest they divide the swarm and stir up rebellions. How they produce offspring has been a great and subtle question among the learned. For the mating of bees has nowhere been seen. Most have thought it more fitting to suppose that they are made and produced from flowers; others, however, have said that there is one male, called the emperor, distinguished by his size, and that the females accompany him as a male, not as a leader. But this opinion is improbable, since mating, among such subtle investigators, could hardly have remained hidden. They brood their offspring like hens. What first hatches appears as a small white worm, so that it seems merely to be feeding. But the emperor's offspring is at once of a honey color, made from the choicest flower and from every abundance, and does not have, at the start, the worm-like appearance the others have, but at once takes on, feathered, the form of the mature, along with the crowd. The obedience of the common bees toward their emperor is remarkable. When he goes out, the whole column is one and gathers around him, surrounding and protecting him. At other times, when the people are at work, he goes around among the workers, similar to them, as if encouraging them, alone exempt from work. Around him are certain attendants and guards, constant custodians of his authority. He does not easily let himself be seen, nor does he go out, except when the swarm is about to migrate. This is understood by much noise: for some days beforehand they murmur within, choosing, as a sign of preparation, a fitting day.

Ambrose: none then dare leave their dwellings, unless the king has gone out first and claimed the leadership of their flight. Their procession, then, is through fragrant countryside, where gardens open to flowers, where a stream flees through the grasses, where the pleasant riverbanks are: there is the eager play of youth, there the exercise of the fields, there the sweet excursion among flowers. Among the sweet herbs they busy themselves curiously testing the fragrances. Then, after feeding, gathered together again, they sing sweetly. For they have a pleasing and wondrous sweetness of voice in their murmur, which we seem, by making the sound of trumpets, at first to imitate somewhat sluggishly, by which sound it is thought more fitting to rouse spirits to vigor. With these trumpet-like songs the throngs of bees surround their emperor and each is eager to encourage their great-hearted king to become also glorious.

If anyone passing by destroys the wing of the emperor nearby, the swarm will not flee. When they go forth, each one desires to be nearest to him and rejoices to be seen in his service. They lift the tired on their shoulders, the stronger ones carry them entirely. If one has grown weary or has by chance wandered off, they follow by scent. Wherever he goes, there is the camp of the rest. As long as the emperor is safe, the whole swarm holds together; once lost, it disperses and migrates to others, wherever an emperor is; and indeed they cannot exist without an emperor. Pliny: but if honey is ever lacking in a hive, they make an attack and rush upon the nearest hives with plunder in mind. But these, in turn, draw up their ranks against them. They also fight for other reasons, and two emperors draw up opposing battle lines. This quarrel arises most from the gathering of flowers. This fighting is entirely dispelled by throwing dust or smoke. They are reconciled, however, with milk or water. There are also rustic or wild bees, rough in appearance, much more irascible, but more excellent in labor and work. There are two kinds of domestic bees: the best are short, varied, and, for all their shortness, compact; the worse are long, resembling wasps, and the worst of these are hairy. In Pontus there are bees that make honey twice a month. There are some that make honey in trees, others that make it underground with a triple row of combs, most abundantly. Nature gave bees a sting, joined to the belly, for a single strike. Once this is embedded, some say they die at once; others say this is not so, unless it is driven in so deeply that the intestine follows it out. Once the sting is lost, they say bees make no more honey thereafter. They hate foul smells and flee them from afar; false perfumes also trouble them. Their natural enemies that attack them are the butterfly, the wasp, hornets. Swallows too, and similarly other birds, prey upon them. Frogs also lie in wait for them as they drink water, and it is said that bees do not feel the strike of frogs. Sheep are hostile to them, since they entangle themselves with difficulty in their wool. They are also killed by the smell of crabs, if these are cooked nearby. They also die together at the smell of the dead. If anyone pours oil-juice over them, they are nearly killed, since, their pores blocked, they cannot draw in the airy breath; and at once, if anyone pours vinegar (and oil) over the dead ones, they revive immediately, since the force of vinegar is said quickly to open, with its moisture, the pores that were blocked by the constriction of the oil.
A bee's wing, as Aristotle says, if cut off or if it falls out, never grows back.

The bee stays in its cave during the cold days and does not eat from its prepared food. It stays in caves from the setting of the Pleiades until springtime. It also has an enemy in the butterfly, and not in one way only; for it also feeds on the wax and leaves excrement, from which wood-worms are bred. Sadness and sluggishness are a sign of these things. They accompany funerals in the manner of mourners. When their emperor is destroyed by this plague, the common people grieve. These are the signs of their sorrow: they do not gather food nor go out; sad, they cluster around the emperor's body, and, gazing at him lifeless, mourn. Then, unless they are helped, they die of hunger. As the Experimentator says, bees fall ill especially when the flowers are swelling with bud.

The great Basil: bees, when they have stung someone, sometimes give up their life together with their sting in the wound. Let Christians listen, who are commanded to render evil to no one for evil, but to overcome malice with goodness.

Pliny: an echo with resounding sound is their enemy. A mist, too, is their enemy. Spiders too are especially hostile to them: when they have gained the upper hand and woven their webs around them, they kill them. Health is judged by their liveliness and brightness. They delight in applause and the ringing of bronze, and are summoned by it, whence it is remarkable that they have a sense of hearing. Once the work is finished, the brood raised, every duty performed, they hold a kind of solemn exercise, wandering in the open and rising up high, then finally return to food. Their life is longest at seven years; they are said never to last beyond ten years. Some say that dead ones revive, if kept under a roof in winter and then placed in the sun in springtime; they are thought to revive. Bees can be produced from the fresh bellies of buffalo, buried with dung; Virgil says these are produced from the lifeless body of a beast of burden, just as wasps and hornets come from the bodies of horses, and beetles from the bodies of asses. But it should be noted that bees produced from buffalo and beasts of burden mate like flies; but in their offspring they have nearly the same nature as true bees. Honey should be gathered at the full moon on a clear day. That it breaks off at once and springs back is a sign of poor quality. The proof of good quality, however, is that it be fragrant, of sweet substance, sticky, and translucent. When the honey is removed, it is most useful to drive away the bees with smoke, lest they grow angry and greedily devour the honey. With darker smoke their sluggishness is roused to work; for when they brood too much, they make the combs discolored. Again, with too much smoke they are harmed, whose injury the honey feels most quickly. Honey is hot in the first degree and dry in the second. Honey preserves and cleanses. It is used in medicines, so that the bitterness of the ingredients is tempered by its sweetness. In electuaries too it is mixed with powders, so that they are preserved longer and with greater efficacy. Against the cold humors of the stomach, honey should be given with warm water; for it cleanses and dissolves. It is also good for clearing the complexion, washed with honey and water. A suppository, too, made of honey roasted in a shell mixed with salt, is very effective for the feverish.
The spider, so as to catch flies, weaves a most delicate net from its own entrails. For it eviscerates itself for the catching of flies so often that, entirely emptied, it fails and dies.

What, then, of you, preacher and teacher of the word of God: should you not take care to weave nets, as it were, from your own inmost heart, not to catch the vanities of empty glory as if they were flies, but so that, with diligent and gentle admonitions, you may untiringly catch your hearers? Blessed indeed is the man who will meditate in wisdom, etc.

For within spiders there is a certain wool-bearing material, subtle and sufficient for the work. This they draw out with so measured a claw, so round a thread, so even a warp, that they mock every human art that imitates them. Beginning to weave from the middle, they attach the crossing threads in a rounded circle, at equal intervals. And if prey should fall into it meanwhile, how alert and ready is their response! But once sated, they are accustomed to carefully entangle the other flies that have fallen into the net, the surplus, so that they do not escape, so that, when hungry again, they may find food already desired and prepared. The one that weaves is thought to be the female, the one that hunts the male: thus the merits of the spider's pairing are made equal. They join at the haunches, and bear little worms similar to eggs. They lay their eggs among their webs. [Spiders are also born without mating, from corruption, as it were from the dust of atoms and the spittle of a man who has just eaten.]

Aristotle says that the mating of spiders occurs mostly at the end of spring, that is, at the beginning of summer. When they wish to mate, then, the female draws the male toward her by the threads of the web, and the male likewise draws the female, and they do not stop until they are joined. The spider flees heavy moisture and dry substance, but delights in a moderate, temperate condition.

Likewise it weaves in clear weather, and does not weave in cloudy weather, Pliny [says]. There are also false omens the pagans draw from it, since, as the years progress, they raise their webs higher. They live on juice; therefore none dies of hunger. The spider does not hunt until it has repaired what has been spent of its web.

As the Experimentator says, a spider's web placed on a wound keeps it from swelling and corruption. The spider balances itself by a thread over the head of a serpent stretched out in a tree's shade, and its bite has such power that it seizes hold of its brain and does not let go until its death. It is a sign of rain when spiders raise their webs higher.
The 'adlacta,' though different in color from the locust, nevertheless leaps like the locust; it has longer hind legs, like the locust.

And by these are signified those who, according to the Apostle, straining forward toward the eternal life to come, are by no means stretched out with the longest affections toward passing, temporal things.
The adlacta lays eggs for its offspring, from which young come forth in springtime.
And blessed works, done only in hope of reward, so that from these they may receive the fruit of eternal salvation.

Toads, as the Book of Properties says, are counted among the other worms. It is a venomous reptile, with a pestilential look and a filthy touch. It feeds on earth, and this by weight and measure. For as much as it can hold in its front foot, this is its daily food. For it fears that earth may fail it as food; and in this it signifies the miserly and the greedy.

div.head: 6. De buffonibus minoribus, qui et ‘cornuti’ dicuntur

cit.quote: There is a kind of toad in the regions of Gaul, which has the name 'cornuti' [horned]; and this from the sound of its voice, in that they seem to sound like a horn. They have two colors, dark and saffron. They come forth in spring, and then give out sounds like trumpets. They answer each other's calls, two by two. They live, croaking, only in Gaul. Raised up, they lose their voices and are silent.

And these signify preachers who are unwilling to preach unless among their acquaintances and in their own land, not heeding the judgment of the prophet Jonah, who, disobedient in this, was given by God to the whale to be devoured.

The 'borax' is of the toad kind, having a frog's face, as the Experimentator says. It is a venomous animal, [a near-duplicate repetition follows in the source, again attributed to the Experimentator]. Whence, because of the quantity of its venom, when touched, it swells up. It fights with the spider and is overcome by it; and this because, when the spider has repeatedly stung the borax and it cannot take revenge, it swells up so much with inflation that it bursts in the middle. The borax's bite is most severe and becomes incurable. It nurtures a precious stone in its forehead, for which it is killed. There are two kinds of these stones, one white, and this the better, the other dark and black, and it has in its middle an eye, which somewhat resembles a sky-blue color; and this one, of the dark kind, is the better. This stone, taken as food, is said to heal the internal ailments of man. For it travels around the intestines and, the cure accomplished, exits through the lower region. It must, however, be swallowed whole. The borax, then, uses a special herb when its eye is blinded, and by this recovers its sight. It is killed by rue. It gladly dwells in damp and rotting places. It hates the brightness of the sun and does not easily bear to see it. It walks at night, and this more on the paths worn by human footsteps; by day it rests in hidden places. It flees the scent of a flowering vineyard. It sometimes grows to nearly a cubit in size. In the regions of Spain is the best kind of borax, and especially that which bears the stone we call in French 'crapaudine,' but in Latin 'borax,' from the animal from which, once hardened, it is taken. It is also said to be an antidote to poison.

Cockroaches are worms named from their color, as Isidore says, since, when caught, they stain the hand; whence they are also said to have the color 'blatteus.' This worm cannot bear to see the light, and this is the opposite of the fly. For the fly seeks the light, the cockroach flees the light. For it walks only by night.
He who walks in darkness is ignorant and does not know where he is going. But he who walks in the day of understanding does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world, Christ.

The silkworm, as Pliny says, is a small worm found in Assyria. It shapes its nest from clay with such hardness that it cannot be pierced by darts. In this they make wax more abundantly than bees, and afterward a larger worm. In the manner of spiders, it weaves webs for the clothing and luxury of women, which is called 'silk.'

Weave for yourself, then, O soul, with diligent practice, an ordered arrangement of body and soul, so that, according to Isaiah, Christ, in his members, may be clothed, by your example, as with an adornment, and it may be said to you in the Song of Songs: How beautiful are your steps in your sandals, daughter of the prince (Christ).

The 'brucus' [young locust], as the Gloss says, is smaller in body than the adlacta, and has less strength for leaping. It is of a tawny color. This one grazes on vegetables, plants, and the foliage of trees with a bitter bite, and there is no remedy in the place where a multitude gathers. And in this it signifies slanderers, hateful to God, according to the Apostle.
The brucus does more harm than the locust, as the Experimentator says.

The stag-beetle is a worm the size of a human thumb. It is black, has wings, and flies, its forehead roughened with horns like a stag's. Once its head is cut off, it is said to live for some time still, even having lost its body. It grips firmly with its horns whatever it seizes.

The glow-worm is a kind of beetle, as Isidore says, [named] from the fact that it shines while flying or walking. [It is a worm found in Italy.] It is, however, a worm like a small fly. It is seen in many parts of the world, but especially in Italy. It flies for fifteen days before the summer solstice and fifteen days after. It never flies by day, but only by night, and shines among the darkness like sparks, so brightly that, if you saw it in the dark, you would think it a shower of sparks. [That brightness is especially in its tail, and more so while it flies; but when it folds its wings, it is seen less. It is found endowed with a marvelous power; for if anyone eats three of these worms, his lust will be entirely extinguished; and many who have tried this have proven it.]

Blessed, then, is he who, bright with works and the reputation of virtues, dwells amid the darkness of the world, not overtaken by darkness. Let your works, then, (good ones) shine before men, that they may glorify the Father who is in heaven.

The dog-fly is a worm, as Isidore says, called in Greek 'canine fly,' for 'cyno' in Greek means 'dog.' This fly is troublesome to the ears of puppies, and although they frequently shake it off, it nevertheless always flies back, insistent; but where it finds puppies too lazy to shake it off, it presses on, insistent, even to the point of blood and wounds.

And in this it signifies the devil, whose suggestions, if anyone, careless in shaking them off, receives into the ear of the mind, will inflict a wound reaching even to consent to sin or to delight in it. As Abraham, then, drive away flies and the winged creatures of evil thoughts, and this with the rod that is the sign of the cross. For with a staff David came to Goliath, and with a staff Jacob crossed the Jordan, that is, the onslaught of temptations and evil thoughts, which, according to the wise man, separate from God.
Gnats, as the Book of Properties says, are very tiny, flying worms. Egypt is recorded to have been scourged by these through Moses. They follow the breath of livestock, and this especially of man.

They sting, as Aldhelm says, sleeping people with certain stings, with a fairly sharp pain as best they can. Whence, in places where their impudence abounds, delicate people are accustomed to have a net stretched, finely woven, around their beds, so that through it gnats cannot pass to do harm. Weave for yourself, then, from constant reading and prayer, a guard for the mind, so that the devil cannot enter to do harm.

The mosquito is a worm, as Isidore says, and takes its name from its sting, in that it sucks blood. For it has, in its mouth, a tube like a goad, with which it bores into the flesh of animals, so as to drink blood.
As the Experimentator says, the mosquito loves the light so much that it sometimes burns itself at a flame.
Mosquitoes seek out sour things and flee sweet ones (as Pliny says).

And in these, woe to the slanderers of dragons, who are always occupied in spreading the evil deeds of men, and care for no good, so as to recount it as an example; of such men it is said in the song of Deuteronomy: their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps.
If you wish to be freed from mosquitoes on the road or while sleeping, eat garlic, and they will not trouble you.

Blister-beetles [cantharides] are worms that are generated at the tips of the branches of the ash or alder tree, from the tree's moisture in the leaves, and grow like caterpillars, but develop full wings and fly by day. At night, however, they gather together into a single cluster. These worms, of a green color, shine like gold in the sun's rays. Around the month of August they are gathered at night as a remedy and are killed, steeped in vinegar. Once dead, however, poured over with wine, they are placed on whatever limb you wish, beneath a small wax vessel shaped like a cup, and, by their application, raise a blister on the skin. This blister, pierced in several places with a golden needle or the point of a straw, discharges bad humor like a cautery; and its discharge over fifteen days is as effective as any cautery within a year.

Hornets, as Pliny says, live in caves or underground. Their cells are six-sided, of a bark-like, spider-web-like wax. Their offspring itself is uneven and rough: one flies out, another is still in water, another remains a little worm. They feed on flesh. They grow at the full moon. In winter they hide away. Authorities say that a two-year-old child is killed by nine stings of hornets. Hornets and wasps have no kings, as bees do, but are governed by their own individual rule, whence it happens that they are subject to many more dangers. They emit horrid sounds and murmurs, and more so in hollow places. Their honey is useless for human purposes, and whoever wishes to steal it exposes himself to a foolish danger, for he is pierced by their stings.
The bed-bug is a worm, as Isidore says, named from its resemblance to a certain plant, and has its stench.
It signifies the vice of the lustful, who rotted like beasts of burden in their own dung, so that their stench troubled the heavens (that is, spiritual beings).

Cicadas, as the Book of Properties says, are worms, of which there are two kinds: some are similar to locusts. These dwell in houses and in places that are warmer, namely where there is constant heat. There is another kind, dark in color, similar to butterflies.

Pliny: the males sing, the females are silent. They mate lying on their backs. They have white eggs, but corrupted. They hollow out a place for their brood in the ground and produce their offspring there. In their chest they have something spine-like, resembling tongues, with which they lick the dew. Their chest itself is hollow like a pipe, and by this indeed they sing. Sweet is the melody in the tiny throat of the cicada

by whose songs, as Ambrose says, the groves are shattered in the midday heat, since they sing more in the midday heat; and in the way that, at that time of day, it draws in purer air with its breath, its songs resound more clearly.
In the territory of Reggio, as Pliny says, all cicadas are silent. Cicadas also fly with membranes. Their torn-out wings never grow back for any of them.

[a fragmentary note on] a kind [confused in the source with the stag-beetle] that we call 'stag-beetles,' which indeed the Experimentator calls 'scabrones.' Beneath their thicker wings, as he says, they have thin and delicate wings (like the young locust). They fly especially toward evening. In flying they make a noise. They have medicinal horns, long and curved legs. These have large, very long, cloven, toothed (and shining) horns, meeting like pincers at the tip when they wish to bite. Their sides and haunches shine at night like fire, glowing like fireflies' wings in color; sometimes, folded together, they are darkened. Their severed head lives longer, even having lost its body; but the body itself also lives without the head, though not as long as the head.

The caterpillar, as the Book of Properties says, is a long worm, set apart by its many feet. It is varied in color. It grazes on vegetables as well as the leaves of trees. Around the month of September, drenched by heavenly dew or rain, it is said suddenly to change its color and form, so that, having crawled on countless feet, it can now fly, wings having formed.
By worm, locust, and caterpillar, at the hand of Moses, Egypt is recorded to have been scourged.

Likewise, as Isidore says, the caterpillar is a worm of the foliage, devouring crops, cabbage, and vine-leaves. It does not fly off, like the locust, so as, running here and there, to leave things half-eaten, but stays with the crops as they perish and, with a slow crawl and lazy bites, consumes everything. And the caterpillar itself is finally consumed, after it has left, at the tops of trees, something like silk and woven material, which the following summer develops into worms. Sometimes, too, certain caterpillars, entering the roofs of houses, their form entirely changed, hang on the walls with a golden-yellow color, and there are reduced to nothing.
As the Experimentator says, a caterpillar passing over a man's flesh infects it and leaves pustules behind it, and this is a sign of venom, even if not potent enough for great harm.

The 'engula' [tick] is a worm that can take its name from the fact itself in this way. For, as Pliny says, it is a creature that always has its head in blood and, sucking continuously, swells up so much that it bursts in the middle; for it has no outlet for its surplus. It is called by some the 'wild louse'; some, however, call it the 'theca.' In beasts of burden - that is, oxen - it is never bred; but in wolves and dogs, frequently.
Solomon commands us to imitate the ant, where he says: Go to the ant, O sluggard, and learn wisdom. It is, then, a worm of wondrous foresight and watchfulness for its own life.

And so ants, as Pliny says, share their labor like bees; but bees make food, ants store it. But if anyone compares the loads to their bodies, he will admit that no animals have proportionally greater strength.

And in this it is greatly to be praised, since, though tiny and weak in body, it dares things greater than its strength, as Ambrose says. Nature giving them reason, they store seeds already gnawed, so that they do not sprout again into crops from the earth; they split the larger ones at the entrance to their den, and, once wetted by rain, bring out their seeds and dry them, lest they contract rot. For it knows how to detect times of clear weather.

The ant has a sense of smell, as Aristotle says; which is proven thus: take sulphur and wild oregano, and, powdered, place them over their dwellings, and at once they will flee and abandon their homes. Ants always cease working at the new moon. Among other animals, this alone grows stronger and increases with age. They work at the full moon; at the new moon they cease. What labor, then, in their work, what diligence! For indeed, since they carry burdens from different directions, certain days are given for mutual recognition; what a gathering there is then among them, what careful conversation and inquiry with those they meet! For we see the path worn by their traffic and made by their labor, so that no one may doubt how much even the smallest constancy can accomplish in a matter. They carry out their dead and bury them, and this alone, among all animals, they do, except man.

The ant-lion, also called 'mirmicoleon,' is explained by Aldhelm from 'mirmin,' which means ant, and 'leon,' which means lion, as if 'lion of the ants.' This worm is of the ant kind, but much larger. While it is still small and weak in strength, it feigns peace and modesty. But once it has gained strength, power, and size of body, it scorns its former companions and now keeps company with the greater crowd. Then, growing bolder, it hides in concealment and, after the example of robbers, lies in wait for the ants laboring for the common good, and, like a plunderer, seizes their loads or even kills and eats the ants themselves. But in winter, when the ants have stored their food in the ground as if in a granary, and the ant-lion, which had prepared nothing for itself in summer for the needs of life, plunders and destroys their labors.
This kind of animal signifies hypocrites and deceitful men within the cloister.

There are ants in India around the golden mountains. They are larger than foxes, strong and exceedingly fierce, having four feet and hooked claws on their feet. These beasts are of such strength that they tear apart men they see. But other beasts, such as horses, or asses, or bulls, they do not easily harm, well aware that they do not take away, against their will, the gold which they guard in the aforesaid mountains against mankind. These beasts are stationed there by God. Isidore and Aldhelm write of these ants.

Pliny also says of these: once hidden away in wintertime, the Indians come and steal the gold. But the beasts, roused by the scent, fly out and often tear apart even those fleeing on the swiftest horses or camels.

The slug is a kind of tortoise-like creature, as the Experimentator says, named from 'slime' [limus], because it is born in slime. It eats earth. It has four horns, but two longer ones. In crawling it extends its horns, but as soon as it is touched, it draws in its horns and curls itself up. It hides in winter, comes forth in spring. Its blood closes the pores and effectively prevents hair from growing. Crushed and ground, it heals abscesses in certain wounds.
The locust - as Pope Gregory says, is called as if 'standing in place' [loco stans] -

shaped like a horse. It is green in color, having longer hind legs. It leaps through fields and thickets. It lays eggs, as Pliny and Aldhelm say, densely packed in autumn, which last through the whole winter. At the end of spring the young burst forth, tiny in form, crawling without legs or wings. It is certain that the mothers die once they have laid their eggs, a small worm at once growing near their throat that strangles them. Locusts, carried up by the wind, fall into seas or rivers. It is certain that they cross vast seas from this, continuing for the hunger of many days, which we marvel at especially, that for the sake of foreign pastures they know how to seek out such distant places. And what wonder, if for the sake of the food of eternal life and hunger for the word of God the faithful do this? Locusts fly with such a rustling of wings that they are believed to be other birds; but peoples, when they see them coming from afar, grow anxious, lest they cover their lands. For wherever they touch the land like a dread cloud, they scorch and gnaw at everything they touch. In the region of Cyrenaica it is the law to fight them three times a year: first the eggs, then the young, finally the adults; whoever ceases from this law is condemned to the penalty of a deserter. In Syria the inhabitants are compelled, by military command, to fight them. The Parthians eat them as food. They are said to have something like teeth at the joints of their shoulders, and to produce a rasping sound by rubbing these together. The mating of locusts is around the solstice. They mate with the female carrying the male. The males are smaller than the females.

As the Experimentator says, locusts eat one another, and the larger eat the smaller. The locust has a mouth arranged in the shape of a small square; it has a sting instead of a tail. It has legs bent back toward itself. Locusts are generated by the south wind, and die from the north and northeast wind. They fatten more quickly on the blossoms of almond trees. They have a single intestine, filled with filth and matter.
Locusts also have, as Ambrose says, a remedy for their sickness: for gnawed laurel leaves free them from illness.

The wool-worm [silkworm] is a long, spotted worm, set apart by its many feet, scattered white in color. These worms work silk wool from their own entrails. They use, as food, the leaves of the mulberry tree, which food, through the mediation of the worms' entrails, is turned into silk wool. They make spindles of their wool on small branches and work around themselves, so that, once the spindles are complete, they are enclosed on every side by their own work. After this they make an exit for themselves at the top of the spindles, and, emerging, appear, by a marvelous nature, entirely changed from their former shape, so much so that the worms that had before crawled on countless feet now, having wings, are fit for flight. Finally, entering into mating, they join for three days. Once this is done, the male dies. The female, however, lays countless eggs in an ordered pattern, laid upon a small cloth either white or red; then she too dies. Then the little cloth, with its eggs, is taken up and placed where the cold of winter cannot reach the eggs. But after winter, when the spring season has grown warm, the stored eggs are set out in the sun and warmed by its heat, until, given life, they form into worms. The silk worm's wool takes on only two colors: white and saffron. The rest are made by artifice; but nature forms only these two in the worm. It is said, however, that the eggs take on a white or saffron color from the cloth placed beneath them at their conception.

The 'multipes' or 'centipes,' as some prefer, is rather a worm than a beast, though it exceeds worms in form. This animal lacks blood. It seems to take its name from the fact itself: for it is set apart by many, nearly innumerable feet. Of this animal the blessed Augustine, in the book Against the Academics, says that it was brought before him and, in his presence and while he watched, the animal was cut into many parts, and yet each part lived on its own, separated from the others. From this occasion it came to be rightly asked whether the soul is simple and uncomposed, or composed, distributed among parts. It is established, however, that it is simple.

The fly flies impudently, as the Book of Properties says. It loves the light and does not know how to move in darkness. It gladly betakes itself to warmth. It settles on damp things; it craves blood. It is hostile to every animal, and this especially to man. Wherever it touches freshly cut flesh, worms follow at once, which corrupt the infected flesh, and this especially in the dog days. It flees salty and rough things; it gladly defiles white and cleaner things, nor can the stain of this filth be washed away as long as that same cycle of the year turns.

As the Experimentator says, a fly, submerged in water and then set out, revives. They are generated from the corruption of dung. Flying around, it makes a noise, and this from the air stirred between its wings.

It has a snout like a hollow reed. With its hind legs it sharpens its wings, and with its front legs its snout and head. Pliny: they hide in winter, most similar to dead things. In the month of August, however, they fly out in troublesome numbers. They lay little worms, from which flies come; and these little worms are hard and black. [Flies have no memory.]

There is a kind of fly in the regions of Cyprus that is four-footed, as Pliny says, and winged, much larger than our flies. These are called 'pyrallis' from 'pyr,' which means fire. For, staying in furnaces, they fly unharmed in the midst of the flames. And this is marvelous: as long as it is in the fire, it lives in the fire; when it flies out even a little beyond it, then it dies.

The 'opimacus' is a worm, as the Gloss says, quite small in body, but exceedingly bold in spirit and vigorous in cunning. For it is said to have a contest with serpents and to defend its life by the skill of fighting; and though small in body and unequal in strength to the serpent, it nevertheless overcomes, through the exercise of combat, one stronger than itself, and lives secure through boldness rather than natural strength.

Butterflies, as the Book of Properties says, are flying worms, which rely mostly on flowers and take their food from them. They mate after August, and, the male dying after mating, the female lays eggs; once these are laid, she dies. The eggs, however, enduring through the winter, produce worms in summertime, which, growing strong with the sun's heat and the night dew, take on wings and fly off.

The 'phalangium' [venomous spider], as Pliny says, is a kind of spider, venomous and harmful in its bite, small and sharp-pointed in body. It gladly enters the nostrils of men, as of livestock. When it has bitten stags in the woods, unless they eat crabs as food, their life is in danger. They brood in caves and lay eggs in great number, sometimes thirty, sometimes fewer. And as soon as the young hatch, they consume their father and mother: for the father helps to brood the offspring.

Fleas, as the Book of Properties says, dark in color, leap rather than fly. And by these too man is scourged, given as a punishment to the tiniest and basest of creatures. For they trouble a man more at night than by day, and, unless a heavy numbness or deep sleep is in his limbs, he cannot protect himself. When someone raises a hand for vengeance, they suddenly slip away in flight and cannot be found; but where rest is trusted, their quick return to troubling him shows well enough that a man driven to fury can do nothing. They sting a man with a sharp bite and draw blood by the power of their mouthparts, and they do this so subtly that, the skin between remaining whole, they draw out blood only through the pores and natural openings. In moist air and softened earth they thrive with greater vigor. [They are said to be bred from heated dust and afterward corrupted moisture.]
The chief remedy against fleas is that the whole body be rubbed in the evening with wormwood, as Ambrose says: fleas will not touch you, if you boil wormwood herb with oil and anoint your body.

As the Experimentator says, fleas leave a mark on the flesh of the man they settle on. A flea, divided into two parts, revives. If there is cold around the month of June, fleas quickly perish, and there will not be an abundance of their offspring for the rest of the summer.

Lice, as the Book of Properties says, are named from the multitude of their feet: for they consist of countless feet. This evil is created from man's own flesh, and though this is beyond doubt, the creation of lice is nevertheless invisible. Some say these are born, invisibly, from man's sweat, others from the pores and vapors of the body.

The chief remedy against these, as the philosopher says, is frequent washing of the body with sea water or strongly salted water; or quicksilver boiled for a long time in olive oil, and a belt dipped in this; or egg white and quicksilver carefully mixed together, and a woolen belt dipped in this and worn; or butter mixed with quicksilver, and garments infused with this and worn.

The frog, as the Book of Properties says, is counted among the other worms. It is green in color, and sometimes reddish, but the reddish kind is worse. It is talkative and troublesome with its voice. It fears everything that breathes, suspecting itself hated by all. In the month of August it can never open its mouth for any purpose of food, drink, or voice, and if you even try to open it with your hand or a stick, you will be able to do so only with difficulty.

The frog has its own voice, 'coax,' and can say nothing else but this voice 'coax,' except when pressed or hurt: for then it changes its voice and gives out a thin sound like a mouse's. The reason for its voice 'coax' can be understood from this, as Aristotle says: with its mouth closed and its sides inflated, it sounds 'co' in the throat; but for the syllable 'ax' it opens its mouth and, like bellows, presses in its sides, so that, with a stronger breath, the raised voice is produced. It amplifies its voice when it places its lower jaw level in the water and extends the upper; and when it extends both, its eyes shine like candles. Their mating occurs more by night than by day, and in this the modesty of their mating is noted.

This is against those who mate indiscriminately and shamelessly by day as by night. In the mating of frogs there is a long delay, and they discharge much seed. The male frog calls the female frog by a recognized voice. The male has frogs that have wings [sic, garbled in source]. Every fish nourishes its young, except the frog. This is noted, from Aristotle's statements, as showing that the frog is a fish. [The tongue of the water-frog, if placed beneath the head of a sleeping person, makes him talkative in his sleep and reveal secrets, as the old rustic tradition ambiguously puts it.]
The frog that is called 'rubeta' by Pliny is a frog whose life is both on land and in water, and is rich in many remedies.
This one, as the Book of Kyranides says, dwells in dry fields. The ash of its burning, sprinkled in a bath, removes body hair.

It lays aside and takes up again these remedies when it wishes, and this is said to happen constantly as it feeds. But it never lays aside its venoms, keeping them by it as its weapons, so to speak. It is certain that purple-fish are especially attracted when its flesh is placed on a hook. Authors relate marvelous things about these, competing with one another; they say that if the little bone of its right side is thrown into boiling water, the vessel is cooled and does not boil again unless the rubeta bone is removed. Against the poisons of the sea-hare and the rubeta, their ash, drunk in water, is a remedy.

div.head: 38. De rana parvula muta et nociva

cit.quote: There is a very small frog, as Pliny says, living mostly in reed-beds and grasses, mute and voiceless, green, which, if by chance swallowed by oxen, causes their bellies to swell to an enormous size.

There is also a very small frog called the 'running frog' [corriens]. This one climbs trees and rests there among the leaves. Sensing rain by a natural foresight in the clouds, it cries out loudly, announcing, namely, the coming of a flood; at other times, however, it scarcely ever sings. This one, thrown before the mouths of dogs, is commonly believed to take away their voice. This frog is green and small.

[The star-shaped worm] is a worm, as Pliny says, that shines like a star at night. It appears only after heavy rains, and marks the return of clear weather. It has such coldness in it that, touching fire, it extinguishes it no differently than ice would. Of the same matter, [if human flesh] which is vomited from its mouth, milk-white, touches any part of a man, all his hair falls out wherever touched, and what was touched changes color to green. These worms produce nothing, nor is there male or female among them.

The 'snake-despoiler' is a worm, as the Book of Properties says, of a golden color, whence it is called by some the 'golden worm.' It also has a greenish hue in the shade. This creature, called the snake-despoiler, is said to take its name from the fact itself, for wherever it sees a snake lying in the heat, climbing up its tail it runs to its head and first caresses it, as if stroking it; then it attacks its flesh with bites. And when the snake feels the injury, it tries to escape by fleeing, but in vain, for its pursuer follows the fleeing creature and presses on with a fatal bite, until it penetrates the inner parts of the brain and kills the deceived creature, and is sated on its flesh. Thus a small and weak worm deceives the snake by cunning. And from this it is that they have named this worm the snake-despoiler.

Aristotle seems to say something about this worm that is remarkable to many; for he says that when these worms, which he names of a golden color, are born, they are first fed by their parents, then remain without food for many days and lie thus motionless, and seem dead. But after the time that nature has set for them, they revive and rise to seek food for themselves.

The 'seta' [hair-worm] is a worm, or rather a serpent, as some prefer. It takes its name from the fact itself: for it is a tiny creature like a bristle, or like one of the hairs of a horse's mane. It is a worm nearly a cubit long, slender, thin, hard and white like a needle, and no different at either end, since indeed it has no head, but crawls with a tail at both ends. This is often found born in springs that come from mountain torrents, in unspoiled but not foul-smelling waters. It is so tough that it can scarcely be crushed underfoot. If placed in boiling water to be cooked, it cannot be cooked. The strength of its venom is such that, taken in a drink, it makes a man languish and waste away, until it strips him of life with dire torment. It brings death only in this way, and no other.

The 'buprestis' is a small worm in Italy, as Isidore says, very similar to a beetle, having long legs. It deceives, hidden among the grasses, animals, but especially the ox, whence it also gets its name. For when an ox has devoured it, hidden among the grasses, and its gall has touched it, the ox becomes so inflamed and swollen that it soon bursts, its innards split open.

The leech is a worm living in water. It lacks bones, feet, and wings. It attacks man and beasts, so as to drink their blood. By drinking their blood to excessive satiety, it often brings death upon itself. Men are accustomed to offer themselves willingly to these worms, so that they may drink the surplus blood of the body. But some do this less wisely, unless they sense an excessive corruption of the blood. For in a healthy man they draw out the nobler and well-digested blood. It is called 'sanguisuga' [blood-sucker] from the nature of its work, sucking blood. The better ones, and those said to be less harmful, are those wrinkled and lined on the back; the worse are the black ones; of these the philosopher Aldhelm writes.

But the Experimentator says of these that the leech vomits up the blood it has drawn, so as to drink fresher blood. It is pricked with nettles and caltrops, so that it vomits up any venom it has drawn from beasts, toads, or water-serpents. When it has attached itself to flesh, the more it is pulled, the more firmly it clings, until it bursts. It draws out putrid blood: in healing another, it kills itself. It has a mouth shaped like a triangle, whence it leaves a triangular wound.
The Book of Kyranides says that if you burn leeches and rub their ash mixed with vinegar on a place where hairs have been plucked out, they will not grow back again.

The 'thamur,' or 'samier' as some say, is a worm also called Solomon's worm, taking its name from the fact itself. For when Moses, in the Law, had forbidden that the stones from which the Lord's altar was made be cut with iron, and Solomon, aware of this prohibition, had ordered the most precious, hardest, and whitest marble - a kind of marble called Parian - to be brought from distant parts of the world for the building of the altar and the temple, and the hardest stones could not easily be cut to the required shape, Solomon himself sought out a technique among worms, which human skill did not know. He took, then, a chick of the ostrich bird, which he had, and shut it in a glass vessel; and when the ostrich saw it but could not reach it, it naturally attempted a skill it knew. Running, then, to the desert and returning, it brought back a little worm, with whose blood it smeared the glass, and it broke, and thus it rescued its young. When Solomon saw this, he took note of the kind of worm the bird had used in cutting the glass, and used that same technique in cutting the hardest marble, and achieved his result.
This worm can indeed fittingly bear the figure of Christ, whose blood is of such power that it softens the adamantine hearts of men to compassion and contrition for themselves.

The 'tappula' [water-strider] is a worm supported on four feet. This worm, having soles, walks boldly upon the water and does not fear the depths of the waters. It lives equally on land and in water. On land, indeed, it runs most swiftly, and yet more so upon the water, so that in a short time it crosses long stretches of water at a run; it pauses, however, in its running upon the water and, tired, recovers its strength. And it is quite remarkable about this worm that, although it runs upon the water, it remains with a dry body and feet. And if you hold this worm forcibly under the waves for a long time, it is nevertheless not wetted or does it die, but, as it returns to the surface, dry and unencumbered, it carries on its usual swift and untroubled life.

The tortoise-beetle is a worm born from the corruption of grasses through excessive moisture and heat. It is a slow animal, thick with much fat, some red, some white, some black, some saffron-colored according to changes in the air and corruptions. It shapes for itself a dwelling, marvelously vaulted like a tortoise-shell, of a bony or rather marble-like substance; and this is remarkable: from its own spittle, which is slippery and thick, it makes itself a dwelling, and, by the sun's heat, this gradually hardens somewhat into stone.

This creature, as the blessed Ambrose relates, feeding on the entrails of a serpent, when it perceives the venom creeping through it, applies oregano as a remedy for its health; and though it wallows in marshy mire, it nevertheless knows how to heal itself with its own antidote, and, by this certain aid to health, proves that it too knows the powers of herbs.
If you throw salt upon it, it nearly all dissolves into nothing, and you will scarcely find anything of it left but fat; and this is useful as a remedy.

The moth is a worm, as Isidore says, so named because it 'holds fast' [teneat]. This worm is created in garments, from corrupted air, out of the decaying moisture that is in the wool, and settles there and gnaws at it.

Wood-worms are called by the Greeks the worms of wood, as Isidore says, and are so named because they eat by wearing away [terendo]. We call these 'termites.' For thus, among the Latins, the worms of wood are named, which trees cut at an unsuitable time produce.

As the Experimentator says, wood-worms have a red head and a white body. By successive boring they pierce wood, and, reducing it to dust, the wood-worm builds itself a home, purifying itself by consuming itself and casting out the dust. Few woods of the eastern regions breed worms; but in the regions of Italy, Germany, Gaul, and Spain, nearly all trees, except oak and linden, and a few other woods, breed worms. And this is quite remarkable, that boxwood and hawthorn, which are among the hardest of trees, breed wood-worms; but the linden, one of the most tender of trees, wherever its wood is kept dry, never breeds worms from it, but remains permanently free of worms. [And in this a secret of nature is noted.]

The 'tharmus' is a worm, as Isidore says, [taking its name from the fact itself. For wherever it bites, the washed place burns so much that blisters rise there, and] which is born in lard. We call 'lardum' the fat of the pig, which lies immediately beneath the skin, between the skin and the red flesh; and the name is taken from the Gallic tongue.
The 'uria' is a worm of the pig, as Isidore says. It takes its name from the fact itself, for wherever it bites, the place burns so much that blisters rise there.

Wasps, as Pliny says, make their nests of mud, raised on high; and in these, useless wax, but not gathered from flowers, and therefore useless. Their life centers on dung. They feed on flesh. They hunt larger flies; having cut off and discarded the head, they eat the rest of the body. They are said to grow larger at the full moon.
Wasps are sometimes produced from the flesh of horses, as Pope Clement says.

div.head: 53. De verme qui proprie vermis dicitur

cit.quote: The name 'worm' [vermis], though it indeed applies to all worms, is nevertheless properly and specifically given to that worm which is generated from pure and clean earth, with no mixing of seed. With this worm the fisherman's hook is baited, to deceive fish.

To this the Lord himself compared himself, through the prophet, saying: I am a worm, and not a man - and not without reason, since he was generated from the pure and clean flesh of his mother, without the seed of corruption. Whence it is also read that manna generated a worm in the desert.

The worms of Celidonia are worms, as the blessed Augustine attests in the book On the City of God, which are found in certain naturally boiling waters in the region of Celidonia. Just as fish live in cold water, so these live in hot and boiling water: outside the boiling water, when they come into cold air, they die at once.

Fear not, worm of Jacob - you, I say, humble and despised soul, strong wrestler and supplanter of vices: fear not. Only remain in the warm waters of tears, sigh devoutly to the Lord, grow warm with the saving fire of charity, and do not depart, lest the cold of sluggishness overtake you. Fear not, I say, for if the Lord is your light, for the knowledge of himself, and salvation even in dangers: whom shall you fear? As if to say: no one. Here ends the book on worms.
